## Definition

Let $n\ge1$, let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$A,B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$. The **matrix pencil** determined by $(A,B)$ is
$A-\lambda B$. Its determinant polynomial is
$f(\lambda)=\det(A-\lambda B)$, with real coefficients viewed as complex
coefficients when $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. The pencil is **regular** if $f$ is
not the zero polynomial; otherwise it is **singular**.

For $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$ not both zero, put
$$p(\alpha,\beta)=\det(\beta A-\alpha B).$$
A **homogeneous generalized eigenvalue pair** is an equivalence class of such
pairs satisfying $p(\alpha,\beta)=0$, where $(\alpha,\beta)$ and
$(c\alpha,c\beta)$ represent the same pair for every $c\in\mathbb C\setminus
\{0\}$. If $\beta\ne0$, the associated finite generalized eigenvalue is
$\lambda=\alpha/\beta$; if $\beta=0$, the pair is an infinite generalized
eigenvalue. The pair $(0,0)$ is never an eigenvalue pair.
Write $\sigma(A,B)$ for the set of finite ratios $\alpha/\beta$ among these
homogeneous eigenvalue pairs.

The QZ results on this page assume a regular pencil. They make no assertion
about Kronecker structure or eigenvalues of a singular pencil.

id: lem-block-upper-triangular-pencil-determinant-factorizes
kind: lemma

status: draft

      url: "https://pages.mtu.edu/~struther/Courses/OLD/Other/Sp2012/5627/BlockQR/Work/kressner_daniel.pdf"
    - title: "Peter Arbenz, Lecture Notes on Solving Large Scale Eigenvalue Problems, §12.8"
      url: "https://people.inf.ethz.ch/arbenz/ewp/Lnotes/lsevp.pdf"
---

## Statement

Let $n_1,n_2\ge1$, $n=n_1+n_2$, and let $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be
block upper triangular with the same two-block partition of sizes $n_1,n_2$,
with diagonal blocks $A_{11},A_{22}$ and
$B_{11},B_{22}$. For every $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$,
$$\det(\beta A-\alpha B) =\det(\beta A_{11}-\alpha B_{11})\det(\beta A_{22}-\alpha B_{22}).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A block upper triangular pair with a common two-block partition.

[F1] [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]: the determinant is the signed
finite sum over permutations.

## Proof

1.1 The matrix $M=\beta A-\alpha B$ is block upper triangular, so every entry in its lower-left block is zero. In a nonzero Leibniz term, each of the first block's columns must therefore be paired with one of the first block's rows. Since the block sizes agree, these choices are a permutation of exactly those rows, and the remaining columns are paired with the remaining rows. Thus every nonzero permutation term splits into one term from each diagonal block. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Summing the split terms in [F1] gives the product of the two signed permutation sums for $M_{11}$ and $M_{22}$. These sums are their determinants, which proves the identity. [step 1.1, F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

If $M\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and $\det M=0$, then there is a nonzero vector $v\in\mathbb F^n$ with
$Mv=0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A square real or complex matrix $M$ of positive order.

[F1] [[cor-matrix-rank-nullity]]: $\operatorname{rank}(M)+\dim\ker M=n$.

[F2] [[cor-matrix-rank-equals-the-rank-of-its-linear-map]]: matrix rank is
the dimension of the image of the associated linear map.

[F3] [[thm-operator-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]]: a finite-dimensional
operator over a field is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero.

## Proof

1.1 Suppose $\ker M=\{0\}$. By [F1], $\operatorname{rank}(M)=n$; by [F2] the image of $M$ has dimension $n$ in the $n$-dimensional space $\mathbb F^n$, so $M$ is surjective. It is also injective by the supposition, hence invertible. [given, F1, F2, algebra, assume-contra]

2.1 By [F3], invertibility implies $\det M\ne0$, contradicting the given $\det M=0$. Therefore $\ker M\ne\{0\}$ and a nonzero $v$ with $Mv=0$ exists. [step 1.1, F3, contradiction, discharge-contradiction] ∎

## Definition

Let $B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
be Hermitian positive definite, with Cholesky factor $B=LL^*$ and $L$ lower
triangular with positive diagonal. This factor exists and is unique by
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]].
Define the linear-first **B-inner product** by
$$\langle x,y\rangle_B:=y^*Bx,$$
the **B-norm** by
$$\|x\|_B:=\|L^*x\|_2=\sqrt{x^*Bx},$$
and the **B-dual residual norm** by
$$\|r\|_{B^{-1}}:=\|L^{-1}r\|_2 =\sqrt{r^*B^{-1}r}.$$
The B-orthogonality condition is $x^*By=0$; since $B=B^*$ it is equivalent
to $\langle x,y\rangle_B=0$.

      url: "https://pages.mtu.edu/~struther/Courses/OLD/Other/Sp2012/5627/BlockQR/Work/kressner_daniel.pdf"
    - title: "LAPACK Users' Guide, Generalized Nonsymmetric Eigenproblems"
      url: "https://www.netlib.org/lapack/lug/node35.html"
---

## Definition

Input $A,B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, with
$\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. All transformations here are exact.
Let $Q=Z=I_n$.

For a target pair $(a,b)$, define the left factor $L(a,b)$ deterministically. Use $I_2$ if $a=b=0$. Otherwise put $r=(|a|^2+|b|^2)^{1/2}$ and $L=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-\overline s&c\end{pmatrix}$. Over $\mathbb R$, take $c=a/r$, $s=b/r$. Over $\mathbb C$, if $a=0$ take $c=0$, $s=\overline b/|b|$; otherwise take $\phi=a/|a|$, $c=|a|/r$, $s=\phi\overline b/r$. Thus $L(a,b)(a,b)^T=(\gamma,0)^T$ with $|\gamma|=r$. Set $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and define the right factor
$$R(a,b)=J L(\overline b,\overline a)^*J.$$
Then $(a,b)R(a,b)=(0,\eta)$ with $|\eta|=r$; the zero pair again uses identity. These factors are real orthogonal over $\mathbb R$ or unitary over $\mathbb C$, as direct multiplication shows in [[thm-householder-reflectors-and-givens-transformations-are-unitary-and-annihilate-targeted-entries]]; the right identity follows by taking adjoints of the left annihilation of $(\overline b,\overline a)^T$ and reversing the coordinates. Use their identity embeddings on the two rows or columns specified by each step below.
1. Triangularise $B$ by left rotations. For $j=1,\ldots,n$ and, in descending
order, $i=n,n-1,\ldots,j+1$, set
$$L=L(B_{i-1,j},B_{i,j}),\quad A\leftarrow LA,\quad B\leftarrow LB, \quad Q\leftarrow QL^*.$$

2. Reduce $A$ to upper Hessenberg form while restoring triangularity of $B$.
For $j=1,\ldots,n-2$ and, in descending order, $i=n,n-1,\ldots,j+2$, set
$$L=L(A_{i-1,j},A_{i,j}),\quad A\leftarrow LA,\quad B\leftarrow LB, \quad Q\leftarrow QL^*,$$
then set
$$R=R(B_{i,i-1},B_{i,i}),\quad A\leftarrow AR,\quad B\leftarrow BR, \quad Z\leftarrow ZR.$$

Return $Q,Z,H=A,T=B$, where $H$ is upper Hessenberg and $T$ is upper
triangular in the senses of
[[def-upper-hessenberg-and-real-symmetric-tridiagonal-matrices]] and
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]. The outputs are represented by the exact products of
the recorded Givens factors; no dense rounded factor is asserted unitary.

      url: "https://www.netlib.org/lapack/lug/node35.html"
---

## Definition

Let $(A,B)$ be a regular pencil of order $n$. A **complex generalized Schur
form** is a factorisation
$$Q^*AZ=S,\qquad Q^*BZ=T,$$
where $Q,Z\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ are unitary in the sense of
[[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]], and $S,T$ are
upper triangular as in
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]. For its
$i$th one-by-one diagonal block, $[s_{ii}:t_{ii}]$ is the
**diagonal homogeneous pair**.

For real $A,B$, a **real generalized Schur form** has
$$Q^TAZ=S,\qquad Q^TBZ=T,$$
where $Q,Z$ are orthogonal, $S$ is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks
of size one or two, and $T$ is upper triangular. Each one-by-one diagonal
block has a nonzero real homogeneous pair. For a two-by-two diagonal block
$(S_{kk},T_{kk})$, the **diagonal homogeneous roots** are the zeros of
$\det(\beta S_{kk}-\alpha T_{kk})$ in $[\alpha:\beta]$; such a block has a
nonreal conjugate pair of finite roots. A singular pencil is outside this
definition.

      url: "https://www.netlib.org/lapack/lug/node35.html"
---

## Statement

For $A,B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, let
$p(\alpha,\beta)=\det(\beta A-\alpha B)$. For every $c\in\mathbb C$,
$$p(c\alpha,c\beta)=c^n p(\alpha,\beta).$$
Consequently the zero condition is independent of the nonzero representative
of a homogeneous pair. If $\beta\ne0$, then
$$p(\alpha,\beta)=\beta^n\det(A-(\alpha/\beta)B).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $n\ge1$, $A,B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, and
$(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb C^2$.

[F1] [[def-regular-generalized-eigenvalue-pencil]]: $p(\alpha,\beta)$ is
$\det(\beta A-\alpha B)$, and homogeneous pairs are identified by nonzero
complex scaling.

[F2] [[thm-leibniz-determinant-is-alternating-multilinear-and-normalized]]:
the determinant is multilinear in each column.

## Proof

1.1 Scaling $(\alpha,\beta)$ by $c$ scales every column of $\beta A-\alpha B$ by $c$. Applying [F2] to its $n$ columns gives $\det(c(\beta A-\alpha B))=c^n\det(\beta A-\alpha B)$, which is the first identity by [F1]. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 If $c\ne0$, then $c^n\ne0$, so $p(c\alpha,c\beta)=0$ exactly when $p(\alpha,\beta)=0$. If $\beta\ne0$, factor $\beta A-\alpha B=\beta(A-(\alpha/\beta)B)$ and apply the same column multilinearity to obtain the finite-eigenvalue identity. [step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

If $(A,B)$ is a regular pencil and $x\in\mathbb C^n$ satisfies $Ax=0$ and
$Bx=0$, then $x=0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A regular pencil $A-\lambda B$ of order $n\ge1$.

[F1] [[def-regular-generalized-eigenvalue-pencil]]: regularity means
$\det(A-\lambda B)$ is a nonzero polynomial.

[F2] [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]: determinant is defined by the
finite Leibniz sum.

[F3] [[thm-root-bound-for-polynomials-over-a-domain]]: a nonzero polynomial of
degree $d$ over an integral domain has at most $d$ distinct roots.

[F4] [[thm-operator-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]]: a finite-dimensional
operator is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero.

## Proof

1.1 Suppose $x\ne0$ and $Ax=Bx=0$. Then $(A-\lambda B)x=0$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb C$, so $A-\lambda B$ is not invertible. By [F4], $f(\lambda)=\det(A-\lambda B)=0$ for every complex $\lambda$. [given, F1, F4, algebra, assume-contra]

2.1 By [F2], $f$ has degree at most $n$. If $f$ were nonzero, [F3] would bound its number of distinct complex roots by $n$, while step 1.1 gives every $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ as a root. Since $\mathbb C$ has more than $n$ distinct elements, this contradicts [F1]. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, contradiction, discharge-contradiction] ∎

id: lem-two-sided-unitary-equivalence-errors-accumulate-for-pencil

status: draft

      url: "https://pages.mtu.edu/~struther/Courses/OLD/Other/Sp2012/5627/BlockQR/Work/kressner_daniel.pdf"
    - title: "Peter Arbenz, Lecture Notes on Solving Large Scale Eigenvalue Problems, §12.8"
      url: "https://people.inf.ethz.ch/arbenz/ewp/Lnotes/lsevp.pdf"

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, $m\ge0$, $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and
$A,B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$. Put $A_0=A$, $B_0=B$. For
$j=1,\ldots,m$, suppose exact unitary/orthogonal factors $Q_j,Z_j$ and local
arithmetic/deflation perturbations satisfy
$$A_j=Q_j^*(A_{j-1}+E_j^A+D_j^A)Z_j,$$
$$B_j=Q_j^*(B_{j-1}+E_j^B+D_j^B)Z_j.$$
Then with $Q=Q_1\cdots Q_m$ and $Z=Z_1\cdots Z_m$ (empty products are $I_n$)
there are perturbations
$\Delta_A,\Delta_B$ such that
$$A_m=Q^*(A+\Delta_A)Z,\qquad B_m=Q^*(B+\Delta_B)Z,$$
and
$$\sqrt{\|\Delta_A\|_F^2+\|\Delta_B\|_F^2} \le\sum_{j=1}^m\left( \sqrt{\|E_j^A\|_F^2+\|E_j^B\|_F^2} +\sqrt{\|D_j^A\|_F^2+\|D_j^B\|_F^2}\right).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Finite sequences of square matrices and exact unitary update factors
as in the statement.

[F1] [[lem-unitary-similarity-error-accumulation]]: a sequence
$H_j=P_j^*(H_{j-1}+E_j+D_j)P_j$ with unitary $P_j$ has a global unitary
similarity representation whose Frobenius perturbation is bounded by
$\sum_j(\|E_j\|_F+\|D_j\|_F)$.

[F2] [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]: block matrix multiplication
uses the usual row-by-column products.

[F3] [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]: the Frobenius norm is the square root of
the sum of squared moduli of all matrix entries.

## Proof

1.1 If $m=0$, take $Q=Z=I_n$ and $\Delta_A=\Delta_B=0$; the equations and bound hold. For $m\ge1$, form the $3n\times3n$ block matrix $M_j=\begin{pmatrix}0&A_j&B_j\\0&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $P_j=\operatorname{diag}(Q_j,Z_j,Z_j)$. Put the local $E_j^A,E_j^B$ in the first block row of $\mathcal E_j$ and the local $D_j^A,D_j^B$ in the first block row of $\mathcal D_j$, with all other blocks zero. Then [F2] and the stated updates give $M_j=P_j^*(M_{j-1}+\mathcal E_j+\mathcal D_j)P_j$. Each $P_j$ is unitary/orthogonal because its diagonal blocks are unitary/orthogonal. [given, F1, F2, construct, algebra]

2.1 For $m\ge1$, apply [F1] to the augmented sequence. Its accumulated perturbation has only the two first-row, off-diagonal blocks, because conjugation by each block diagonal $P_j$ preserves those block positions. Call them $\Delta_A,\Delta_B$. By [F3], $\|\mathcal E_j\|_F=\sqrt{\|E_j^A\|_F^2+\|E_j^B\|_F^2}$ and likewise for $\mathcal D_j$. Therefore the global bound from [F1] is exactly the displayed pair bound, and the accumulated block products are $Q,Z$. [given, F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $A=A^*$ and let $B=B^*$ be positive definite in
$\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, where $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
If $B=LL^*$ is its Cholesky factorisation, then
$$C=L^{-1}AL^{-*}$$
is self-adjoint and has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues
$\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$. The vectors
$$x_i=L^{-*}y_i\quad (i=1,\ldots,n)$$
form a basis satisfying $Ax_i=\lambda_iBx_i$ and
$x_i^*Bx_j=\delta_{ij}$. The generalized eigenvalues of $(A,B)$ are exactly
$[\lambda_i:1]$; none is infinite.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real symmetric or complex Hermitian matrix $A$ and a Hermitian
positive-definite matrix $B$ of the same positive order.

[F1] [[def-b-inner-product-and-dual-norm-for-definite-pencil]]: for the unique
Cholesky factor $B=LL^*$, $\|x\|_B=\|L^*x\|_2$, and B-orthonormality means
$x_i^*Bx_j=\delta_{ij}$.

[F2] [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]:
$B=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and positive diagonal, and $L$ is unique.

[F3] [[thm-determinant-of-a-triangular-matrix]]: the determinant of a
triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries.

[F4] [[thm-operator-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]]: a finite-dimensional
operator over a field is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero.

[F5] [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]: a real
self-adjoint endomorphism has an orthonormal eigenbasis.

[F6] [[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]: a complex
normal endomorphism has an orthonormal eigenbasis.

[F7] [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]]: determinants multiply under matrix
products.

[F8] [[def-regular-generalized-eigenvalue-pencil]]: homogeneous roots of
$\det(\beta A-\alpha B)$ are the generalized eigenvalues.

## Proof

1.1 By [F2], $L$ is lower triangular with positive diagonal. [F3] gives $\det L\ne0$, and [F4] therefore makes $L$ invertible. Hence $C=L^{-1}AL^{-*}$ is defined. Taking adjoints and using $A=A^*$ gives $C^*=L^{-1}AL^{-*}=C$. [given, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Regard $C$ as a real or complex endomorphism with the Euclidean inner product. In the real case [F5] applies; in the complex case $C=C^*$ implies $C$ is normal, so [F6] applies. Thus there are orthonormal $y_i$ and real $\lambda_i$ with $Cy_i=\lambda_i y_i$. [step 1.1, F5, F6, algebra]

3.1 Set $x_i=L^{-*}y_i$. Then $Ax_i=AL^{-*}y_i=L Cy_i=\lambda_iLy_i=\lambda_iBx_i,$ and $x_i^*Bx_j=y_i^*L^{-1}LL^*L^{-*}y_j=y_i^*y_j=\delta_{ij}.$ The invertible change of variables $L^{-*}$ sends the basis $(y_i)$ to a basis $(x_i)$. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra, construct]

4.1 For every $\lambda\in\mathbb C$, $A-\lambda B=L(C-\lambda I)L^*$, so $\det(A-\lambda B)=\det(L)\det(C-\lambda I)\det(L^*).$ The diagonalisation from step 2.1 expresses $C=UDU^*$ with $D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)$ and $U$ unitary. By [F7], $\det(C-\lambda I)=\det(U)\det(D-\lambda I)\det(U^*)$ and $\det(U)\det(U^*)=\det(UU^*)=\det I=1$. Applying [F3] to the diagonal matrix gives $\det(C-\lambda I)=\prod_i(\lambda_i-\lambda)$. Also $\det(L)$ and $\det(L^*)$ are nonzero by step 1.1, so the finite roots of $\det(A-\lambda B)$ are exactly the real $\lambda_i$. Finally $\det(B)=\det(L)\det(L^*)\ne0$, so $[1:0]$ is not a homogeneous root. [F2, F3, F7, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every input of [[alg-generalized-hessenberg-triangular-reduction]], the
algorithm terminates and returns orthogonal/unitary $Q,Z$, an upper Hessenberg
matrix $H$, and an upper triangular matrix $T$ such that
$$H=Q^*AZ,\qquad T=Q^*BZ.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $A,B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$ with $n\ge1$ and
$\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

[F1] [[alg-generalized-hessenberg-triangular-reduction]] performs a finite
sequence of left Givens rotations and paired right Givens restorations, with
the accumulators updated as $Q\leftarrow QL^*$ and $Z\leftarrow ZR$.

[F2] [[thm-householder-reflectors-and-givens-transformations-are-unitary-and-annihilate-targeted-entries]]:
each selected Givens factor is unitary and zeros its targeted coordinate.

## Proof

1.1 The triangularisation loops range over finitely many pairs $(i,j)$. For fixed $j$, descending $i$ zeros $B_{i,j}$ without changing already cleared entries below it. The rotations act on rows with indices at least $j$, whose entries in columns less than $j$ are zero by upper triangularity; hence they do not create below-diagonal entries in earlier columns. After all columns, $B$ is upper triangular. [given, F1, F2, choose]

2.1 For $j=1$ there are no earlier Hessenberg columns, so the base condition is vacuous. For general $j$, assume every earlier column already has the Hessenberg pattern. Descend through $i$; the left factor zeros $A_{i,j}$. Since $B$ was upper triangular, this left factor can create below-diagonal fill only at $B_{i,i-1}$; the paired right factor zeros that entry. It creates no further below-diagonal entries in $B$, because rows below $i$ are zero in columns $i-1,i$. The right factor does not touch column $j$ because $i-1\ge j+1$, and the left factors preserve all earlier Hessenberg columns, whose entries in rows $i-1,i$ are already zero. Thus after the loop, column $j$ of $A$ is zero below row $j+1$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra, base, ih]

3.1 Induction over $j=1,\ldots,n-2$ proves that the final $A$ is upper Hessenberg and $B$ remains upper triangular. Each left update $A\leftarrow LA$ is matched by $Q\leftarrow QL^*$, and each right update $A\leftarrow AR$ is matched by $Z\leftarrow ZR$; direct substitution preserves $A_{\rm current}=Q^*A_{\rm input}Z$ and $B_{\rm current}=Q^*B_{\rm input}Z$. The finite loops terminate, proving the claim. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, F2, algebra, induction, discharge-induction] ∎

## Statement

Every regular finite square pencil $(A,B)$ over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ has
at least one homogeneous generalized eigenvalue pair $[\alpha:\beta]$ over
$\mathbb C$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $n\ge1$ and a regular pencil $A-\lambda B$ with
$A,B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

[F1] [[def-regular-generalized-eigenvalue-pencil]]: regularity means
$f(\lambda)=\det(A-\lambda B)$ is not the zero polynomial, and a homogeneous
eigenvalue pair is a nonzero projective zero of $p(\alpha,\beta)$.

[F2] [[lem-projective-determinant-is-homogeneous-and-scale-invariant]]:
$p(\alpha,\beta)=\beta^n f(\alpha/\beta)$ when $\beta\ne0$.

[F3] [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra-minimum-modulus-proof]]: every
nonconstant complex polynomial has a complex root.

[F4] [[thm-leibniz-determinant-is-alternating-multilinear-and-normalized]]:
the determinant is multilinear in its columns.

## Proof

1.1 By the Leibniz formula in [F1], every term of $f(\lambda)=\det(A-\lambda B)$ is a product of $n$ entries affine in $\lambda$. Thus $f$ has degree at most $n$; regularity makes it a nonzero polynomial. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 If $\deg f=n$, [F3] gives $\lambda_0\in\mathbb C$ with $f(\lambda_0)=0$. Set $[\alpha:\beta]=[\lambda_0:1]$; [F2] gives $p(\alpha,\beta)=0$. [step 1.1, F2, F3, construct, assume-case degree]

2.2 If $\deg f<n$, its coefficient of $\lambda^n$ is $(-1)^n\det B$: in the Leibniz expansion this coefficient is obtained by choosing the $-\lambda B$ entry in every column, and [F4] factors out $(-1)^n$. Hence $\det B=0$. Setting $[\alpha:\beta]=[1:0]$ gives $p(1,0)=\det(-B)=(-1)^n\det B=0$, so this is an infinite homogeneous eigenvalue pair. [step 1.1, F1, F4, algebra, construct, assume-case lower]

3.1 The two degree cases exhaust the nonzero polynomial $f$ and each produces a nonzero projective pair with $p(\alpha,\beta)=0$. [step 2.1, step 2.2, cases-exhaustive] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$A,B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$ be Hermitian with $B$ positive definite. For
$x\in\mathbb F^n\setminus\{0\}$ and $\mu\in\mathbb R$, put
$r=Ax-\mu Bx$. Then
$$\operatorname{dist}(\mu,\sigma(A,B)) \le \frac{\|r\|_{B^{-1}}}{\|x\|_B},$$
where $\sigma(A,B)$ is the finite generalized spectrum and
$\operatorname{dist}(\mu,S):=\min_{\lambda\in S}|\mu-\lambda|$. Equivalently, the
interval with centre $\mu$ and radius $\|r\|_{B^{-1}}/\|x\|_B$ contains at
least one generalized eigenvalue.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A Hermitian-definite pencil $(A,B)$, a nonzero vector $x$, and a
real scalar $\mu$.

[F1] [[def-b-inner-product-and-dual-norm-for-definite-pencil]]: for $B=LL^*$,
$\|x\|_B=\|L^*x\|_2$ and $\|r\|_{B^{-1}}=\|L^{-1}r\|_2$.

[F2] [[thm-hermitian-definite-pencil-has-real-spectrum-and-b-orthogonal-eigenbasis]]:
$C=L^{-1}AL^{-*}$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis and its eigenvalues are the
generalized eigenvalues of $(A,B)$.

[F3] [[def-regular-generalized-eigenvalue-pencil]]: $\sigma(A,B)$ is the set
of finite ratios $\alpha/\beta$ from homogeneous roots with $\beta\ne0$.

## Proof

1.1 Let $y=L^*x$ and $C=L^{-1}AL^{-*}$. Since $L^{-1}Bx=L^*x=y$, the transformed residual is $L^{-1}r=L^{-1}(Ax-\mu Bx)=(C-\mu I)y.$ By [F1], $\|y\|_2=\|x\|_B$ and $\|L^{-1}r\|_2=\|r\|_{B^{-1}}$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Let $u_1,\ldots,u_n$ be the orthonormal eigenbasis of $C$ from [F2], with real eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$. By [F3], these are exactly the finite generalized eigenvalues in $\sigma(A,B)$. Write $y=\sum_i c_i u_i$. Then $\|(C-\mu I)y\|_2^2 =\sum_i |c_i|^2|\lambda_i-\mu|^2 \ge \operatorname{dist}(\mu,\{\lambda_i\})^2\sum_i|c_i|^2 =\operatorname{dist}(\mu,\sigma(A,B))^2\|y\|_2^2.$ Taking square roots and applying step 1.1 proves the bound. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

$$a_2=\frac{1+u}{(1-u)^2}-1,\qquad q=\max\left\{\left(\frac{1+u}{1-u}\right)^3-1,\frac{(1+a_2)(1+6u)(1+u)}{(1-u)^3}-1\right\},$$
$$v=q+2(7u+6u^2)(1+q),\qquad h=u+2q+v,\qquad \eta=v+h.$$

$$C_+=Q_0^*(C+E^C)Z_0,\qquad D_+=Q_0^*(D+E^D)Z_0,\qquad P(E^C,E^D)\le\ell P(C,D),$$

Post-action zero writes are pulled back by the exact local factor adjoints before they enter a pre-action perturbation ledger. $$e_a=g_n\|A\|_F\|\widehat z\|_2+\|A\|_F e_z,\qquad g_n=\frac{1+6u}{1-(n-1)u}-1.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Successful source arithmetic, including normal nonzero exact intermediates and admissible stored basis constants $0,1$ for residual evaluation. All controller arithmetic is exact, separate from rounded matrix/vector updates.

[F2] [[lem-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-local-backward-error]] proves the unitary representative, raw application coefficient $q+\sqrt2(7u+6u^2)(1+q)$ and target-write bound $u+2q$ plus that raw coefficient.

The one actual target write has norm at most $h$ times its two-entry target norm, hence at most $hP(C,D)$. The triangle inequality gives $\eta P(C,D)$. This uses one generated factor for both arrays; no similarity relation between $C,D$ is assumed. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Permutations and conjugate transposes preserve Euclidean/Frobenius norms and use exact copies of stored coefficients. requires $0<u<1$; otherwise retain diagnostics with `certificate-inconclusive`. Record each elementary
rotation separately. If the source cannot produce its admissible factor,
return `range-failure` or `certificate-inconclusive` with diagnostics.

1. Execute the finite index loops of
[[alg-generalized-hessenberg-triangular-reduction]] with these COMPUTED common
rotations: triangularize $B$ with left targets $B_{i,j}$; then reduce $A$ with
left targets $A_{i,j}$ followed by right targets $B_{i,i-1}$. Every application
updates both whole arrays. The exact initializer and
[[prop-generalized-hessenberg-triangular-reduction-preserves-form-and-equivalence]]
supply the index schedule and support induction, not exact rounded
reconstruction. Retain each local factor and residual defined against its
exact representative. Include structural target writes in that local
arithmetic residual. Record all OTHER explicit zero writes separately: their
post-action perturbations are pulled back by the local factor adjoints before
entering the pre-action $D_j^A,D_j^B$ ledger. A pure tolerance write is an
identity-factor stage. Never count a structural write twice.

Initialize the sweep counter to zero. Process active blocks in increasing first
index, splitting them at exact zero subdiagonals of $H$. In each deflation
pass execute step 2, then repeat step 3 for the smallest available non-isolated
zero diagonal of $T$ until none remains or a status exits. Test step 5 before
starting a sweep: if the target is absent and the counter equals $N$, return
`budget-exhausted`. Otherwise increment the counter, execute step 4 on all
remaining active blocks, and repeat the deflation pass. In particular $N=0$
permits initialization/deflation but no step-4 sweep.

2. On each active block $H_{a:b,a:b},T_{a:b,a:b}$, apply the following deflation
tests before a sweep. For $i=a,\ldots,b-1$, set $H_{i+1,i}$ to zero when
$$|H_{i+1,i}|\le\tau\bigl(|H_{i,i}|+|H_{i+1,i+1}|\bigr),$$
and record its old value in $D^A$. For $k=a,\ldots,b$, set $T_{k,k}$ to zero when
$$|T_{k,k}|\le\tau\bigl(|T_{k-1,k}|+|T_{k,k+1}|\bigr),$$
using zero for a missing boundary term, and record the old value in $D^B$.
Evaluate each displayed modulus by the canonical rounded scaled two-component
norm; evaluate its additions and tolerance product with the declared rounded
real operations, then compare the stored finite values exactly. Excluded
operations return `range-failure`. The tests mean these rounded comparisons,
not an assertion about exact moduli at the threshold. Save the actual old
entries, so their deflation perturbations remain exact regardless of the test.
A one-by-one diagonal pair at $k$ is isolated when $H_{k,k-1}=0$ and
$H_{k+1,k}=0$, omitting a boundary entry when $k=a$ or $k=b$. If it has
$T_{k,k}=0$ and $H_{k,k}\ne0$, report an infinite candidate for the computed pencil and deflate it
from the active block. If the isolated diagonal pair is $(0,0)$, return
`singular-pencil-suspected` without assigning an eigenvalue.

3. To move a non-isolated zero $T_{k,k}$ to the top of its active block, for
$j=k-1,k-2,\ldots,a$ apply a right Givens factor on columns $j,j+1$ that
zeros $T_{j,j}$, then, when $j+2\le b$, a left Givens factor on rows
$j+1,j+2$ that zeros the resulting bulge $H_{j+2,j}$. Finally, when $a<b$,
apply a left Givens factor on rows $a,a+1$ to zero $H_{a+1,a}$. Record all rounded update residuals and target writes. If this isolates $(H_{a,a},T_{a,a})=(h,0)$ with $h\ne0$, report
the infinite candidate and remove the first row/column from the active block.
If the isolated pair is $(0,0)$, return `singular-pencil-suspected`; if isolation
fails, return `certificate-inconclusive`. Each successful isolation removes
one index, so at most $n$ such removals occur.

4. For each remaining active block with more than one row in the current
sweep, choose the homogeneous shift $[\alpha:\beta]=[H_{b,b}:T_{b,b}]$ if this pair is nonzero and
$T_{b,b}\ne0$; if $T_{b,b}=0$, use $[0:1]$. Form
$$x=(\beta H_{a:b,a:b}-\alpha T_{a:b,a:b})e_1.$$
Compute the first two components of $x$ using the declared rounded complex
products/subtractions and generate a left Givens factor from that stored
external vector. Apply it to both matrices without a matrix-target overwrite.
Its rounding changes the selected factor, not its application certificate. Apply a right Givens factor to columns $1,2$ to restore triangularity
of $T$. For $j=2,\ldots,b-a$, alternate a left Givens factor on rows $j,j+1$
to zero the current Hessenberg bulge and a right Givens factor on columns
$j,j+1$ to zero the resulting subdiagonal entry of $T$. Update and retain the
products $Q,Z$; record every local residual including its structural target
write. Indices $1,2,j,j+1$ here are relative to the active block; apply the
embedded transformations to the entire pair, retaining the transformed off-block data. All divisions by a generalized eigenvalue ratio are avoided.

5. After each infinite isolation and before every successful return, scan all
isolated diagonal pairs. Any $(0,0)$ pair returns `singular-pencil-suspected`
without an eigenvalue. Stop with `qz-computed` only when $H$ is upper triangular
and every diagonal pair is nonzero. Otherwise stop after $N$ sweeps with
`budget-exhausted`. Range failures return `range-failure` with partial factors;
unavailable local certificates return `certificate-inconclusive`. Neither a
rounded diagnostic nor a tolerance-induced infinite candidate asserts an exact
infinite eigenvalue of the original pencil.

For local-accumulation bounds use $\ell_j=\eta$ for matrix-target actions and
$\ell_j=v$ for external-vector/raw actions, plus the separately saved actual
tolerance perturbations. For an independent residual certificate execute the
factor-action/column procedure of
[[lem-qz-two-sided-local-computed-update-bound]]: use stored raw kernels without
zero overwrites, propagate their $v$ allowances, use
[[lem-rounded-linear-and-normal-residual-certificates]] only on STORED matvec
inputs, and include the final subtraction allowance. Exact normalized factor
entries are not silently treated as stored inputs. Evaluate each certificate
using the finite exact real-controller expression trees/loops in the local
lemma and component absolute sums as norm upper bounds. Controller operations
are separate from rounded update arithmetic; for rational/binary stored data
and rational $u$ this is exact rational computation. No opaque certification
oracle is used. Failure of this residual route's dimension/range hypotheses
makes that route inconclusive and does not invalidate a valid independent
local-accumulation bound. Always retain available diagnostics.

The output is $(Q,S,T,Z,\text{status})$, the exact factor products when
available, the raw residuals $R_A=Q^*AZ-S$ and $R_B=Q^*BZ-T$, and the recorded
local arithmetic and deflation perturbations. The procedure asserts no
unconditional convergence or small-roundoff bound.

## Statement

Let $(A,B)$ be a regular $n\times n$ pencil over $\mathbb C$. Then there are
unitary $Q,Z$ such that $Q^*AZ$ and $Q^*BZ$ are upper triangular. If
$A,B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, there are orthogonal $Q,Z$ such that $Q^TAZ$
is block upper triangular with one-by-one real blocks and two-by-two blocks
whose generalized determinant polynomial has a nonreal conjugate root pair,
while $Q^TBZ$ is upper triangular. In either form, the homogeneous roots of
the diagonal block determinant polynomials are exactly the homogeneous
generalized eigenvalues of $(A,B)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A regular finite square pencil $(A,B)$ of order $n\ge1$ over
$\mathbb C$ or $\mathbb R$.

[F1] [[lem-regular-pencil-has-projective-eigenvalue]]: a regular pencil has a
nonzero homogeneous pair $[\alpha:\beta]$ with
$\det(\beta A-\alpha B)=0$.

[F2] [[lem-regular-pencil-has-no-common-kernel-vector]]: regularity excludes
a nonzero vector in both $\ker A$ and $\ker B$.

[F3] [[lem-block-upper-triangular-pencil-determinant-factorizes]]: the
homogeneous determinant of a block upper triangular pair is the product of
the determinants of its diagonal block pairs.

[F4] [[thm-householder-reflectors-and-givens-transformations-are-unitary-and-annihilate-targeted-entries]]:
Householder transformations are unitary and can align a nonzero vector with
the first coordinate; Givens transformations can annihilate a prescribed
coordinate.

[F5] [[thm-gram-schmidt-orthonormalisation]]: Gram–Schmidt converts finite
independent lists to orthonormal lists with the same successive spans.

[F6] [[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]]:
every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an
orthonormal basis.

[F7] [[thm-operator-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]]: a finite-dimensional
operator over a field is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero.

[F8] [[thm-root-bound-for-polynomials-over-a-domain]]: a nonzero polynomial of
degree at most $n$ has at most $n$ distinct roots.

[F9] [[def-generalized-schur-form]]: the required complex and real block
structures and homogeneous diagonal roots are as defined there.

[F10] [[lem-zero-determinant-matrix-has-nonzero-kernel-vector]]: over either
$\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, zero determinant gives a nonzero kernel vector.

[F11] [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]]: determinants multiply under matrix
products.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** induction on the pencil order, splitting one real
eigenvalue or one nonreal conjugate pair at each step.

1.1 We prove the statement by induction on $n$, with the empty trailing pencil allowed after a final block is removed. For $n=1$, regularity says the scalar pair $(A,B)$ is not $(0,0)$, and $Q=Z=[1]$ gives the required form. Now let $n>1$ and assume the result for smaller regular pencils. [given, F9, induction, base, ih]

1.2 Choose a homogeneous eigenvalue pair $[\alpha:\beta]$ by [F1]. Its homogeneous determinant is zero, so [F10] gives a nonzero vector $v$ in the kernel over $\mathbb C$. For real input and a real projective root, rescale $[\alpha:\beta]$ to real coordinates and apply [F10] over $\mathbb R$. If $\beta\ne0$, put $\lambda=\alpha/\beta$; then $Av=\lambda Bv$. If $Bv=0$, this also gives $Av=0$, contrary to [F2], so $Bv\ne0$. If $\beta=0$, then $Bv=0$ and [F2] gives $Av\ne0$. [given, F1, F2, F10, algebra, cases]

2.1 If the input field is complex, or if the selected root for real input is real, use a one-dimensional block. Set $q=Bv$ in the finite case and $q=Av$ in the infinite case. Both vectors are nonzero by step 1.2. By [F4], choose unitary/orthogonal alignments $Lq=\gamma e_1$ and $Rv=\eta e_1$ and set $Q=L^*$, $Z=R^*$. Then $Q^*q=\gamma e_1$ and $Z^*v=\eta e_1$, so $Q^*AZ$ and $Q^*BZ$ have zeros below their first entries in the first column. The leading diagonal pair is nonzero: in the finite case its $B$ entry is nonzero, and in the infinite case its $A$ entry is nonzero. [step 1.2, F4, construct, cases]

2.2 If the input is real and the selected root is nonreal, then $\beta\ne0$; write $\lambda=\alpha/\beta=a+ib$ with $b\ne0$ and write the vector from step 1.2 as $v=x+iy$ in $\ker(A-\lambda B)$. The real vectors $x,y$ are linearly independent. If they were dependent, $v$ would be a nonzero complex multiple of a nonzero real vector $w$, so $(A-\lambda B)w=0$. If $Bw=0$, then $Aw=0$, contradicting [F2]. If $Bw\ne0$, a coordinate with $(Bw)_i\ne0$ gives $\lambda=(Aw)_i/(Bw)_i\in\mathbb R$, contradicting $b\ne0$. Put $X=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{x,y\}$ and $Y=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{Bx,By\}$. Separating real and imaginary parts gives $Ax=aBx-bBy$ and $Ay=bBx+aBy$, so $A(X)\subseteq Y$. If $\dim Y<2$, then for each $\mu\in\mathbb C$ the map $(A-\mu B):X_{\mathbb C}\to Y_{\mathbb C}$ has a nonzero kernel because its domain has dimension two and its range has dimension at most one. Hence $A-\mu B$ is not invertible, so [F7] gives $\det(A-\mu B)=0$ for every $\mu$, contradicting regularity and [F8]. Thus $\dim Y=2$. [given, F2, F7, F8, step 1.2, algebra, contradiction]

3.1 Apply [F5] to obtain orthonormal bases $z_1,z_2$ of $X$ and $q_1,q_2$ of $Y$, choosing $q_1,q_2$ by Gram–Schmidt on $Bz_1,Bz_2$. The restriction $B|_X:X\to Y$ sends a basis to the independent pair $Bz_1,Bz_2$ and is therefore an isomorphism. Its matrix in these bases is $B_{11}=Q_1^TBZ_1$, so $B_{11}$ is invertible and [F7] gives $\det(B_{11})\ne0$; the Gram–Schmidt choice makes this matrix upper triangular. Extend these bases by orthonormal bases of $Y^\perp$ and $X^\perp$ using [F6]. In these full bases, the first two columns of both transformed matrices are supported in the first two rows. Let $P$ be the invertible change-of-basis matrix from $(x,y)$ to $(z_1,z_2)$. The equations in step 2.2 give $A[z_1\ z_2]=B[z_1\ z_2]C$, where $C=P^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}P$. Thus the leading blocks satisfy $A_{11}=B_{11}C$, and $C$ is similar to $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}$. Consequently $\det(A_{11}-\mu B_{11}) =\det(B_{11})\det(C-\mu I) =\det(B_{11})\bigl((a-\mu)^2+b^2\bigr)$ is a nonzero polynomial with roots $a\pm ib$. [step 2.2, F5, F6, F7, F11, algebra, construct]

4.1 In either the one-dimensional case of step 2.1 or the two-dimensional case of step 3.1, the transformed pair has a nonzero leading block determinant polynomial $g$. The transformed full pencil is regular: by [F8] choose $\mu$ with $\det(A-\mu B)\ne0$; the unitary or orthogonal changes of basis preserve invertibility. By [F7], the transformed determinant at this $\mu$ is also nonzero, so the transformed full determinant polynomial is nonzero. If there is no trailing block, the transformed pencil is just its leading block and this already proves regularity. If the trailing block is nonempty, both block sizes are positive, so [F3] factors the full determinant polynomial as $g$ times the trailing determinant. A product of two nonzero complex polynomials is nonzero because their leading nonzero coefficients have nonzero product. Since $g$ and the full determinant are nonzero, the trailing determinant is nonzero, so the trailing pencil is regular. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F3, F7, F8, algebra]

5.1 If the trailing block is nonempty, apply the induction hypothesis to it and extend its left and right transformations by identity matrices on the leading block. If it is empty, no further transformation is needed. This produces the stated upper triangular complex form or real block upper triangular form with upper triangular second factor. [step 1.1, step 4.1, induction, construct, ih]

6.1 The left and right basis changes are invertible, so [F7] shows that they preserve singularity of every homogeneous pencil matrix. If there is one diagonal block, its determinant is the full determinant. With at least two blocks, split off the first diagonal block and apply [F3] repeatedly; every split has positive block sizes. The resulting product is the nonzero determinant polynomial of the regular transformed pencil, so each factor is nonzero by the leading-coefficient argument in step 4.1. Thus a homogeneous pair is a root of the full determinant exactly when it is a root of at least one diagonal block determinant. The basis changes preserve this root set, which proves the claim. [step 4.1, step 5.1, F3, F7, F9, algebra, discharge-induction] ∎

## Statement

Every run of [[alg-finite-budget-qz-iteration-with-deflation-and-residual]]
terminates with a declared status. After each successful initialization or
QZ/infinite-deflation sweep, the stored pair is Hessenberg-triangular, except
at explicitly isolated blocks. For any run with a certified exact-unitary
factor record and local update residuals, the returned pair $(S,T)$ satisfies
$$S=Q^*(A+\Delta_A)Z,\qquad T=Q^*(B+\Delta_B)Z,$$
where $(\Delta_A,\Delta_B)$ is the accumulated arithmetic and explicit
deflation perturbation pair. This proposition gives no bound on its size.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite input, budget $N$, tolerance $\tau$, and operationwise
finite-arithmetic model stated in the algorithm.

[F1] [[alg-finite-budget-qz-iteration-with-deflation-and-residual]] has finite
loops, a finite sweep budget, explicit range-failure handling, and records each
arithmetic residual and each assigned structural zero.

[F2] [[prop-generalized-hessenberg-triangular-reduction-preserves-form-and-equivalence]]:
the exact initialization gives the finite index schedule and support induction; numerical reconstruction instead uses [F5].

[F3] [[thm-householder-reflectors-and-givens-transformations-are-unitary-and-annihilate-targeted-entries]]:
left and right Givens factors can annihilate the prescribed bulge entries.

[F4] [[lem-two-sided-unitary-equivalence-errors-accumulate-for-pencil]]:
local left/right unitary updates with local arithmetic and deflation residuals
give a global perturbation pair bounded by the sum of their pair norms.

[F5] [[lem-qz-two-sided-local-computed-update-bound]] supplies common computed
left/right factors for both matrices, correct row-target orientation, exact
target writes, pulled-back perturbations, and explicit local norm bounds.

## Proof

1.1 The initialization uses finitely many Givens loops by [F2]. In a QZ sweep, the first left rotation is chosen from the computed first two components of $(\beta H-\alpha T)e_1$, whose only possibly nonzero entries are the first two. The following right rotation removes the new $T_{2,1}$ entry and can create only the bulge $H_{3,1}$. [F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]

1.2 For an infinite-deflation step with $T_{k,k}=0$, the descending right rotations make $T_{j,j}=0$ for $j=k-1,\ldots,a$. At each such stage, $T_{j+1,j}=T_{j+1,j+1}=0$, so the right rotation does not create a subdiagonal entry in $T$. It can create only $H_{j+2,j}$, which the paired left rotation zeros; that left rotation preserves triangularity because the affected entries of column $j+1$ of $T$ are both zero. The final left rotation zeros $H_{a+1,a}$ while column $a$ of $T$ remains zero, isolating the top one-by-one pair $(H_{a,a},0)$. The mandatory post-isolation scan reports the $(0,0)$ branch as `singular-pencil-suspected`, so it is not assigned an eigenvalue. The targeted zeros are explicit assignments; applying rounded rotations to other already-zero coordinate pairs preserves them exactly. [F1, F3, F5, induction]

1.3 There are finitely many initialization loops, at most $2n$ rotations per infinite isolation or per active-block sweep, at most $n$ successful infinite removals, and at most $N$ sweeps over at most $n$ active blocks. An unsuccessful isolation exits rather than repeating indefinitely. Each residual/controller evaluation uses finite prescribed factor/column loops. Every scalar operation either succeeds or exits with `range-failure`; missing unitarity or arithmetic certificates exit with `certificate-inconclusive`. Thus every branch terminates with a declared status. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 If the current bulge is $H_{j+1,j-1}$, [F3] supplies a left Givens factor on rows $j,j+1$ that zeros it. This can create the single $T_{j+1,j}$ entry; a right Givens factor on columns $j,j+1$ zeros that entry and can create only the next Hessenberg bulge $H_{j+2,j}$. The final rotation pair has no row below the active block, so the sweep ends Hessenberg-triangular. Computed target entries are explicitly zeroed with [F5], so this support induction also holds in rounded storage. Structural writes are included in their arithmetic allowance; only separate tolerance writes enter the deflation ledger. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.1, induction]

2.2 For a run with certified factors, each local update has the form $A_j=Q_j^*(A_{j-1}+E_j^A+D_j^A)Z_j$ and $B_j=Q_j^*(B_{j-1}+E_j^B+D_j^B)Z_j$, where $E_j$ includes the structural target write and $D_j$ is the saved separate tolerance write, pulled back from post-action coordinates as required by [F5]. Applying [F4] to this finite list gives $S=Q^*(A+\Delta_A)Z$ and $T=Q^*(B+\Delta_B)Z$ for the accumulated pair $(\Delta_A,\Delta_B)$. No bound is asserted without local norm certificates. [F1, F4, F5, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Before `qz-computed`, both arrays are triangular and all diagonal pairs are nonzero. Their homogeneous determinant is $\prod_k(\beta S_{kk}-\alpha T_{kk})$, a product of nonzero linear polynomials, hence is not identically zero. The returned pencil is regular; any label with second coordinate zero is an infinite candidate of this returned perturbed pencil. This proves no exact original-input infinite-eigenvalue or forward-error claim. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Suppose [[alg-finite-budget-qz-iteration-with-deflation-and-residual]]
returns exact unitary factor products $Q,Z$, factors $S,T$, and exact local
arithmetic and deflation residuals as specified there. If each local residual
pair has a certified bound, then the accumulated theorem
[[lem-two-sided-unitary-equivalence-errors-accumulate-for-pencil]] gives
perturbations $\Delta_A,\Delta_B$ such that
$$Q^*(A+\Delta_A)Z=S,\qquad Q^*(B+\Delta_B)Z=T,$$
with combined Frobenius error bounded by the sum of the certified local pair
errors and deflation errors. This implication is conditional: it does not
assert such a bound for an arbitrary unspecified rotation implementation. For the specified successful canonical Givens implementation, [[lem-qz-two-sided-local-computed-update-bound]] supplies $\ell_j=\eta$ for actual matrix annihilations and $\ell_j=v$ for external-vector/raw actions. With structural writes included there and only separate tolerance writes $D_{\mathrm{tol},j}$, it gives the concrete bound
$$P(\Delta_A,\Delta_B)\le\sum_j\ell_jP(A_{j-1},B_{j-1})+\sum_j P(D^A_{\mathrm{tol},j},D^B_{\mathrm{tol},j}),$$
where $P(C,D)=(\|C\|_F^2+\|D\|_F^2)^{1/2}$. Tolerance deflations need not be $O(u)$.

Independently, if the exact raw residuals are
$$R_A=Q^*AZ-S,\qquad R_B=Q^*BZ-T,$$
then the choices $\Delta_A=-Q R_A Z^*$ and $\Delta_B=-Q R_B Z^*$ satisfy the
same equations and
$$\sqrt{\|\Delta_A\|_F^2+\|\Delta_B\|_F^2} =\sqrt{\|R_A\|_F^2+\|R_B\|_F^2}.$$
Certified upper bounds on the two residual norms therefore give an
a-posteriori backward-error certificate for the pair.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A run with exact unitary factor records, computed factors $(S,T)$,
local arithmetic/deflation residuals, and any claimed certified residual norm
upper bounds.

[F1] [[prop-finite-budget-qz-iteration-terminates-and-preserves-pencil-equivalence]]:
the completed run has the stated accumulated perturbation representation
whenever all local residual certificates are available.

[F2] [[lem-two-sided-unitary-equivalence-errors-accumulate-for-pencil]]: the
global pair perturbation is bounded by the sum of the local pair and deflation
norms.

[F3] [[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]]:
left or right unitary multiplication preserves the Frobenius norm.

[F4] [[lem-qz-two-sided-local-computed-update-bound]] proves the actual common
real/complex Givens pair update and target-write coefficients, and a stored
factor-action residual evaluation with explicit norm/controller allowances.

The specified canonical implementation instantiates them by [F4] whenever its
successful-operation hypotheses hold; alternative implementations require their
own certificates.

1.2 For the specified implementation, [F4] gives $P(E_j^A,E_j^B)\le\ell_jP(A_{j-1},B_{j-1})$. 2.1 From the definitions of $R_A,R_B$, set $\Delta_A=-QR_AZ^*$ and $\Delta_B=-QR_BZ^*$. Exact unitarity gives $Q^*\Delta_A Z=-R_A$ and $Q^*\Delta_B Z=-R_B$, so adding the residuals proves both displayed backward equations. By [F3], $\|\Delta_A\|_F=\|R_A\|_F$ and $\|\Delta_B\|_F=\|R_B\|_F$; squaring and adding proves the exact pair equality. [given, F3, algebra, construct]

2.2 Under the independent residual route's successful-operation hypotheses, [F4] bounds each exact residual column by its computed diagnostic norm plus the propagated factor, stored-input matvec and subtraction allowances. ## Example

Take $A=I_2$ and $B=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$. The matrix $B$ is singular,
but the pencil is regular and has one finite eigenvalue and one infinite
eigenvalue.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The pair $(A,B)$ and the homogeneous eigenvalue convention of
[[def-regular-generalized-eigenvalue-pencil]].

[F1] [[def-regular-generalized-eigenvalue-pencil]]: regularity means
$\det(A-\lambda B)$ is not identically zero, and homogeneous eigenpairs solve
$\det(\beta A-\alpha B)=0$ with $(\alpha,\beta)\ne(0,0)$.

## Verification

1.1 Direct calculation gives $\det(A-\lambda B)=1-\lambda$, a nonzero polynomial, so the pencil is regular although $\det B=0$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The homogeneous determinant is $\det(\beta A-\alpha B)=\det\begin{pmatrix}\beta-\alpha&0\\0&\beta\end{pmatrix} =\beta(\beta-\alpha).$ Its projective roots are $[1:1]$, the finite eigenvalue $1$, and $[1:0]$, the infinite eigenvalue. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

The pair $(I_2,0)$ is regular and has only infinite generalized eigenvalues.
The pair $(\operatorname{diag}(1,0),0)$ has an identically zero determinant
pencil and is singular. Thus a singular second matrix is compatible with
regularity, while the determinant polynomial decides pencil regularity.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The regularity definition for finite square pencils in
[[def-regular-generalized-eigenvalue-pencil]].

[F1] [[def-regular-generalized-eigenvalue-pencil]]: a pencil is regular
exactly when $\det(A-\lambda B)$ is not the zero polynomial.

## Verification

1.1 For $(A,B)=(I_2,0)$, $\det(A-\lambda B)=\det I_2=1$, so the pencil is regular. Its homogeneous determinant is $\det(\beta I_2)=\beta^2$, which vanishes only at $[1:0]$, the infinite eigenvalue pair. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 For $(A,B)=(\operatorname{diag}(1,0),0)$, $\det(A-\lambda B)=\det A=0$ for every $\lambda$, so the determinant polynomial is identically zero and the pencil is singular. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let the stiffness and mass matrices be
$$K=\begin{pmatrix}4&-2\\-2&3\end{pmatrix},\qquad M=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
The generalized eigenvalues are $1$ and $4$, with $M$-orthogonal modes. The
trial pair $(x,\mu)=(e_1,2)$ also illustrates a B-metric residual enclosure.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The displayed real symmetric stiffness and mass matrices.

[F1] [[thm-hermitian-definite-pencil-has-real-spectrum-and-b-orthogonal-eigenbasis]]:
a symmetric $K$ and positive-definite $M$ have real generalized eigenvalues
and an $M$-orthonormal eigenbasis.

[F2] [[thm-b-metric-residual-encloses-definite-pencil-eigenvalue]]: a nonzero
trial vector and real trial value have spectral distance bounded by the
$M$-dual residual norm divided by the $M$-norm of the vector.

[F3] [[def-regular-generalized-eigenvalue-pencil]]: the pencil is regular when
its determinant polynomial is nonzero.

## Verification

1.1 The matrix $M$ is positive definite because $u^TMu=2u_1^2+u_2^2>0$ for $u\ne0$. Also $u^TKu=2u_1^2+2(u_1-u_2)^2+u_2^2>0$ for $u\ne0$. The determinant polynomial is $\det(K-\lambda M)=(4-2\lambda)(3-\lambda)-4 =2(\lambda-1)(\lambda-4),$ so the pencil is regular and its eigenvalues are $1,4$. [given, F3, algebra]

2.1 For $x_1=(1,1)^T$, $Kx_1=(2,1)^T=Mx_1$. For $x_2=(1,-2)^T$, $Kx_2=(8,-8)^T=4Mx_2$. Their mass inner product is $x_1^TMx_2=2-2=0$. Thus they are distinct generalized eigenmodes and are $M$-orthogonal; [F1] gives the general real-spectrum and orthogonal-basis conclusion for this pencil. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

3.1 For $x=e_1$ and $\mu=2$, the residual is $r=Kx-\mu Mx=(0,-2)^T$. Hence $\|x\|_M=\sqrt2$ and, since $M^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1)$, $\|r\|_{M^{-1}}=2$. The theorem [F2] therefore bounds the distance from $2$ to $\{1,4\}$ by $2/\sqrt2=\sqrt2$; indeed that distance is $1$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

## Statement

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$,
$$\operatorname{rank}(A)+\dim_F N(A)=n.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The linear map $L_A:F^n\to F^m$, $x\mapsto Ax$.

[L1] Matrix rank equals the rank of $L_A$ ([[cor-matrix-rank-equals-the-rank-of-its-linear-map]]).

[L2] Rank–nullity gives $\dim V=\operatorname{rank}T+\dim\ker T$ for a linear map with finite-dimensional domain ([[thm-rank-nullity]]).

[L3] $N(A)=\{x:Ax=0\}$ ([[def-row-space-column-space-nullspace-and-matrix-ranks]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Apply rank–nullity to $L_A:F^n\to F^m$ to obtain $n=\operatorname{rank}L_A+\dim\ker L_A$. [L2]

2.1 By [L1] the first term is $\operatorname{rank}A$, and by [L3] the kernel is $N(A)$. Substitution proves the formula, including $n=0$. [step 1.1, L1, L3] ∎

## Statement

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, the matrix rank of $A$ equals the rank of the linear map $L_A:F^n\to F^m$ defined by $L_A(x)=Ax$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and its associated linear map $L_A$.

[L1] Matrix rank is row rank, which equals column rank ([[def-row-space-column-space-nullspace-and-matrix-ranks]]).

[L2] Row rank equals column rank ([[thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank]]).

[L3] The rank of a linear map is the dimension of its image ([[def-rank-and-nullity]]).

[L4] Matrix multiplication is given entrywise by $(Ax)_i=\sum_{j<n}a_{ij}x_j$ ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]).

[L5] Matrix multiplication distributes over addition and is compatible with scalar multiplication ([[thm-matrix-multiplication-laws]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fact [L5] shows that $L_A(x)=Ax$ is linear. By [L4], every value $Ax$ is a linear combination of the columns of $A$, with coefficients $x_j$, and every such combination is $Ax$ for that coefficient column. Hence $\operatorname{im}L_A=\operatorname{Col}(A)$. [L4, L5, algebra]

2.1 Taking dimensions and using [L1]–[L3] gives $\operatorname{rank}L_A=\dim\operatorname{Col}(A)=\operatorname{rank}A$. [step 1.1, L1, L2, L3] ∎

## Statement

Let $T:V\to V$ be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space over
a field $F$. Then $T$ is invertible if and only if $\det(T)\neq0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $T,V,F$ as in the statement.

[L1] If $T$ is invertible, its representing matrix is invertible ([[thm-invertible-matrices-correspond-to-linear-isomorphisms]]).

[L4] Every square matrix is the representing matrix of a unique operator, and composition of operators becomes multiplication of their matrices ([[thm-matrix-representation-is-a-vector-space-isomorphism]], [[thm-matrix-of-a-composite-is-the-product]]).

[L2] A positive-sized square matrix over a commutative ring is invertible exactly when its determinant is a unit ([[cor-square-matrix-invertible-iff-determinant-is-a-unit]]).

[F1] A field is a commutative ring and its units are precisely its nonzero elements ([[lem-field-is-a-commutative-ring]]).

[L3] The operator determinant is the determinant of a representing matrix and is basis independent ([[thm-operator-determinant-is-basis-independent]]).

[F2] In dimension zero, the operator determinant is defined to be $1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Suppose $\dim V\geq1$ and choose an ordered basis, writing $A=[T]$. If $T$ is invertible, then $A$ is invertible by [L1]. Conversely, if $A$ is invertible, [L4] gives an operator $S$ with $[S]=A^{-1}$; the composite formula gives $[S\circ T]=I=[T\circ S]$, and injectivity of matrix representation gives $S\circ T=I_V=T\circ S$. Thus $T$ is invertible exactly when $A$ is invertible. [L1, L4, algebra]

1.2 If $\dim V=0$, the unique endomorphism is the identity and is invertible, while [F2] gives $\det(T)=1\neq0$. [F2, algebra]

2.1 By [L2] and [F1], $A$ is invertible exactly when $\det(A)\neq0$; by [L3], this is exactly $\det(T)\neq0$. [step 1.1, L2, F1, L3]

3.1 Steps 2.1 and 1.2 establish the equivalence in every finite dimension. [step 2.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

For $n\ge1$ and every commutative ring $R$, the Leibniz determinant $\det:M_n(R)\to R$ is column-multilinear, alternating and normalized.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Leibniz determinant of an $n\times n$ matrix over a commutative ring.

[L1] Determinant is the finite signed sum over $S_n$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

[L2] Multilinear, alternating and normalized have the stated columnwise meanings ([[def-multilinear-alternating-normalized-and-antisymmetric-matrix-functions]]).

[L3] Sign is a homomorphism on $S_n$ ([[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]).

[L4] Finite sums may be distributed and reindexed by bijections ([[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]]).

[L5] Composing a permutation on either side with a transposition reverses its inversion sign ([[lem-a-transposition-reverses-inversion-sign]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 With every column but column $q$ fixed, each Leibniz monomial contains exactly one entry from column $q$. Distributing finite sums therefore proves additivity and scalar compatibility in that column, and $q$ was arbitrary. [L1, L2, L4, algebra]

2.1 Suppose columns $p,q$ are equal. Pair each $\sigma$ with $\sigma\circ(p\ q)$. Commutativity makes the paired monomials equal, while [L5] makes their signs opposite, so every pair sums to zero and the determinant vanishes. [step 1.1, L3, L4, L5, algebra]

3.1 At $I_n$, every nonidentity permutation selects an off-diagonal zero, while the identity term is $1$. Thus $\det(I_n)=1$. This also covers $n=1$ and the zero ring, where the equality reads $0=0$. [step 2.1, L1, L2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $D$ be an integral domain. A nonzero polynomial $f\in D[x]$ of degree $n$ has at most $n$ distinct roots in $D$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integral domain $D$ and a nonzero polynomial $f\in D[x]$ of degree $n$.

[L1] If $a$ is a root of $f$, then $f=(x-a)q$ for some polynomial $q$ ([[cor-factor-theorem-over-a-commutative-ring]]).

[L2] Degrees add when nonzero polynomials over a domain are multiplied ([[thm-polynomial-degree-of-a-product-over-a-domain]]).

[L3] In an integral domain, a product is zero only if one factor is zero ([[def-zero-divisor-and-integral-domain]]).

[L4] If a property holds at $0$ and passes from $n$ to $n+1$, it holds for every natural number ([[thm-induction-principle]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** induction.

1.1 If $n=0$, then $f$ is a nonzero constant and has no root, proving the base case. [base, given]

2.1 For $n>0$, if $f$ has no root the claim is immediate; otherwise choose a root $a$, use [L1] to write $f=(x-a)q$, and use [L2] to obtain $\deg q=n-1$. [step 1.1, ih, L1, L2, choose]

3.1 If $b\ne a$ is another root, then $0=f(b)=(b-a)q(b)$, and [L3] gives $q(b)=0$ because $b-a\ne0$; the induction hypothesis bounds the roots other than $a$ by $n-1$, so $f$ has at most $n$ roots, and [L4] completes the induction. [step 2.1, ih, L3, L4, discharge-induction] ∎

      url: https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~demmel/ma221_Fall10/Lectures/Lecture_16.html
    - title: "David Bindel, CS 6210 Matrix Computations, Hessenberg QR iteration"
      url: https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs6210/2025fa/lec/2025-10-29.html
---

## Statement

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, let $U_0$ be unitary, and set $H_0=U_0^*AU_0$. For $j=1,\ldots,m$, suppose

$$H_j=P_j^*(H_{j-1}+E_j+D_j)P_j,$$

where each $P_j$ is unitary, $E_j$ is a local arithmetic perturbation, and $D_j$ is a local deflation perturbation. Then for $U_m=U_0P_1\cdots P_m$ there is a matrix $\Delta$ such that

$$H_m=U_m^*(A+\Delta)U_m,\qquad \|\Delta\|_F\le\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(\|E_j\|_F+\|D_j\|_F\bigr).$$

The assertion also holds over $\mathbb R$ with orthogonal factors.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The matrices and update relations in the statement.

[F1] [[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]]: each $P_j$ and $U_0$ is unitary.

[F2] [[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]]: unitary multiplication on either side preserves the Frobenius norm.

## Proof

1.1 Set $\Delta_0=0$ and $U_j=U_{j-1}P_j$. If $H_{j-1}=U_{j-1}^*(A+\Delta_{j-1})U_{j-1}$, then the stated update gives $H_j=U_j^*(A+\Delta_{j-1}+U_{j-1}(E_j+D_j)U_{j-1}^*)U_j$. Thus define $\Delta_j=\Delta_{j-1}+U_{j-1}(E_j+D_j)U_{j-1}^*$. The base case holds by the definition of $H_0$, so induction gives the displayed representation for $j=m$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], $\|U_{j-1}(E_j+D_j)U_{j-1}^*\|_F=\|E_j+D_j\|_F\le\|E_j\|_F+\|D_j\|_F$. Applying the triangle inequality to the sum defining $\Delta_m$ proves the stated bound. [step 1.1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

## Definition

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

## Remarks

- **The name records the entry-sum definition.** Different sources write
  $\lVert A\rVert_F$, $\lVert A\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}$, or
  $\lVert A\rVert_{2,\mathrm{HS}}$; this library uses $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$
  exclusively and does not fold it into the induced $p$-norm notation.

- **Zero-sized shapes are included.** At $m=0$ or $n=0$ the double sum is the
  empty sum $0$, so the unique empty matrix has Frobenius norm $0$; this is the
  value of the inner-product norm of the zero space.

## Statement

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, with the real case obtained by
restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and
   positive real diagonal.
2. $A$ is Hermitian positive definite.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A matrix $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$.

[L1] Hermitian positive-definite matrices and Cholesky factorisations with positive diagonal are defined in [[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]].

[L2] The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries ([[thm-determinant-of-a-triangular-matrix]]).

[L3] Determinants are multiplicative ([[thm-determinant-multiplicative]]).

[L4] Matrix multiplication uses the convention of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]].

[L5] A finite-dimensional operator over a field is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero ([[thm-operator-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]]), applied to the operator represented by a square matrix.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** block induction with a quotient comparison for uniqueness.

1.1 Suppose $A=LL^*$ as in [L1]. Then $A^*=LL^*=A$, so $A$ is Hermitian. For any nonzero $x$, one has $$x^*Ax=x^*LL^*x=(L^*x)^*(L^*x)=\|L^*x\|_2^2.$$ The diagonal of $L$ is positive, hence nonzero; [L2] and [L3] give $\det L\ne 0$, so [L5] makes $L$ invertible and $L^*x\ne 0$ when $x\ne 0$. Therefore $x^*Ax>0$. [L1, L2, L3, L4, L5, algebra]

1.2 For the converse, use induction on $n$. The case $n=1$ is immediate: $A=[a]$ is Hermitian positive definite exactly when $a>0$, in which case $A=[\sqrt a][\sqrt a]^*$. [base, L1, algebra]

1.3 Assume $n>1$ and the converse for size $n-1$. Write $$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&r^*\\ r&C\end{pmatrix}.$$ Positive definiteness of $A$ at $x=e_0$ gives $a>0$. Set $\ell:=r/\sqrt a$ and $S:=C-\ell\ell^*$. For nonzero $y\in\mathbb C^{n-1}$, apply positive definiteness to $x=\binom{-a^{-1}r^*y}{y}$: $$0<x^*Ax=y^*Sy.$$ Thus $S$ is Hermitian positive definite. By the induction hypothesis, $S=\widetilde L\widetilde L^*$ with $\widetilde L$ lower triangular and positive diagonal. [ih, L1, algebra]

2.1 Define $$L:=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt a&0\\ \ell&\widetilde L\end{pmatrix}.$$ Direct multiplication gives $$LL^*=\begin{pmatrix}a&r^*\\ r&\ell\ell^*+\widetilde L\widetilde L^*\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}a&r^*\\ r&C\end{pmatrix}=A.$$ The matrix $L$ is lower triangular and its diagonal is positive real, so this is a Cholesky factorisation. [step 1.3, L1, L4, algebra]

3.1 For uniqueness, suppose $A=L_1L_1^*=L_2L_2^*$ are two such factorizations. By [L2] and [L5], both factors are invertible. Forward substitution in $L_2u=e_j$ gives $u_i=0$ for $i<j$ and $u_j=1/(L_2)_{jj}$, so $L_2^{-1}$ is lower triangular with reciprocal diagonal. Hence $M:=L_2^{-1}L_1$ is lower triangular with positive real diagonal, and $MM^*=I$ follows by multiplying $L_2MM^*L_2^*=L_1L_1^*=L_2L_2^*$ by the inverses. Its first row contains only $M_{11}$, so $MM^*=I$ gives $|M_{11}|=1$ and $M_{i1}\overline{M_{11}}=0$ for $i>1$. Removing this first row and column leaves a lower triangular block satisfying the same identity; induction gives zero strict-lower entries and unit-modulus diagonal throughout. Every diagonal entry is positive real, hence $1$, so $M=I$ and $L_1=L_2$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L2, L3, L4, L5, algebra]

4.1 Step 1.1 proves that a Cholesky factorisation implies Hermitian positive definiteness. Steps 1.2-2.1 prove the converse by induction, and step 3.1 gives uniqueness. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, discharge-induction] ∎

## Statement

If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A triangular $n\times n$ matrix $A$ over a commutative ring.

[L1] Upper triangular means $a_{ij}=0$ for $i>j$, while lower triangular means $a_{ij}=0$ for $i<j$ ([[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]).

[L2] Determinant is the sum of the signed products $\prod_i a_{\sigma(i),i}$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

[L3] The identity permutation has sign $1$ ([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For an upper triangular matrix, a nonzero Leibniz term requires $\sigma(i)\le i$ for every $i$. A permutation with these inequalities is the identity: starting at $i=0$ and proceeding upward, bijectivity forces $\sigma(i)=i$. Thus every nonidentity term contains a zero entry. [L1, L2, L3]

2.1 The identity term has sign $1$ and equals $\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}$, so it is the whole determinant. [step 1.1, L2, L3]

3.1 For a lower triangular matrix the same argument uses $\sigma(i)\ge i$ and proceeds downward, again forcing the identity. The argument includes $n=1$ and makes no cancellation assumption, so zero divisors and the zero ring cause no exception. [step 2.1, L1, L2] ∎

## Statement

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite-dimensional real inner product space $V$ and a self-adjoint endomorphism $T:V\to V$.

[L1] Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal ([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]).

[L2] A real normal endomorphism admits an orthonormal block decomposition by $1\times1$ real blocks and $2\times2$ blocks $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}$ ([[thm-real-normal-endomorphism-classification]]).

[L3] In an orthonormal basis, self-adjointness means symmetry of the matrix ([[prop-self-adjoint-and-normal-matrix-criteria-in-orthonormal-bases]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1] and [L2], there is an orthonormal basis in which the matrix of $T$ is block diagonal with $1\times1$ real blocks and $2\times2$ blocks $B=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}$. [L1, L2]

2.1 Because $T$ is self-adjoint, [L3] says that the same matrix is symmetric. A block $B$ above is symmetric exactly when $b=0$, so every $2\times2$ block collapses to the scalar block $[a]$. Therefore the whole matrix is diagonal. [L3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 A diagonal matrix acts on each basis vector by scalar multiplication, so the orthonormal basis from step 2.1 is an orthonormal eigenbasis of $T$. [step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite-dimensional complex inner product space $V$ and a linear endomorphism $T:V\to V$.

[L1] The field $\mathbb C$ is algebraically closed ([[thm-the-complex-numbers-are-algebraically-closed]]).

[L2] If the characteristic polynomial splits, then some orthonormal basis makes the matrix upper triangular ([[thm-schur-triangularisation]]).

[L3] A normal upper-triangular complex matrix is diagonal ([[lem-normal-upper-triangular-matrix-is-diagonal]]).

[L4] In an orthonormal basis, a linear map is normal exactly when its matrix commutes with its conjugate transpose ([[prop-self-adjoint-and-normal-matrix-criteria-in-orthonormal-bases]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Assume $T$ is normal. By [L1], the characteristic polynomial of $T$ splits over $\mathbb C$, so [L2] gives an orthonormal basis in which the matrix of $T$ is upper triangular. Because $T$ is normal, [L4] makes that matrix normal, and then [L3] makes it diagonal. Hence the chosen orthonormal basis consists of eigenvectors of $T$. [L1, L2, L3, L4]

2.1 Conversely, assume $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of $T$, with $Te_j=\lambda_j e_j$. Then the matrix of $T$ in that basis is the diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$, and every diagonal matrix commutes with its conjugate transpose. By [L4], $T$ is normal. [L4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A fixed matrix $A\in M_n(R)$ and a variable matrix $B\in M_n(R)$.

[L1] Determinant is the unique normalized alternating column-multilinear matrix function ([[thm-determinant-is-the-unique-normalized-alternating-multilinear-function]]).

[L2] Every alternating column-multilinear $F$ satisfies $F(B)=F(I_n)\det(B)$ ([[lem-rigidity-of-alternating-multilinear-matrix-functions]]).

[L3] Matrix multiplication is associative, distributive and unital ([[thm-ring-matrix-arithmetic-laws]]).

[L4] Determinant is defined for every square matrix over the commutative ring ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Define $F(B):=\det(AB)$. Each column of $AB$ is $A$ times the corresponding column of $B$, so distributivity makes $F$ column-multilinear; equal columns of $B$ give equal columns of $AB$, so $F$ is alternating. [L1, L2, L3, L4]

2.1 Since $AI_n=A$, one has $F(I_n)=\det(A)$. [step 1.1, L3, L4]

3.1 Apply [L2] to $F$: $\det(AB)=F(B)=F(I_n)\det(B)=\det(A)\det(B)$. Neither matrix was assumed invertible. [step 2.1, L2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$.

1. Every Householder reflector $H_v=I-2vv^*$ is orthogonal or unitary.
2. For every nonzero $z\in \mathbb F^m$, there is a Householder reflector $H$
   such that $Hz=\alpha e_1$ with $|\alpha|=\|z\|_2$.
3. For every pair $(a,b)\in \mathbb F^2$ not both zero, there is a real or
   complex Givens transformation $G$ such that
   $$G\binom{a}{b}=\binom{\alpha}{0}$$
   with $|\alpha|=(|a|^2+|b|^2)^{1/2}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, a unit vector $v$, a nonzero vector $z\in\mathbb F^m$, and a pair $(a,b)\in\mathbb F^2$ with not both entries zero.

[L1] Householder reflectors and Givens transformations are defined in [[def-householder-reflector]] and [[def-real-and-complex-givens-transformations]].

[L2] An orthogonal or unitary operator is an invertible linear isometry ([[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct matrix multiplication and explicit parameter choice.

1.1 For $H_v=I-2vv^*$ with $v^*v=1$, one has $H_v^*=I-2vv^*=H_v$ and $H_v^2=I-4vv^*+4v(v^*v)v^*=I$. Hence $H_v^*H_v=I$, so $H_v$ is orthogonal or unitary. [L1, L2, algebra]

1.2 In the real case, for $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$ set $r=(a^2+b^2)^{1/2}$, $c=a/r$, and $s=b/r$. Then $c^2+s^2=1$ and $$ \begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-s&c\end{pmatrix}\binom{a}{b} =\binom{r}{0}. $$ In the complex case put $r=(|a|^2+|b|^2)^{1/2}$. If $a=0$, take $c=0$ and $s=\overline b/|b|$; then the transformed pair is $(|b|,0)^T$. If $a\ne0$, put $\phi=a/|a|$, $c=|a|/r$, and $s=\phi\overline b/r$; then $|\phi|=1$, $c^2+|s|^2=1$, and $$ \begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-\overline s&c\end{pmatrix}\binom{a}{b} =\binom{\phi r}{0}. $$ In each case direct multiplication gives $G^*G=I$, so the selected Givens transformation is unitary and annihilates the second entry with the stated output modulus. [L1, L2, algebra]

Both cases give the required first-coordinate alignment and output modulus. Otherwise put $\phi=z_1/|z_1|$ when $z_1\ne0$ and $\phi=1$ when $z_1=0$, and set $\alpha=\phi\|z\|_2$, $w=z-\alpha e_1$, $v=w/\|w\|_2$. ## Statement

Every nonconstant complex polynomial has a complex root. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[lem-complex-polynomial-growth-and-minimum-modulus]], [[lem-dalembert-minimum-modulus-descent]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonconstant complex polynomial $p$.

[L1] [[lem-complex-polynomial-growth-and-minimum-modulus]] states that $|p|$ attains a global minimum on $\mathbb C$.

[L2] [[lem-dalembert-minimum-modulus-descent]] states that, if $p(a)\ne0$, then $|p|$ is not minimal on any neighbourhood of $a$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** contradiction.

1.1 By [L1], let $a$ minimize $|p|$ globally. [L1]

1.2 Suppose $p(a)\ne0$. [assume-contra]

2.1 By [L2], there is a point arbitrarily near $a$ with strictly smaller modulus, contradicting step 1.1. [L2, step 1.1]

3.1 Therefore $p(a)=0$, proving the theorem. [discharge-contradiction] ∎

## Statement

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite linearly independent list $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$.

[L1] An orthonormal list is orthogonal and every listed vector has norm one ([[def-orthogonal-vectors-sets-and-orthonormal-bases]]).

[L2] A finite list $v$ is linearly independent when every list of scalars with $\sum_{i<n}\lambda_iv_i=0_V$ has $\lambda_i=0_F$ for all $i<n$ ([[def-linear-independence]]).

[L3] For a nonzero vector $u$, positive definiteness gives $\lVert u\rVert>0$, so $u/\lVert u\rVert$ is defined and has norm one ([[def-inner-product-norm]]).

[L4] Every finite orthogonal list of nonzero vectors is linearly independent ([[thm-orthogonal-nonzero-vectors-are-linearly-independent]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** induction.

1.1 For $r=0$ there is nothing to construct, and the successive-span assertion at $k=0$ is equality of zero subspaces. [base]

1.2 Suppose $e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1}$ have been constructed orthonormally with the required span equalities. Define $u_k$ by the displayed formula. For $i<k$, linearity and orthonormality give $\langle u_k,e_i\rangle=\langle v_k,e_i\rangle-\langle v_k,e_i\rangle=0$. [ih, L1, algebra]

2.1 If $u_k=0$, then $v_k$ lies in $\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1})$, say $v_k=\sum_{i<k}\mu_iv_i$; then the scalars $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for $i<k$, $\lambda_k=-1_F$ and $\lambda_i=0_F$ for $i>k$ satisfy $\sum_i\lambda_iv_i=0_V$ with $\lambda_k\ne0_F$, contradicting the independence of $v$ through [L2]. Hence $u_k\ne0$, and [L3] makes $e_k=u_k/\lVert u_k\rVert$ a unit vector orthogonal to its predecessors. [step 1.2, ih, L2, L3]

3.1 The formula for $u_k$ shows $e_k$ lies in $\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_k)$, while its rearrangement shows $v_k$ lies in $\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_k)$. Together with the induction hypothesis these give both inclusions in the span equality at $k+1$. [step 2.1, ih, algebra]

4.1 Induction constructs the stated list and proves every successive-span equality. Its vectors are nonzero and orthogonal, so [L4] also confirms their independence; their unit norms make the list orthonormal. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, L1, L4, discharge-induction] ∎
