## Statement

Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite-dimensional inner product space $V$.

[L1] A finite-dimensional vector space has a finite basis, with the empty list serving when $V=0$ ([[def-linear-basis]]).

[L2] Gram–Schmidt converts every finite independent list into an orthonormal list with the same span ([[thm-gram-schmidt-orthonormalisation]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Choose a finite basis $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ of $V$ using [L1]. [L1, choose]

2.1 Apply [L2]. The resulting orthonormal list has the same span as the basis, namely $V$, and therefore is an orthonormal basis. This also covers $r=0$. [step 1.1, L2] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with singular values $\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$.

[L1] There is a singular value decomposition $A=U\Sigma V^{*}$ with $U,V$ unitary (orthogonal over $\mathbb R$) and $\Sigma$ the diagonal matrix of the singular values ([[thm-singular-value-decomposition]]).

[L2] The operator norm of a map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces equals its largest singular value ([[thm-operator-norm-is-the-largest-singular-value]]).

[L3] The rank of a linear map is the number of its positive singular values ([[cor-rank-equals-number-of-nonzero-singular-values]]).

[L4] A unitary (orthogonal) operator preserves norms: $\lVert Qv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$ for every vector $v$ ([[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]]).

[L5] Compositions and adjoints of unitary operators are unitary ([[cor-orthogonal-and-unitary-operators-form-groups-and-have-unit-determinant-modulus]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Claim 1 is [L2] applied to the map $x\mapsto Ax$: $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$. [L2]

1.2 Left invariance of the Frobenius norm. For unitary $Q\in M_m(\mathbb F)$, each column of $QA$ is the image under $Q$ of the corresponding column of $A$, so by [L4] $\lVert(QA)\text{ column }j\rVert_2=\lVert A\text{ column }j\rVert_2$ for every $j<n$; summing over $j$ gives $\lVert QA\rVert_F^{2}=\sum_{j<n}\lVert(QA)_j\rVert_2^{2}=\sum_{j<n}\lVert A_j\rVert_2^{2}=\lVert A\rVert_F^{2}$, using the entry formula of [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]. [L4, algebra]

1.3 Right invariance of the Frobenius norm. For unitary $Z\in M_n(\mathbb F)$, the $i$-th row of $AZ$ is $\operatorname{row}_i(A)Z$, and by [L4] applied to $Z^{*}$, $\lVert\operatorname{row}_i(A)Z\rVert_2=\lVert\operatorname{row}_i(A)\rVert_2$ for every $i<m$; summing over $i$ gives $\lVert AZ\rVert_F^{2}=\sum_{i<m}\lVert\operatorname{row}_i(A)\rVert_2^{2}=\lVert A\rVert_F^{2}$. [L4, algebra]

1.4 Singular values of $UAV$. If $A=U_0\Sigma V_0^{*}$ is the decomposition of [L1], then $UAV=(UU_0)\Sigma(V_0^{*}V)=(UU_0)\Sigma(V^{*}V_0)^{*}$, and by [L5] the factors $UU_0$ and $V^{*}V_0$ are unitary, so this is a singular value decomposition of $UAV$ with the same singular values as $A$. [L1, L5, algebra]

2.1 From [L1], $A=U\Sigma V^{*}$, so steps 1.2 and 1.3 give $\lVert A\rVert_F^{2}=\lVert U\Sigma V^{*}\rVert_F^{2}=\lVert\Sigma\rVert_F^{2}$, and the diagonal entries of $\Sigma$ are $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_r$ followed by zeros, so $\lVert\Sigma\rVert_F^{2}=\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}$ by the entry formula of [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]. This is claim 2. [L1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Claim 3 follows: by step 1.4 the singular values of $UAV$ are those of $A$, so claim 1 gives $\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\sigma_1=\lVert A\rVert_2$ and claim 2 gives $\lVert UAV\rVert_F=\bigl(\sum_j\sigma_j^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}=\lVert A\rVert_F$. [step 1.4, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.2 The lower inequality. The maximum $\sigma_1$ is at most the Euclidean total $\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$, each term being nonnegative, so claims 1 and 2 give $\lVert A\rVert_2\le\lVert A\rVert_F$. Equality holds exactly when $\sigma_2=\cdots=\sigma_r=0$, that is exactly when $r\le 1$ by [L3]. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L3, algebra]

3.3 The upper inequality. Each $\sigma_j\le\sigma_1$, so $\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\le r\sigma_1^{2}$, and claims 1 and 2 give $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{r}\,\sigma_1=\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$. Equality holds exactly when $\sum_{j\le r}(\sigma_1^{2}-\sigma_j^{2})=0$, a sum of nonnegative terms, hence exactly when every $\sigma_j=\sigma_1$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Since $r\le\min(m,n)$ by [L3], the upper bound also gives $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$. [step 3.3, L3]

5.1 Claims 1, 2, 3 and 4 are steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1 and steps 3.2, 3.3 and 4.1. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 3.3, step 4.1] ∎

## Definition

Use the operationwise real/complex arithmetic model, with six-real-operation complex products and componentwise division by positive real scalars. A scaled norm of a nonzero complex vector first chooses the largest absolute real or imaginary component $s>0$, rounds every real component divided by $s$, sums their rounded squares sequentially, rounds the positive square root, and rounds multiplication by $s$. A norm of already scaled components omits the last multiplication. Zero input has exact norm zero. Reject every nonzero exact intermediate outside the normal range, nonfinite/invalid operation, and nonpositive required norm; return the first range-failure. All sign changes and conjugations are exact.

For a Householder active block $C=[x\;B]$, $x\in\mathbb C^r$, a zero $x$ copies the block with identity action. Otherwise compute $\widehat N$ by the scaled norm. If $x_1=0$ put $\widehat\phi=1$; otherwise compute its modulus $\widehat a$ by its own two-component scaled norm and divide its real and imaginary parts by $\widehat a$. Set $\widehat\alpha=-\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\phi\widehat N)$ using real-scalar component multiplication, and $v=\operatorname{fl}(x-\widehat\alpha e_1)$. Compute $w$ by sequential summation of all $2r$ rounded real component squares of $v$, and $\widehat\tau=\operatorname{fl}(2/w)$. Compute $d=\operatorname{fl}(v^*B)$, $p=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau v)$, $Z=\operatorname{fl}(pd)$, and $\widehat B=\operatorname{fl}(B-Z)$. Return $C_+=[\widehat\alpha e_1\;\widehat B]$, writing exact zeros below the target diagonal, and store $v,\widehat\tau$. Its theoretical representative is $H(v)=I-2vv^*/(v^*v)$. For a separate block application omit the column overwrite. For a right step apply these instructions to the conjugate-transposed block and transpose back.

For a Givens target pair $(a,b)$, use the identity when $b=0$, including $(0,0)$. Otherwise choose $\lambda$ as the largest absolute real/imaginary component of $(a,b)$, round $z=a/\lambda$ and $w=b/\lambda$ componentwise, and compute $h$ as the norm of their four already scaled components. If $z\ne0$, compute $n_z$ as the norm of its two components, $\widehat\phi=\operatorname{fl}(z/n_z)$, $c=\operatorname{fl}(n_z/h)$ and $s=\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\phi\overline w)/h)$. If $z=0$, set $c=0$ and $s=\operatorname{fl}(\overline w/h)$. Store $T=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-\overline s&c\end{pmatrix}$ and apply it to the chosen two rows using two complex products and one rounded componentwise addition for each output entry. For an actual target column, set its intended annihilated entry to exact zero after the update. The initial shift-vector rotation is formed from the shift vector but applied to the matrix without zeroing an unrelated matrix entry. Right applications use the conjugate-transposed form. Its exact unitary representative is $Q=T/\sqrt{c^2+|s|^2}$; this normalization defines a mathematical representative and is not an additional rounded operation.

These are arithmetic realizations of the canonical Householder and Givens methods. Returned dense transformation accumulators may be rounded; the exact unitary products used in backward-error statements are represented by the stored local data. Additional discarded matrix entries must be recorded separately, including their magnitudes. Their omission is never implicit in a sparsity convention.

## Statement

Use [[alg-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-updates]] successfully, with $0<u<1$ and $(r-1)u<1$ for every Householder dimension $r$. For a nonzero Householder column define
$$e=(1+u)^{r+3}-1,\quad a_\phi=\frac{1+u}{(1-u)^4}-1,\quad a_\alpha=(1+a_\phi)(1+e)(1+u)-1,\quad d_v=a_\alpha+u(2+a_\alpha),$$
$$a_\tau=\frac{1+u}{(1-u)^{2r}}-1,\quad g=\frac{1+6u}{1-(r-1)u}-1,\quad c_U=2\bigl((1+a_\tau)(1+u)(1+6u)(1+g)-1\bigr),$$
$$\eta_H(r)=\max\{a_\alpha+8d_v,(1+u)c_U+3u\}.$$
For a Givens step define
$$a_2=\frac{1+u}{(1-u)^2}-1,\quad q=\max\left\{\left(\frac{1+u}{1-u}\right)^3-1,\frac{(1+a_2)(1+6u)(1+u)}{(1-u)^3}-1\right\},$$
$$\epsilon=\sqrt2(7u+6u^2)(1+q),\quad v=q+\epsilon,\quad \eta_G=2v+u+2q.$$
Each complete left update, including its target zero write, has an exact unitary representative $W$ and perturbation $E$ with
$$W(C+E)=C_+,\qquad \|E\|_F\le\eta\|C\|_F,$$
where $\eta=\eta_H(r)$ or $\eta_G$. Identity branches have $E=0$. The corresponding right relation follows by conjugate transposition. For a Givens application without an annihilation overwrite use the smaller coefficient $v$; for a Householder separate-block application use $(1+u)c_U+3u$. All coefficients are explicit and $O(ru)$ or $O(u)$ for fixed dimensions.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated real/complex arithmetic realization and successful no-underflow operations.

[F1] [[alg-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-updates]] fixes the scaled norm, coefficient formation, product order, zero branches and exact target writes.

[F2] [[lem-product-of-one-plus-deltas-gives-theta-n]] bounds products of rounding factors and sequential addition expansions.

## Proof

1.1 A complex product's real/imaginary error is at most $2(2u+u^2)|z||w|\le6u|z||w|$: bound each of its four real products and then its two component additions. A sequential complex dot of length $r$ therefore has error at most $[6u+\gamma_{r-1}(1+6u)]\sum_i|z_i||w_i|=g\sum_i|z_i||w_i|$. These expansions include exact zeros. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 A scaled norm with $2r$ real components has its positive squared sum multiplied termwise by between $(1-u)^{2r+2}$ and $(1+u)^{2r+2}$, including two scaling factors. Square root and rescaling give relative norm error at most $e$. The independently scaled modulus of $x_1$ has lower/upper factors $(1-u)^4,(1+u)^4$, so the phase division error relative to $x_1/|x_1|$ is at most $a_\phi$; when $x_1=0$ it is zero. Thus for $N=\|x\|$, $\alpha_0=-\operatorname{phase}(x_1)N$ and $v_0=x-\alpha_0e_1$, one has $|\widehat\alpha-\alpha_0|\le a_\alpha N$ and $\|v-v_0\|\le d_vN$. For exponents at least one the lower deviation is bounded by the upper by convexity, justifying these two-sided estimates. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The identity $H(v)^*H(v)=I$ follows by multiplying $I-2vv^*/(v^*v)$. The exact phase choice gives $H(v_0)x=\alpha_0e_1$ and $\|v_0\|\ge N$ by direct inner-product expansion. Normalization gives $\|a/\|a\|-b/\|b\|\|\le2\|a-b\|/\|b\|$; expanding the difference of unit-vector projectors therefore gives $\|H(v)-H(v_0)\|\le8d_v$. The target-column error is at most $(a_\alpha+8d_v)N$. [step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 For Givens formation at stored $z,w$, the norm $h$ has relative factors between $(1-u)^3$ and $(1+u)^3$, since its unscaled four-component squared sum has at most four rounding factors per term. The norm $n_z$ has exponents two. Let $G_0$ be the exact canonical Givens annihilator for $(z,w)$, with coefficients $c_0=|z|/\|(z,w)\|$ and $s_0=(z/|z|)\overline w/\|(z,w)\|$ when $z\ne0$. The phase error is at most $a_2$; the coefficient numerator, denominator, six-operation complex product and division errors therefore give $|c-c_0|\le q c_0$ and $|s-s_0|\le q|s_0|$. If $z=0$, $c=0$ and $s_0=\overline w/|w|$; the smaller bound $(1+u)/(1-u)^3-1\le q$ applies. Hence $\|(c,s)-(c_0,s_0)\|\le q$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The positive real sum defining $w$ has bounds $(1-u)^{2r}\|v\|^2\le w\le(1+u)^{2r}\|v\|^2$. The final division gives $|\widehat\tau\|v\|^2/2-1|\le a_\tau$. The dot-product error in step 1.1, the componentwise real multiplication by $\widehat\tau$ and the final complex multiplication bound the rank-one update error by $c_U\|B\|_F$. Final subtraction adds at most $u(3+c_U)\|B\|_F$. Combine this with step 2.1 over disjoint columns to get the Householder bound. For the zero column take the identity exactly. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Put $t=\sqrt{c^2+|s|^2}>0$ and $Q=T/t$. Direct multiplication gives $T^*T=t^2I$, so $Q$ is canonical unitary, $\|T-Q\|=|t-1|\le q$ and $\|T\|\le1+q$. Normalization also gives $\|Q-G_0\|\le2q$; differences of canonical blocks have norm equal to the Euclidean norm of their coefficient differences. Each computed output entry has error at most $(7u+6u^2)(|c||C_{1j}|+|s||C_{2j}|)$, by two products and their addition. The absolute coefficient block has norm at most $\sqrt2t$. Thus the raw update differs from $QC$ by at most $v\|C\|_F$. [step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Scaling introduced $\|\lambda(z,w)-(a,b)\|\le u\|(a,b)\|$. Because $G_0$ annihilates $(z,w)$, its exact target residual for $(a,b)$ is at most $u\|(a,b)\|$; under $Q$ it is at most $(u+2q)\|(a,b)\|$. Writing the rounded target to zero adds at most $(u+2q+v)\|(a,b)\|$ to the raw update discrepancy, so the total is at most $\eta_G\|C\|_F$. No unrelated matrix entry is zeroed for a shift-vector rotation. Identity branches have zero discrepancy. [F1, step 2.2, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 In every left case choose $E=W^*C_+-C$, with $W=H(v)$ or $Q$; unitarity gives the stated equation and equal error norm. Right updates follow by conjugate transposition and invariance of Frobenius norm. All coefficients are finite explicit functions under the stated conditions, vanish at $u=0$, and have first derivatives bounded by a fixed multiple of the active dimension, proving the asymptotics. [step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra, construct] ∎

id: lem-rounded-linear-and-normal-residual-certificates
kind: lemma
title: Rounded matrix products give certified linear and normal-equation residual allowances
status: draft

    url: https://www.seehuhn.de/publications/StuaVo08/numlinalg.pdf

## Statement

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $x\in\mathbb F^n$, $y\in\mathbb F^m$ have stored real or complex entries, with $m,n\ge1$. Use the operationwise arithmetic model, successful sequential dot products, and $0<u<1$ with $(\max(m,n)-1)u<1$. Define
$$g_k=\frac{1+6u}{1-(k-1)u}-1,\qquad F=\|A\|_F,\quad X=\|x\|_2,\quad Y=\|y\|_2.$$
For $\widehat v=\operatorname{fl}(Ax)$ and $\widehat w=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-y)$, put $V=g_nFX$ and $W=V+u(\|\widehat v\|_2+Y)$. Then
$$\|\widehat w-(Ax-y)\|_2\le W.$$
For a stored real $\lambda>0$, also compute $\widehat z=\operatorname{fl}(A^*\widehat w)$, $\widehat l=\operatorname{fl}(\lambda x)$ and $\widehat r=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat z+\widehat l)$, rounding scalar multiplication componentwise. The exact intended normal residual $r=A^*(Ax-y)+\lambda x$ satisfies
$$\|\widehat r-r\|_2\le\rho:=FW+g_mF\|\widehat w\|_2+u\lambda X+u(\|\widehat z\|_2+\|\widehat l\|_2).$$
Norms in these certificates mean exact norms or certified upper bounds. Uncontrolled rounding of the certificate itself is not authorized. The linear bound applies columnwise to certify $\|I-AB\|_2\le\|I-AB\|_F$ from stored basis-solve columns $B$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated stored inputs, evaluation order and successful operations; every nonzero exact intermediate is normal, and zero operations are exact.

[F1] [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]] specifies real component operations and six-real-operation complex multiplication.

[F2] [[lem-product-of-one-plus-deltas-gives-theta-n]] bounds sequential addition coefficient errors.

[F3] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: for real or complex Euclidean vectors, $|\langle v,w\rangle|\le\|v\|_2\|w\|_2$. Applying this rowwise gives $\|Mz\|_2\le\|M\|_F\|z\|_2$, also for $M=A^*$.

## Proof

1.1 For $(a+ib)(c+id)$, each rounded real product has error at most $u$ times its absolute exact value. Each final real addition contributes at most $u(1+u)$ times the two corresponding product magnitudes. The Euclidean norm of the resulting real/imaginary error is at most $2(2u+u^2)|a+ib||c+id|\le6u|a+ib||c+id|$, since $u<1$. Conjugation is exact. Real products obey this conservative bound as well. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 In a length-$k$ dot product, each product error from step 1.1 is propagated through at most $k-1$ additions. Expansion of each real component and [F2] bound the dot discrepancy by $[6u+\gamma_{k-1}(1+6u)]\sum_i|a_i||x_i|=g_k\sum_i|a_i||x_i|$, with $\gamma_0=0$. Combining rows and applying Cauchy-Schwarz gives $\|\widehat v-Ax\|_2\le g_nFX=V$. Componentwise subtraction has vector error at most $u(\|\widehat v\|_2+Y)$, so the linear residual allowance is $W$. Zeros cause no difficulty in this expansion. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Apply step 2.1 to $A^*\widehat w$ to get $\|\widehat z-A^*\widehat w\|_2\le g_mF\|\widehat w\|_2$. Transporting the earlier error through $A^*$ adds at most $FW$. The scalar product error is at most $u\lambda X$; the last addition adds at most $u(\|\widehat z\|_2+\|\widehat l\|_2)$. Their sum proves $\rho$. For basis columns, the triangle inequality combines each computed linear residual with its allowance; summing the squared column bounds gives a Frobenius certificate for $I-AB$, which bounds its induced Euclidean norm by Cauchy-Schwarz. [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Use $\mathbb N$ for the natural-number index set (including zero) ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $\mathbb R$ for the real scalar field ([[def-real-numbers]]), and $\mathbb C$ with its real embedding and modulus ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]).

Let $N\ge2$, $h>0$, $k>0$, and $t_n=nk$. For the finite periodic grid put $J_N=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$ and reduce every shifted index modulo $N$. A periodic grid function is a map $v:J_N\to\mathbb C$, with weighted norm
$$ \|v\|_{2,h}=\left(h\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}|v_j|^2\right)^{1/2}. $$
The infinite uniform grid has indices $j\in\mathbb Z$ and positions $x_j=jh$. On the periodic and infinite grids define
$$ (D_+v)_j=\frac{v_{j+1}-v_j}{h},\qquad (D_-v)_j=\frac{v_j-v_{j-1}}{h},\qquad (D_0v)_j=\frac{v_{j+1}-v_{j-1}}{2h},\qquad (\Delta_hv)_j=\frac{v_{j+1}-2v_j+v_{j-1}}{h^2}. $$
Use the inner product linear in its first entry,
$$ \langle p,q\rangle_{2,h}=h\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}p_j\overline{q_j},\qquad \langle D_+p,D_+q\rangle_{e,h}=h\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(D_+p)_j\overline{(D_+q)_j}, $$
where the indices in $D_+$ are reduced periodically, and set $\|D_+p\|_{e,h}^2=\langle D_+p,D_+p\rangle_{e,h}$. The same definitions apply to real-valued grid functions.

For a finite interval of length $L=Nh$, use physical nodes $x_j=jh$ with indices $j=0,\ldots,N$. On its edges $j=0,\ldots,N-1$ define $(D_+v)_j=(v_{j+1}-v_j)/h$, and on interior nodes $j=1,\ldots,N-1$ use $(\Delta_hv)_j=(v_{j+1}-2v_j+v_{j-1})/h^2$. At the right endpoint define $(D_-v)_N=(v_N-v_{N-1})/h$. The interior inner product, norm, and edge inner product are
$$ \langle p,q\rangle_h=h\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}p_j\overline{q_j},\qquad \|v\|_h^2=\langle v,v\rangle_h,\qquad \langle p,q\rangle_{e,h}=h\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(D_+p)_j\overline{(D_+q)_j}. $$
Dirichlet grid functions have prescribed endpoint values; when they are zero, the interior norm and edge inner product above are the ones used for the wave energy.

All statements below distinguish these periodic, infinite, and finite-interval index sets. Periodic Fourier calculations are not boundary estimates for the finite-interval grid.

## Definition

Use the index sets and uniform spacings of [[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]]: $x_j=jh$, $j\in\mathbb Z$, or $j$ reduced modulo $N$ in the periodic case. Fix $a>0$, $h,k>0$, and $\nu=ak/h$. The target equation is the one-dimensional constant-velocity transport equation $u_t+a u_x=0$, the constant-coefficient case of [[def-linear-transport-equation-and-its-characteristic-flow]]. Set $U_j^0=u_0(jh)$ and define, for $n\ge0$,
$$ \begin{aligned} \text{upwind: }&U_j^{n+1}=U_j^n-\nu(U_j^n-U_{j-1}^n),\\ \text{downwind: }&U_j^{n+1}=U_j^n-\nu(U_{j+1}^n-U_j^n),\\ \text{centered: }&U_j^{n+1}=U_j^n-\frac{\nu}{2}(U_{j+1}^n-U_{j-1}^n),\\ \text{Lax--Friedrichs: }&U_j^{n+1}=\frac{U_{j-1}^n+U_{j+1}^n}{2}-\frac{\nu}{2}(U_{j+1}^n-U_{j-1}^n),\\ \text{Lax--Wendroff: }&U_j^{n+1}=U_j^n-\frac{\nu}{2}(U_{j+1}^n-U_{j-1}^n)+\frac{\nu^2}{2}(U_{j+1}^n-2U_j^n+U_{j-1}^n). \end{aligned} $$
On a periodic grid, every index in these formulas is reduced modulo $N$; no physical boundary data are present. For $a<0$, reflect the stencil by $j\mapsto-j$ and replace $\nu$ by $|a|k/h$.

For a finite interval $[0,L]$ with $a>0$, the inflow boundary is $x=0$. The upwind initial/boundary rows are $U_j^0=u_0(jh)$ for $j=0,\ldots,N$, $U_0^n=g(t_n)$ with $u_0(0)=g(0)$, and
$$ U_j^{n+1}=(1-\nu)U_j^n+\nu U_{j-1}^n,\qquad j=1,\ldots,N,\quad n\ge0. $$
The outflow node $j=N$ is computed by this row and receives no prescribed value. This item supplies no finite-interval boundary closure or stability statement for centered, Lax--Friedrichs, or Lax--Wendroff updates.

## Definition

Use the uniform-grid indices, physical nodes, and spacings of [[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]]. Fix a wave speed $c>0$, an interval length $L=Nh$ with $N\ge2$, and a time step $k>0$. Write $\nu=ck/h$. The target model is the real scalar wave equation $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$, and grid states are real-valued. Prescribe a real initial displacement row $U^0$ and discrete initial-velocity row $V^0$, and set $U^1=U^0+kV^0$. For smooth Dirichlet data $u_0,u_1:[0,L]\to\mathbb R$ with $u_0(0)=u_0(L)=u_1(0)=u_1(L)=0$, the corresponding sample rows are $U_j^0=u_0(x_j)$ and $V_j^0=u_1(x_j)$; for smooth periodic data, take real $L$-periodic $u_0,u_1$ and sample them at $x_j$. In both cases the discrete initial velocity equals the sampled $u_1$. The centered leapfrog recurrence is
$$ U_j^{n+1}-2U_j^n+U_j^{n-1}=\nu^2(U_{j+1}^n-2U_j^n+U_{j-1}^n),\qquad n\ge1. $$
For the finite Dirichlet interval, require $U_0^0=U_N^0=V_0^0=V_N^0=0$ and impose the recurrence for $j=1,\ldots,N-1$, with $U_0^n=U_N^n=0$ for every $n\ge0$. For the periodic branch, use $j=0,\ldots,N-1$, reduce indices modulo $N$, and impose the recurrence at every node. Fourier analysis of this real periodic update uses its complex-linear extension to the complexified grid space. No convergence order for a particular initialization formula is asserted here.

## Statement

Let $N\ge2$, $h>0$, and let $u=(u_0,\ldots,u_N)$ and $v=(v_0,\ldots,v_N)$ be complex grid functions. With the finite-interval inner products and differences of [[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]],
$$ \langle u,-\Delta_hv\rangle_h =\langle D_+u,D_+v\rangle_{e,h}+u_0\overline{(D_+v)_0}-u_N\overline{(D_-v)_N}. $$
In particular, if $u_0=u_N=0$, the two boundary terms vanish. On the subspace of grid functions with zero endpoints, $-\Delta_h$ is self-adjoint and nonnegative in the interior grid inner product, with $\langle u,-\Delta_hu\rangle_h=\|D_+u\|_{e,h}^2$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $N\ge2$, $h>0$, and complex grid values $u_j,v_j$ on $j=0,\ldots,N$.

[F1] The interior and edge inner products and differences are defined in [[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]].

## Proof

1.1 Put $d_j=v_j-v_{j-1}$ for $j=1,\ldots,N$. Expanding the second difference gives $$ \langle u,-\Delta_hv\rangle_h=-\frac1h\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}u_j\overline{(d_{j+1}-d_j)}. $$ Shift the index in the $d_{j+1}$ sum and telescope: $$ -\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}u_j\overline{(d_{j+1}-d_j)} =\sum_{j=1}^{N}(u_j-u_{j-1})\overline{d_j}+u_0\overline{d_1}-u_N\overline{d_N}. $$ Dividing by $h$ identifies the edge sum and boundary terms in the displayed identity. [F1, algebra]

2.1 When $u_0=u_N=0$, step 1.1 reduces to $\langle u,-\Delta_hv\rangle_h=\langle D_+u,D_+v\rangle_{e,h}$. Applying this identity after exchanging $u,v$ and taking complex conjugates gives $\langle-\Delta_hu,v\rangle_h=\langle u,-\Delta_hv\rangle_h$, so $-\Delta_h$ is self-adjoint on the zero-endpoint subspace. Setting $u=v$ gives $\langle u,-\Delta_hu\rangle_h=\|D_+u\|_{e,h}^2\ge0$. [step 1.1, F1] ∎

## Statement

Let $N\ge2$, $h>0$, $L=Nh$, and let $w=(w_0,\ldots,w_N)$ be a complex grid function with $w_0=w_N=0$. Then
$$ \|w\|_h\le L\|D_+w\|_{e,h}. $$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A complex grid function $w$ on $j=0,\ldots,N$ with zero endpoint values.

[F1] The weighted interior and edge norms are those of [[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]].

## Proof

1.1 For each $1\le j\le N-1$, put $d_i=w_{i+1}-w_i$ for $i=0,\ldots,j-1$. Expanding both expressions shows $$ j\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}|d_i|^2-\left|\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}d_i\right|^2 =\sum_{0\le i<r<j}|d_i-d_r|^2, $$ since each side equals $(j-1)\sum_i|d_i|^2-\sum_{i<r}(d_i\overline{d_r}+d_r\overline{d_i})$. The right side is nonnegative. Since $w_0=0$, $w_j=\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}d_i$, so $$ |w_j|^2\le j\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}|w_{i+1}-w_i|^2 \le N\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}|w_{i+1}-w_i|^2. $$ [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Sum the step 1.1 bound over $j=1,\ldots,N-1$ and multiply by $h$. Since $(N-1)N h\le N^2h$ and $\|D_+w\|_{e,h}^2=h^{-1}\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}|w_{i+1}-w_i|^2$, we obtain $\|w\|_h^2\le N^2h^2\|D_+w\|_{e,h}^2=L^2\|D_+w\|_{e,h}^2$. Taking nonnegative square roots proves the claim. [step 1.1, F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Fix $a\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$. Let $u:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be a $C^6$ solution of $u_t+a u_x=0$ that is periodic in $x$ with period $P>0$, so $u(x+P,t)=u(x,t)$, and whose derivatives through order six are bounded. Let $h,k\to0$ with $0<c_-\le k/h\le c_+<\infty$, and put $\nu=|a|k/h$. For a stencil $S$, define its local residual by
$$ \tau_S(x,t)=\frac{u(x,t+k)-S(u(\cdot,t))(x)}{k}. $$
Then, for the sign-selected stencils of [[def-periodic-one-way-advection-schemes]], the upwind, downwind, centered, and Lax--Friedrichs residuals are $O(h)$ uniformly in $(x,t)$, while the Lax--Wendroff residual is $O(h^2)$. Here a remainder $R=O(\eta(h,k))$ uniformly means $|R(x,t;h,k)|\le C\eta(h,k)$ for all $x,t$ and sufficiently small $h,k$, with $C$ independent of $x,t,h,k$ under the stated ratio bounds. These are smooth-solution consistency statements and imply no convergence result at discontinuities.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated smooth solution, fixed nonzero speed $a$, and two-sided mesh ratio $c_-\le k/h\le c_+$.

[F1] The five periodic stencils use the stated sign convention for $a>0$ and are reflected by $j\mapsto-j$ for $a<0$, with $\nu=|a|k/h$ ([[def-periodic-one-way-advection-schemes]]).

[F2] If derivatives through order $m+1$ are bounded on the segment, the order-$m$ Taylor polynomial has a remainder bounded by the derivative bound times the corresponding power divided by $(m+1)!$ ([[cor-taylor-remainder-bound]]).

[F3] For a function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^2$, $C^6$ means that every iterated partial derivative of total order at most six exists and is continuous ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]).

[F4] For a $C^k$ function, iterated partial derivatives of order $k$ are unchanged by permuting the coordinate differentiations ([[thm-symmetry-of-higher-mixed-partials]]).

## Proof

1.1 If $a<0$, set $A=-a>0$ and $\widetilde u(x,t)=u(-x,t)$. For fixed $x$, its time difference quotient is that of $u$ at $(-x,t)$, so $\widetilde u_t(x,t)=u_t(-x,t)$. In its spatial difference quotient, substitute $s=-h$ to get $\widetilde u_x(x,t)=-u_x(-x,t)$. Repeating these coordinate calculations gives $\partial_x^p\partial_t^q\widetilde u(x,t)=(-1)^p(\partial_x^p\partial_t^q u)(-x,t)$, so the period and derivative bounds are preserved. The PDE gives $\widetilde u_t+A\widetilde u_x=u_t(-x,t)-A u_x(-x,t)=0$. The definition's reflection $j\mapsto-j$ identifies each negative-speed stencil residual with the corresponding positive-speed residual of $\widetilde u$ at the reflected point. If $a>0$, take $A=a$ and $\widetilde u=u$. It is therefore enough to derive the estimates for positive speed $A$. [given, F1, F3, construct, algebra]

2.1 For this positive-speed solution, differentiating $\widetilde u_t=-A\widetilde u_x$ in $t$ and $x$, then using [F4] to commute the order-two mixed partials, gives $\widetilde u_{tt}=-A\widetilde u_{xt}=-A\widetilde u_{tx}=A^2\widetilde u_{xx}$. Differentiating this identity in $t$ and the PDE twice in $x$, then using [F4] to commute the order-three partials, gives $\widetilde u_{ttt}=A^2\widetilde u_{xxt}=A^2\widetilde u_{txx}=-A^3\widetilde u_{xxx}$. By [F3] these derivatives exist, and the bounded derivatives in the hypotheses make the Taylor remainders uniform. Taylor's formula from [F2] yields $$ \frac{\widetilde u(x,t+k)-\widetilde u(x,t)}{k}=\widetilde u_t+\frac{k}{2}\widetilde u_{tt}+\frac{k^2}{6}\widetilde u_{ttt}+O(k^3), $$ $$ \frac{\widetilde u(x+h,t)-\widetilde u(x-h,t)}{2h}=\widetilde u_x+\frac{h^2}{6}\widetilde u_{xxx}+O(h^4),\qquad \frac{\widetilde u(x+h,t)-2\widetilde u(x,t)+\widetilde u(x-h,t)}{h^2}=\widetilde u_{xx}+\frac{h^2}{12}\widetilde u_{xxxx}+O(h^4). $$ The one-sided expansions are $(\widetilde u(x,t)-\widetilde u(x-h,t))/h=\widetilde u_x-\frac h2\widetilde u_{xx}+O(h^2)$ and $(\widetilde u(x+h,t)-\widetilde u(x,t))/h=\widetilde u_x+\frac h2\widetilde u_{xx}+O(h^2)$. [given, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Substituting the step 2.1 expansions into [F1] with speed $A=|a|$ and using $\widetilde u_t+A\widetilde u_x=0$ gives $$ \tau_{\rm up}=\frac{k}{2}\widetilde u_{tt}-\frac{Ah}{2}\widetilde u_{xx}+O(k^2+h^2),\quad \tau_{\rm down}=\frac{k}{2}\widetilde u_{tt}+\frac{Ah}{2}\widetilde u_{xx}+O(k^2+h^2),\quad \tau_{\rm centered}=\frac{k}{2}\widetilde u_{tt}+O(k^2+h^2). $$ For Lax--Friedrichs the symmetric average contributes $-h^2\widetilde u_{xx}/(2k)$ to the residual, so $\tau_{\rm LF}=\frac{k}{2}\widetilde u_{tt}-\frac{h^2}{2k}\widetilde u_{xx}+O(k^2+h^2+h^4/k)$. For Lax--Wendroff the $k\widetilde u_{tt}/2$ term cancels the second-difference term by $\widetilde u_{tt}=A^2\widetilde u_{xx}$, leaving $\tau_{\rm LW}=\frac{k^2}{6}\widetilde u_{ttt}+\frac{Ah^2}{6}\widetilde u_{xxx}+O(k^3+h^4+kh^2)$. Reflection in step 1.1 transfers these residual bounds to the negative-speed branch. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The mesh ratio bounds imply $k=O(h)$ and $h^2/k=O(h)$. Thus the first four residuals are uniformly $O(h)$, and every displayed Lax--Wendroff term is $O(h^2)$ or smaller. By step 1.1 the same estimates hold for either velocity sign. The conclusion concerns only the sampled smooth solution in the stated periodic setting. [given, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For the homogeneous Dirichlet recurrence of [[def-centered-leapfrog-wave-scheme]], let $0<\nu=ck/h<1$, $V^n=(U^{n+1}-U^n)/k$, and $\bar U^n=(U^{n+1}+U^n)/2$. Define
$$ E^{n+1/2}=\frac12\|V^n\|_h^2+\frac{c^2}{2}\langle D_+U^{n+1},D_+U^n\rangle_{e,h}. $$
Then $E^{n+1/2}$ is independent of $n$ and
$$ E^{n+1/2}\ge\frac{1-\nu^2}{2}\|V^n\|_h^2+\frac{c^2}{2}\|D_+\bar U^n\|_{e,h}^2. $$
Consequently it is a positive quadratic form on adjacent zero-boundary states. For mesh families with fixed wave speed $c>0$, fixed interval length $L$, and $\nu\le\nu_0<1$, it controls the interior state and its discrete velocity with constants independent of $h$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A fixed wave speed $c>0$, mesh sizes $h,k>0$, homogeneous Dirichlet endpoint values, and the source-free centered leapfrog recurrence.

[F1] The recurrence is $\delta_t^2U^n=c^2\Delta_hU^n$, with $U_0^n=U_N^n=0$ ([[def-centered-leapfrog-wave-scheme]]).

[F2] For zero endpoint values, $\langle u,-\Delta_hv\rangle_h=\langle D_+u,D_+v\rangle_{e,h}$; this is symmetric in $u,v$ ([[lem-dirichlet-grid-summation-by-parts]]).

[F3] If $w_0=w_N=0$ on length $L=Nh$, then $\|w\|_h\le L\|D_+w\|_{e,h}$ ([[lem-dirichlet-grid-poincare-inequality]]).

## Proof

1.1 In the quadratic term, $D_+U^{n+1}=D_+\bar U^n+\frac{k}{2}D_+V^n$ and $D_+U^n=D_+\bar U^n-\frac{k}{2}D_+V^n$. Expanding their real edge inner product gives $$ E^{n+1/2}=\frac12\|V^n\|_h^2+\frac{c^2}{2}\|D_+\bar U^n\|_{e,h}^2-\frac{c^2k^2}{8}\|D_+V^n\|_{e,h}^2. $$ [F1, algebra]

2.1 For any zero-endpoint grid function $v$, $(v_{j+1}-v_j)^2\le2v_{j+1}^2+2v_j^2$ and summing over edges gives $$ \|D_+v\|_{e,h}^2=\frac1h\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(v_{j+1}-v_j)^2\le\frac4{h^2}\|v\|_h^2. $$ Apply this to $V^n$, and use $\nu=ck/h$, in step 1.1 to obtain the asserted lower bound. Since $1-\nu^2>0$, zero energy forces $V^n=0$ and $D_+\bar U^n=0$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 A zero-endpoint grid function with $D_+w=0$ is constant across all edges and therefore zero. Hence step 2.1 shows $E^{n+1/2}=0$ only when $V^n=0$ and $\bar U^n=0$, equivalently $U^{n+1}=U^n=0$. For uniform state control, [F3] bounds $\|\bar U^n\|_h$ by $L\|D_+\bar U^n\|_{e,h}$, and $U^{n+1},U^n=\bar U^n\pm(k/2)V^n$; when $\nu\le\nu_0<1$, the lower-bound coefficients and $k\le\nu_0L/(Nc)\le\nu_0L/c$ are uniform in the mesh. [F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $\delta_t^0U^n=(U^{n+1}-U^{n-1})/(2k)$. Taking the interior inner product of $\delta_t^2U^n+c^2(-\Delta_h)U^n=0$ with $\delta_t^0U^n$, the first term is $(\|V^n\|_h^2-\|V^{n-1}\|_h^2)/(2k)$. By [F2], the second is $$ \frac{c^2}{2k}\left(\langle D_+U^{n+1},D_+U^n\rangle_{e,h}-\langle D_+U^n,D_+U^{n-1}\rangle_{e,h}\right). $$ Their sum is $(E^{n+1/2}-E^{n-1/2})/k=0$. Thus the energy is conserved. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

On an $N$-point periodic grid let $z_\ell=\exp(2\pi i\ell/N)$, $C_\ell=\operatorname{Re}z_\ell$, $S_\ell=\operatorname{Im}z_\ell$, and $\nu=ak/h$ with $a>0$. The Fourier vector $j\mapsto z_\ell^j$ is multiplied in one step by
$$ g_{\rm up}=1-\nu+\nu z_\ell^{-1},\quad g_{\rm down}=1+\nu-\nu z_\ell,\quad g_{\rm centered}=1-i\nu S_\ell,\quad g_{\rm LF}=C_\ell-i\nu S_\ell,\quad g_{\rm LW}=1-\nu^2(1-C_\ell)-i\nu S_\ell. $$
Their squared moduli, in the same order, are
$$ 1-2\nu(1-\nu)(1-C_\ell),\quad 1+2\nu(1+\nu)(1-C_\ell),\quad 1+\nu^2S_\ell^2,\quad 1-(1-\nu^2)S_\ell^2,\quad 1-\nu^2(1-\nu^2)(1-C_\ell)^2. $$
The $N$ Fourier vectors form an orthogonal basis under the periodic inner product of [[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]], and each has squared norm $Nh$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $N\ge2$, $a,h,k>0$, and the periodic stencils of [[def-periodic-one-way-advection-schemes]].

[F1] The five one-step formulas and periodic wrap are defined in [[def-periodic-one-way-advection-schemes]].

[F2] The finite root-of-unity sum $\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\exp(2\pi i(\ell-r)j/N)$ equals $N$ if $\ell\equiv r\pmod N$ and $0$ otherwise ([[lem-orthogonality-of-characters-on-a-finite-cyclic-group]]).

[F3] The displayed periodic Fourier modes form a basis of the complexified grid space ([[lem-periodic-heat-difference-amplification-symbol]]).

[F4] For complex numbers, $\bar z=\operatorname{Re}z-i\operatorname{Im}z$ and $z\bar z=|z|^2$; conjugation is multiplicative and modulus obeys the field laws ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

[F5] The periodic grid inner product and norm are $\langle p,q\rangle_{2,h}=h\sum_jp_j\overline{q_j}$ and $\|p\|_{2,h}^2=h\sum_j|p_j|^2$ ([[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]]).

## Proof

1.1 Write $\phi_j=z_\ell^j$. Then $\phi_{j+1}=z_\ell\phi_j$, $\phi_{j-1}=z_\ell^{-1}\phi_j$, and $z_\ell^{-1}=\bar z_\ell$. Substitution into each update in [F1] gives, respectively, $$ 1-\nu+\nu z_\ell^{-1},\quad 1+\nu-\nu z_\ell,\quad 1-\frac{\nu}{2}(z_\ell-z_\ell^{-1}),\quad \frac{z_\ell+z_\ell^{-1}}2-\frac{\nu}{2}(z_\ell-z_\ell^{-1}),\quad 1-\frac{\nu}{2}(z_\ell-z_\ell^{-1})+\frac{\nu^2}{2}(z_\ell+z_\ell^{-1}-2). $$ Since $z_\ell^{-1}=C_\ell-iS_\ell$, these are the displayed factors. [F1, F4, algebra]

2.1 The identity $|z_\ell|=1$ gives $C_\ell^2+S_\ell^2=1$. Multiplying each factor in step 1.1 by its conjugate and simplifying with this identity gives the five displayed squared-modulus formulas. [F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F2] the distinct Fourier modes are mutually orthogonal; by [F3] they form a basis. By [F5], each has squared norm $Nh$, so the normalized modes are an orthonormal basis. Every update is diagonal in this basis with the factors from step 1.1, which therefore describe the full periodic updates. [F2, F3, F5, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

On a periodic grid of length $L=Nh$, let $\nu=ck/h>0$, $V^0=(U^1-U^0)/k$, and write $U^n=\sum_{\ell=0}^{N-1}w_\ell^n\phi_\ell$ in the discrete Fourier basis; write $\widehat V_\ell^0$ for the coefficient of $V^0$ in the same basis. Then
$$ w_\ell^{n+1}-2(1-2\nu^2s_\ell)w_\ell^n+w_\ell^{n-1}=0,\qquad s_\ell=\sin^2(\pi\ell/N). $$
For $0<\nu\le\nu_0<1$, the nonconstant roots are distinct and have modulus one, and
$$ \|U^n\|_{2,h}\le\left(1+\frac{\nu_0}{\sqrt{1-\nu_0^2}}\right)\|U^0\|_{2,h}+t_n\|V^0\|_{2,h}. $$
The mean mode is $w_0^n=w_0^0+t_n\widehat V_0^0$. At $\nu=1$ and even $N$, the Nyquist mode has the repeated root $-1$ and solution $w_{N/2}^n=(-1)^n(A+nB)$, where $B=0$ exactly when $w_{N/2}^1=-w_{N/2}^0$. Thus arbitrary starting pairs do not have a uniform endpoint power bound.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $N\ge2$, fixed $L=Nh$, $c,h,k>0$, and the periodic centered leapfrog scheme.

[F1] The periodic branch obeys $U_j^{n+1}-2U_j^n+U_j^{n-1}=\nu^2(U_{j+1}^n-2U_j^n+U_{j-1}^n)$ ([[def-centered-leapfrog-wave-scheme]]).

[F2] The one-dimensional specialization of the periodic heat symbol lemma with unit diffusivity gives $-\Delta_h\phi_\ell=4h^{-2}s_\ell\phi_\ell$ ([[lem-periodic-heat-difference-amplification-symbol]]).

[F3] The displayed periodic Fourier modes form a basis of the complexified grid space ([[lem-periodic-heat-difference-amplification-symbol]]).

[F4] The finite root-of-unity sum gives orthogonality of distinct periodic Fourier modes ([[lem-orthogonality-of-characters-on-a-finite-cyclic-group]]).

[F5] Complex conjugation and modulus have their coordinate, multiplication, and triangle laws ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

[F6] The periodic grid norm is $\|v\|_{2,h}^2=h\sum_j|v_j|^2$ ([[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]]).

## Proof

1.1 Substituting one mode from [F2] into [F1] uses $-\Delta_h\phi_\ell=4h^{-2}s_\ell\phi_\ell$ and gives the displayed scalar recurrence, whose characteristic polynomial is $$ p_\ell(r)=r^2-2(1-2\nu^2s_\ell)r+1. $$ [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 For $\ell=0$, $s_0=0$, so successive first differences are constant and $w_0^n=w_0^0+n(w_0^1-w_0^0)=w_0^0+t_n\widehat V_0^0$. For $\ell\ne0$ and $\nu<1$, put $q=1-2\nu^2s_\ell$; then $-1<q<1$, and $\rho=q+i\sqrt{1-q^2}$ and $\bar\rho$ are distinct roots with modulus one. [F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For a nonconstant mode the recurrence solution matching $w_\ell^0,w_\ell^1$ is $$ w_\ell^n=w_\ell^0\frac{\rho^n+\bar\rho^n}{2}+(w_\ell^1-qw_\ell^0)\frac{\rho^n-\bar\rho^n}{\rho-\bar\rho}. $$ Indeed both sequences solve the recurrence and the right side equals $w_\ell^0,w_\ell^1$ at $n=0,1$. The quotient is $\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\rho^{n-1-r}\bar\rho^r$, so its modulus is at most $n$. Also $|(\rho^n-\bar\rho^n)/(\rho-\bar\rho)|\le1/\sqrt{1-q^2}$ since $|\rho^n-\bar\rho^n|\le2$ and $|\rho-\bar\rho|=2\sqrt{1-q^2}$. [step 1.1, F5, algebra]

3.1 Since $w_\ell^1-qw_\ell^0=k\widehat V_\ell^0+(1-q)w_\ell^0$ and $$ \frac{1-q}{\sqrt{1-q^2}}=\frac{\nu\sqrt{s_\ell}}{\sqrt{1-\nu^2s_\ell}}\le\frac{\nu_0}{\sqrt{1-\nu_0^2}}, $$ step 2.2 gives $|w_\ell^n|\le(1+\nu_0/\sqrt{1-\nu_0^2})|w_\ell^0|+t_n|\widehat V_\ell^0|$. The same bound holds for the mean mode. [F2, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The modes are a basis by [F3] and orthogonal by [F4]. By [F6], each has squared norm $Nh$, so Parseval's identity holds in $\|\cdot\|_{2,h}$. Squaring the coefficient bounds, summing, and using $$ \left(\sum_\ell a_\ell b_\ell\right)^2\le\left(\sum_\ell a_\ell^2\right)\left(\sum_\ell b_\ell^2\right), $$ which follows by expanding $\sum_{\ell<r}(a_\ell b_r-a_rb_\ell)^2\ge0$, yields the stated weighted-grid norm estimate. [F3, F4, F5, F6, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If $\nu=1$, $N$ is even, and $\ell=N/2$, then $s_\ell=1$ and $p_\ell(r)=(r+1)^2$. Its solutions are $(-1)^n(A+nB)$; the initial values give $B=-w_\ell^1-w_\ell^0$, so $B=0$ exactly when $w_\ell^1=-w_\ell^0$. For $B\ne0$ the mode grows linearly in $n$, proving the endpoint caveat. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For the periodic schemes of [[def-periodic-one-way-advection-schemes]] with $a>0$, upwind powers are contractions in $\|\cdot\|_{2,h}$ for $0\le\nu\le1$ and grow for $\nu>1$. Lax--Friedrichs and Lax--Wendroff powers are contractions for $|\nu|\le1$; when $|\nu|>1$, Lax--Wendroff grows for $N\ge2$ and Lax--Friedrichs grows for $N\ge3$ (the $N=2$ Lax--Friedrichs stencil aliases its nonconstant mode). Downwind powers grow for every $\nu>0$ and $N\ge2$. Centered powers grow for every $\nu\ne0$ when $N\ge3$, while the $N=2$ centered stencil aliases to the identity. Reflection gives the same assertions for $a<0$ with $|\nu|$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite periodic grid with $N\ge2$, fixed $a>0$, $h,k>0$, and the exact amplification formulas.

[F1] The $N$ periodic Fourier vectors form an orthogonal basis ([[lem-periodic-advection-amplification-symbols]]).

[F2] The five amplification factors and squared moduli are those of [[lem-periodic-advection-amplification-symbols]].

[F3] The five periodic updates and their indexing are defined in [[def-periodic-one-way-advection-schemes]].

[F4] For a bounded linear map, its operator norm is the supremum of $\|Tx\|$ over the unit ball ([[def-operator-norm]]).

[F5] For $z=C+iS$ with $|z|=1$, one has $C^2+S^2=1$ and hence $1-C\ge0$, $0\le S^2\le1$; complex conjugation and modulus obey their field laws ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

## Proof

1.1 By [F5], $1-C_\ell\ge0$ and $0\le S_\ell^2\le1$. Thus for $0\le\nu\le1$, the upwind formula gives $|g_{\rm up}|^2\le1$; for $|\nu|\le1$, the Lax--Friedrichs formula gives $|g_{\rm LF}|^2\le1$, and the Lax--Wendroff formula gives $|g_{\rm LW}|^2\le1$. [F2, F3, F5, algebra]

1.2 If $\nu>1$, every nonconstant mode has $C_\ell<1$, so $|g_{\rm up}|^2=1+2\nu(\nu-1)(1-C_\ell)>1$. If $|\nu|>1$ and $N\ge2$, the Lax--Wendroff mode $\ell=1$ has $C_\ell<1$ and $|g_{\rm LW}|^2=1+\nu^2(\nu^2-1)(1-C_\ell)^2>1$. For Lax--Friedrichs with $|\nu|>1$ and $N\ge3$, some mode has $S_\ell\ne0$, so $|g_{\rm LF}|^2=1+(\nu^2-1)S_\ell^2>1$. Downwind has $|g_{\rm down}|^2>1$ for each nonconstant mode whenever $\nu>0$. Centered has $|g_{\rm centered}|^2>1$ on any mode with $S_\ell\ne0$, which exists exactly when $N\ge3$. [F2, F3, F5, algebra]

2.1 Write an arbitrary vector as $v=\sum_\ell c_\ell\psi_\ell$ in the orthonormal Fourier basis [F1]. The $m$-step update sends it to $\sum_\ell c_\ell g_\ell^m\psi_\ell$, so $\|T^mv\|_{2,h}^2=\sum_\ell|c_\ell|^2|g_\ell|^{2m}\le(\max_\ell|g_\ell|^m)^2\|v\|_{2,h}^2$. ## Statement

Fix $a,T>0$. The following two claims hold.

**Strict domain-of-dependence obstruction.** Suppose $h_m,k_m\to0$ and along a subsequence $ak_m/h_m\ge1+\varepsilon$ for some fixed $\varepsilon>0$, and put $R=aT\varepsilon/(4(1+\varepsilon))$. Consider any homogeneous linear nearest-neighbor explicit update on the infinite grid whose value after $n$ steps depends only on initial indices $j-n,\ldots,j+n$. Fix a real-valued datum $u_0\in C_c^\infty((-R,R);\mathbb R)$ with $u_0(0)=1$ and initialize each mesh by $U_j^0=u_0(jh_m)$. The exact samples $u_0(jh_m-at_m)$ and numerical values fail to converge in the sampled maximum error
$$\sup_{j\in\mathbb Z}|U_j^{n_m}-u_0(jh_m-at_m)|$$
at $t_m=n_mk_m\to T$, where $n_m=\lfloor T/k_m\rfloor$.

**CFL insufficiency for centered advection.** For any fixed period $P>0$, set $N_q=4q$, $h_q=P/N_q$, and $k_q=h_q/(2a)$ for $q\ge1$. Let $Q_q$ be the centered advection update on this periodic grid and $r_q=\lfloor T/k_q\rfloor$. Then $0<ak_q/h_q=1/2<1$, but
$$\max_{\substack{r\in\mathbb N\\0\le r k_q\le T}}\|Q_q^r\|_{2,h_q\to2,h_q}\ge\|Q_q^{r_q}\|_{2,h_q\to2,h_q}\ge(\sqrt5/2)^{r_q}\longrightarrow\infty.$$
Thus a fixed strict violation of $ak/h\le1$ prevents convergence for the nearest-neighbor family, while the domain-of-dependence bound does not suffice for uniform finite-time power stability of every periodic nearest-neighbor scheme.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Fixed $a,T>0$; for the first claim, an infinite-grid homogeneous linear nearest-neighbor update and a mesh subsequence with $ak/h\ge1+\varepsilon$; and, independently, for the second claim, the fixed-period centered periodic family with $N_q=4q$.

[F1] The centered advection stencil in [[def-periodic-one-way-advection-schemes]] is a homogeneous explicit nearest-neighbor update.

[F2] For a real-valued $C^1$ function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^2$, the first coordinate partial derivatives exist and are continuous; a classical solution on a neighborhood of a characteristic segment is continuous on that segment ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]).

[F3] Finite induction on the natural-number step count is valid ([[thm-induction-principle]]).

[F4] There is a real cutoff $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $\chi=1$ for $|x|\le1$ and $\chi=0$ for $|x|\ge2$ ([[lem-schwartz-cutoffs-from-the-standard-smooth-step]]).

[F5] For constant velocity $a$, the characteristic ODE is $X'(s)=a$ with terminal value $X(t)=x$, and the transport equation is $u_t+a u_x=0$ ([[def-linear-transport-equation-and-its-characteristic-flow]]).

[F6] A real differentiable function with zero derivative on an interval is constant there, by the mean value theorem ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

[F7] For every real $y$ there is a unique integer $m=\lfloor y\rfloor$ with $m\le y<m+1$ ([[lem-integer-part]]).

[F8] For an open interval $I$, $C_c^\infty(I;\mathbb C)$ consists of smooth functions whose support is a compact subset of $I$; its real-valued functions form the real test-function subspace ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).

[F9] On a periodic grid, the centered advection factor is $g_{\rm centered}=1-i\nu S_\ell$, where $z_\ell=e^{2\pi i\ell/N}$ and $S_\ell=\operatorname{Im}z_\ell$; the modes form an orthogonal basis ([[lem-periodic-advection-amplification-symbols]]).

[F10] The operator norm is the supremum of $\|Qv\|$ over the unit ball in the given norm ([[def-operator-norm]]).

[F11] The periodic grid has indices modulo $N$ and norm $\|v\|_{2,h}^2=h\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}|v_j|^2$ ([[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]]).

## Proof

1.1 Put $R=aT\varepsilon/(4(1+\varepsilon))$ and take $\chi$ from [F4]. Set $u_0(x)=\chi(3x/R)$. Then $u_0$ is smooth, equals $1$ at zero, and is supported in $[-2R/3,2R/3]$, a compact subset of $(-R,R)$; by [F8] it is an admissible real-valued datum. [given, F4, F8, algebra]

1.2 By finite induction [F3], the value at index $j$ after zero steps depends only on $j$. If every value after $n$ steps depends only on initial indices $j-n,\ldots,j+n$, then the next update reads indices $j-1,j,j+1$ at time $n$, whose initial dependence intervals have union $[j-(n+1),j+(n+1)]$. Thus after $n$ steps only initial indices $j-n,\ldots,j+n$ can affect the value. [given, F3, induction]

2.1 Along the violating subsequence put $n_m=\lfloor T/k_m\rfloor$ and $j_m=\lfloor aT/h_m+1/2\rfloor$. By [F7], $j_m\le aT/h_m+1/2<j_m+1$, so $|j_mh_m-aT|\le h_m/2$. Since $n_mh_m\le T h_m/k_m\le aT/(1+\varepsilon)$, the left edge of the numerical dependence interval obeys $$ j_mh_m-n_mh_m\ge\frac{aT\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}-\frac{h_m}{2}. $$ For all sufficiently large $m$, this exceeds $R$. Hence every sampled initial value on which $U_{j_m}^{n_m}$ depends is zero, so $U_{j_m}^{n_m}=0$. [given, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The constant-velocity characteristic is $X(s;t,x)=x+a(s-t)$: it has derivative $a$ and terminal value $x$, and any other solution agrees by [F6] applied to its difference from $X$.
The explicit function $u^*(y,s)=u_0(y-as)$ has partial derivatives $u^*_y=u_0'(y-as)$ and $u^*_s=-a u_0'(y-as)$ by one-variable difference quotients, so it solves $u_t+a u_x=0$ with initial data $u_0$.
To verify uniqueness, let $u$ be any classical solution on an open neighborhood of this characteristic segment with the same initial data, fix $(x,t)$, and set $v(s)=u(x+a(s-t),s)$ on $[0,t]$.
For interior $s$ and small nonzero $\delta$ whose coordinate segments remain in the solution domain, applying [F6] separately in the first and second coordinates gives $$\frac{v(s+\delta)-v(s)}{\delta}=a u_x(\xi_\delta,s+\delta)+u_t(x+a(s-t),\eta_\delta),$$ where $\xi_\delta$ lies between $x+a(s-t)$ and $x+a(s+\delta-t)$, and $\eta_\delta$ lies between $s$ and $s+\delta$.
As $\delta\to0$, these intermediate points tend to $(x+a(s-t),s)$, so continuity of the partials in [F2] yields $v'(s)=a u_x(x+a(s-t),s)+u_t(x+a(s-t),s)=0$.
Then [F6] makes $v$ constant, hence $u(x,t)=u_0(x-at)$. Since $0\le T-n_mk_m<k_m$ and $k_m\to0$, the exact characteristic foot $j_mh_m-a n_mk_m$ tends to $aT-aT=0$. By continuity and $u_0(0)=1$, the exact sample tends to $1$, while step 2.1 gives numerical value zero. Thus the sampled maximum error does not tend to zero. [F2, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For the separate centered-family claim, fix $P>0$ and use $N_q=4q$, $h_q=P/(4q)$, $k_q=h_q/(2a)$, and $r_q=\lfloor T/k_q\rfloor$. Then [F1] gives the centered update with $ak_q/h_q=1/2$, and the Fourier index $\ell=q$ is admissible with $z_\ell=\exp(2\pi i q/(4q))=i$. By [F9] its multiplier is $g=1-i/2$, so $|g|=\sqrt5/2>1$. Repeated application gives $Q_q^{r_q}\phi_q=g^{r_q}\phi_q$. The mode is nonzero, and the finite Fourier basis in [F9] diagonalizes $Q_q^{r_q}$ with finitely many finite multipliers, so this operator is bounded. By [F10] its norm is at least $|g|^{r_q}$. Since [F7] gives $r_q\ge T/k_q-1=8aTq/P-1\to\infty$, these norms are unbounded while all time levels satisfy $r_qk_q\le T$. Thus the domain-of-dependence bound is not sufficient for uniform finite-time power stability. [given, F1, F7, F9, F10, F11, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $N$ be even and consider the periodic centered leapfrog wave scheme. At $\nu=1$, its Nyquist mode has a repeated root $-1$ and admits linear-in-time growth unless the starting coefficient satisfies $w^1=-w^0$. The usual modified quadratic energy is semidefinite there and is indefinite for $\nu>1$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An even periodic grid of real-valued states, $\nu=ck/h>0$, and a Nyquist mode $\phi_{N/2}(j)=(-1)^j$.

[F1] The periodic wave recurrence is defined in [[def-centered-leapfrog-wave-scheme]].

[F2] At $\nu=1$ and even $N$, the periodic wave theorem gives the Nyquist root and compatibility condition ([[thm-periodic-centered-wave-amplification-and-endpoint]]).

[F3] The one-dimensional heat symbol with unit diffusivity gives $-\Delta_h\phi_\ell=4h^{-2}s_\ell\phi_\ell$ ([[lem-periodic-heat-difference-amplification-symbol]]).

[F4] The finite root-of-unity sum gives orthogonality of distinct Fourier modes ([[lem-orthogonality-of-characters-on-a-finite-cyclic-group]]).

[F5] The periodic grid norm is $\|v\|_{2,h}^2=h\sum_j|v_j|^2$ ([[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]]).

[F6] The periodic forward-difference inner product is $\langle D_+p,D_+q\rangle_{e,h}=h\sum_j(D_+p)_j\overline{(D_+q)_j}$ ([[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]]).

## Verification

1.1 For the Nyquist mode, $s_{N/2}=1$, so the recurrence polynomial is $r^2-2(1-2\nu^2)r+1$. At $\nu=1$ this is $(r+1)^2$, with solution $w_n=(-1)^n(A+nB)$; the coefficient $B$ vanishes exactly when $w^1=-w^0$. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 If $\nu>1$, then $q=1-2\nu^2<-1$. The roots of $r^2-2qr+1$ are real and negative because the discriminant is $4(q^2-1)>0$, their product is $1$, and their sum is $2q<-2$. Hence one root has modulus greater than one. [F1, algebra]

1.3 Define the periodic modified energy of adjacent states $X=U^n$, $Y=U^{n+1}$ by $$ \mathcal E_{\rm per}(Y,X)=\frac{1}{2k^2}\|Y-X\|_{2,h}^2+\frac{c^2}{2}\operatorname{Re}\langle D_+Y,D_+X\rangle_{e,h}. $$ For one normalized Fourier mode $\psi_\ell=\phi_\ell/\sqrt L$ with coefficients $x,y$, put $m=(x+y)/2$ and $v=(y-x)/k$. Reindexing the finite periodic sum gives $\langle D_+p,D_+q\rangle_{e,h}=\langle-\Delta_hp,q\rangle_{2,h}$. Thus [F3] gives $\|D_+\psi_\ell\|_{e,h}^2=4h^{-2}s_\ell$, while [F4] gives orthogonality; the $N$ nonzero orthogonal vectors form a basis of the $N$-dimensional space $\mathbb C^{J_N}$. By [F5] they are normalized by $\sqrt L$. Since $x=m-kv/2$ and $y=m+kv/2$, $\operatorname{Re}(y\overline{x})=|m|^2-k^2|v|^2/4$. Summing these diagonal contributions using [F6] gives the modal energy $$ \frac12(1-\nu^2s_\ell)|v|^2+2c^2h^{-2}s_\ell|m|^2. $$ At $\nu=1$, $0\le s_\ell\le1$, so every modal term is nonnegative, while the Nyquist velocity coefficient is zero. Orthogonal Fourier decomposition makes $\mathcal E_{\rm per}$ semidefinite. [F3, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

1.4 Set the real amplitude $A=1$ and take $X=A\phi_{N/2}$ and $Y=-X$. Then $X\ne0$, $\|Y-X\|^2=4\|X\|^2$, and $\langle D_+Y,D_+X\rangle_{e,h}=-4h^{-2}\|X\|^2$, so $$ \mathcal E_{\rm per}(-X,X)=\frac{2}{k^2}(1-\nu^2)\|X\|_{2,h}^2. $$ It is zero at $\nu=1$ and negative at $\nu>1$. [F3, F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 The state $(Y,X)=(0,X)$ has $\mathcal E_{\rm per}(0,X)=\|X\|_{2,h}^2/(2k^2)>0$. Together with step 1.4, this shows that the form is indefinite for $\nu>1$. [F5, step 1.4, algebra] ∎

## Example

On a four-point periodic grid take $\nu=1/2$ and the Fourier mode $z=i$. Its upwind multiplier has modulus $1/\sqrt2$, while its downwind multiplier has modulus $\sqrt{5/2}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $N=4$, $z=\exp(2\pi i/4)=i$, and $\nu=1/2$.

[F1] The upwind and downwind factors are $1-\nu+\nu z^{-1}$ and $1+\nu-\nu z$ ([[lem-periodic-advection-amplification-symbols]]).

[F2] A Fourier multiplier of modulus less than one decays under powers, while a multiplier of modulus greater than one grows under powers ([[thm-periodic-advection-power-stability]]).

## Verification

1.1 Since $z^{-1}=-i$, the upwind factor is $(1-i)/2$, whose squared modulus is $((1)^2+(-1)^2)/4=1/2$. [F1, algebra]

1.2 The downwind factor is $3/2-i/2$, whose squared modulus is $(9+1)/4=5/2$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Taking powers multiplies this mode by the corresponding factor to the same power. Thus the upwind component decays and the downwind component grows geometrically. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

For periodic upwind updates at fixed $0<\nu<1$, every individual grid family is power stable in its grid norm. The family on the varying spaces $\mathbb C^N$ is not, as stated, an instance of the common-space Lax theorem.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The periodic upwind updates on $G_N=\mathbb C^N$ for varying $N$, with fixed $0<\nu<1$.

[F1] A common-space time-scheme family consists of bounded maps $S_\nu:X\to X$ on one Banach space $X$ ([[def-common-space-linear-scheme-interface]]).

[F2] Consistency, stability, and convergence in that interface use the same norm of $X$ ([[def-common-space-linear-scheme-interface]]).

[F3] Under Dependent Choice, a consistent scheme in that common-space interface is convergent on finite time intervals if and only if it is stable there ([[thm-lax-equivalence-for-common-banach-space-schemes]]).

## Statement

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, and suppose $f$ has derivatives through order $n+1$ on the closed interval between $a$ and $x$, with the usual endpoint continuity. If $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ throughout that interval, then
$$|R_{n,a}f(x)|\le \frac{M}{\iota((n+1)!)}|x-a|^{n+1}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated regularity and derivative bound.

[L1] The Lagrange remainder formula is [[cor-taylor-lagrange-and-cauchy-remainders]].

[L2] Absolute value respects products and powers ([[lem-of-abs-value]]), and factorials are positive ([[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]], [[def-canonical-natural]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $x=a$, then $R_{n,a}f(a)=0$, so the estimate is immediate. If $x\ne a$, [L1] gives $$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{\iota((n+1)!)}(x-a)^{n+1}$$ for some point $\xi$ strictly between $a$ and $x$.  [L1]

2.1 In the case $x\ne a$, take absolute values in step 1.1, use $|f^{(n+1)}(\xi)|\le M$, and divide by the positive factorial. Together with the case $x=a$, this proves the estimate.  [step 1.1, L2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

## Statement

Let $k\ge2$. If $f\in C^k(U)$ for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, then every iterated derivative of $f$ of order $k$ is unchanged by any permutation of its coordinate differentiations.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A $C^k$ scalar field on $U$ and a word of $k$ coordinate indices.

[L1] Adjacent second coordinate derivatives commute under the $C^2$ hypotheses ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]).

[L2] A $C^k$ field has every *ordered* iterated partial derivative through length $k$, continuously on $U$ ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** induction.

1.1 Label the $k$ differentiation positions and count inversions of a permutation of these labels. A permutation with zero inversions is the identity, so it leaves the derivative unchanged. [base, algebra]

1.2 Assume every reordering with at most $n$ inversions leaves the derivative unchanged. [ih]

2.1 A reordering with $n+1$ inversions has an adjacent inverted pair; exchanging that pair reduces its inversion count by one. If that pair occupies positions $r,r+1$ in the sequence of differentiation operations, first apply only the operations in positions $1,\ldots,r-1$ and call the resulting field $g$. Every ordered partial of $g$ through order two is an ordered partial of $f$ of length at most $k$, hence is continuous by [L2]; thus $g\in C^2(U)$ and [L1] swaps precisely the operations in positions $r,r+1$. Apply the remaining outer operations in positions $r+2,\ldots,k$ to this equality; their existence is again supplied by [L2]. [step 1.2, L1, L2, algebra]

3.1 The induction hypothesis applies after the swap in step 2.1, so the original reordering leaves the derivative unchanged. Induction on inversion number proves the claim for every finite permutation. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, discharge-induction] ∎

## Statement

Let $N\ge1$ and let $k,\ell\in\mathbb Z$. Then

$$\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)x/N}=\begin{cases}N,&k\equiv\ell\pmod N,\\\\ 0,&k\not\equiv\ell\pmod N.\end{cases}$$

At $N=1$ the congruence holds for all $k,\ell$ and the sum is $1$. The sum is the finite sum of the complex family $x\mapsto e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)x/N}$ over the von Neumann natural $N=\{0,\dots,N-1\}$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]), and $N$ on the right is the natural number $N$ read in $\mathbb C$ as the additive multiple $N\cdot1_{\mathbb C}$, that is, the value at $N$ of the canonical embedding $\mathbb N\to\mathbb C$ ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-integer-multiples-agree-with-canonical-natural]]).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural number $N\ge1$, integers $k,\ell$, the complex number $\omega:=e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)/N}$, the partial sums $S_n:=\sum_{x<n}\omega^x$ for $n\in\mathbb N$, and $S:=S_N$.

[F1] $k\equiv\ell\pmod N$ means $N\mid(k-\ell)$, that is, $k-\ell=Nm$ for some integer $m$; the relation is an equivalence relation and is defined for every integer modulus, including $N\ge1$ ([[def-congruence-modulo-an-integer]], [[lem-congruence-is-an-equivalence-relation]]).

[F2] For complex $z,w$: $\exp z=1$ exactly when $z\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$, and $\exp z=\exp w$ exactly when $z-w\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]], [[def-complex-exponential]]).

[L1] $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\,\exp w$ for all complex $z,w$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]]).

[L2] A finite sum in a commutative monoid is computed from any enumeration of its finite index set and does not depend on it; it is unchanged by reindexing along a bijection, additive over disjoint splittings, and subject to the finite Fubini rule ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]], [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]]).

[L3] Powers in $\mathbb C$: $\omega^0=1$ and $\omega^{n+1}=\omega^n\omega$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-complex-integer-powers]]), and $\omega^{m+n}=\omega^m\omega^n$ for all naturals $m,n$ ([[lem-power-laws]], claim 1). Induction is available ([[thm-induction-principle]]).

[L4] Additive natural powers: in the additive group of $\mathbb C$, the element $N\cdot1_{\mathbb C}$ defined by $0\cdot1_{\mathbb C}=0$ and $\sigma(n)\cdot1_{\mathbb C}=n\cdot1_{\mathbb C}+1_{\mathbb C}$ equals the image of the natural number $N$ under the canonical embedding $\mathbb N\to\mathbb C$ ([[def-group-power]] read additively, [[lem-integer-multiples-agree-with-canonical-natural]]).

[L5] Field laws of $\mathbb C$: multiplication is associative and commutative and distributes over addition, every nonzero element has an inverse, and $1\ne0$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** cases.

1.1 The summands are the powers of $\omega$: $e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)x/N}=\omega^{x}$ for every $x\in\mathbb N$. Indeed, for $x=0$ both sides are $1$ by [F2] (as $0\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$) and [L3]; and if the identity holds at $x$, then the addition law [L1] and the power recursion [L3] give $e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)(x+1)/N}=e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)x/N}e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)/N}=\omega^{x}\omega=\omega^{x+1}$, so induction [L3] proves it for every $x$. Consequently $S=\sum_{x<N}\omega^{x}$ by [L2], since the finite sum depends only on the listed values. [F2, L1, L2, L3, given]

1.2 The geometric identity: $(1-\omega)S_n=1-\omega^{n}$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$. For $n=0$ the sum $S_0$ is empty, hence $0$ by [L2], and $1-\omega^{0}=0$ by [L3]. If the identity holds at $n$, then $S_{n+1}=S_n+\omega^{n}$ by the recursion clause of [L2], so distributivity [L5] gives $(1-\omega)S_{n+1}=(1-\omega)S_n+(1-\omega)\omega^{n}=(1-\omega^{n})+(\omega^{n}-\omega^{n}\omega)=1-\omega^{n+1}$, using the hypothesis, distributivity, associativity and the power recursion [L3]. Induction [L3] gives the identity at every $n$. [L2, L3, L5, given]

2.1 The two alternatives for $\omega$: $\omega=1$ exactly when $k\equiv\ell\pmod N$, and $\omega^{N}=1$ always. For the first, [F2] gives $\omega=1\iff 2\pi i(k-\ell)/N\in2\pi i\mathbb Z\iff(k-\ell)/N\in\mathbb Z\iff N\mid(k-\ell)\iff k\equiv\ell\pmod N$ by [F1]; for the second, $e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)}=1$ by [F2] because $2\pi i(k-\ell)\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$, and step 1.1 identifies $e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)}$ with $\omega^{N}$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

2.2 Case $k\equiv\ell\pmod N$: then $k-\ell=Nm$ for some integer $m$ by [F1], so every exponent $2\pi i(k-\ell)x/N=2\pi imx$ lies in $2\pi i\mathbb Z$ and every summand $\omega^{x}$ equals $1$ by step 1.1 and [F2]. The sum therefore consists of $N$ copies of $1_{\mathbb C}$, and the recursion clause of [L2] computes it as the additive natural power $N\cdot1_{\mathbb C}$ of [L4]. In particular at $N=1$, where every pair $k,\ell$ is congruent, the sum is the single term $1$, the image of the natural number $1$ under the canonical embedding. [assume-case congruent, F1, F2, step 1.1, L2, L4, given]

3.1 Case $k\not\equiv\ell\pmod N$: then $\omega\ne1$ and $\omega^{N}=1$ by step 2.1, so the geometric identity of step 1.2 at $n=N$ gives $(1-\omega)S=1-\omega^{N}=0$. Since $1-\omega\ne0$, the field laws [L5] give $S=(1-\omega)^{-1}\cdot0=0$. [assume-case noncongruent, step 1.2, step 2.1, L5]

4.1 The alternatives of [F1] are exhaustive and mutually exclusive, so steps 2.2 and 3.1 cover every pair $(k,\ell)$: the sum equals the natural number $N$ read in $\mathbb C$ in the congruent case and $0$ otherwise, which is the stated formula. [cases, F1, step 2.2, step 3.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **The case $\omega^{m}=1$ is exactly the case split used by Taylor.** In Taylor's proof of Proposition 11.2 the sum $S_m$ of the powers of $\omega$ satisfies $S_m=\omega^{m}S_m$, so it vanishes whenever $\omega^{m}\ne1$; the coincident case $\omega^{m}=1$ is separated first. Here the split is made on $k\equiv\ell\pmod N$ and the noncoincident case is settled by the geometric identity, which is the same computation in explicit finite-sum form.

- **No dependence on the representation-theoretic orthogonality.** The published orthogonality lemma for finite abelian groups and the real-variable factorisation lemma for $b^{n}-a^{n}$ are stated outside the complex-sum setting used here, so this lemma proves the complex geometric identity directly from the recursion instead of importing them. They are independent cross-checks, not prerequisites.

## Statement

On the finite periodic rectangular $d$-grid of [[def-parabolic-theta-finite-difference-scheme]], let $\ell_j\in\{0,\ldots,N_j-1\}$ and
$$
\phi_\ell(i)=\exp\left(2\pi\mathrm i\sum_{j=1}^d\frac{\ell_ji_j}{N_j}\right).
$$
Then $\phi_\ell$ is an eigenvector of $A_h^{\rm per}$ with eigenvalue
$$
\lambda_\ell=4\sum_{j=1}^d\frac{\kappa_j}{h_j^2}\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi\ell_j}{N_j}\right)\ge0.
$$
For zero source, the $\theta$ update multiplies this mode at each step by
$$
g_\theta(\ell)=\frac{1-(1-\theta)\Delta t\lambda_\ell}{1+\theta\Delta t\lambda_\ell}.
$$
The displayed modes form a basis of the complexified grid space, so this factor describes the full periodic update.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite periodic rectangular grid with $d\ge1$, $N_j\ge2$, $h_j=L_j/N_j$, $\kappa_j>0$, and $\theta\in[0,1]$ as defined in [[def-parabolic-theta-finite-difference-scheme]].

[F1] [[def-parabolic-theta-finite-difference-scheme]] defines $A_h^{\rm per}$ by periodic wraparound and the update $\Delta t^{-1}(U^{n+1}-U^n)+A_h^{\rm per}((1-\theta)U^n+\theta U^{n+1})=0$ when the source is zero.

## Proof

1.1 For each coordinate $j$, the mode satisfies $\phi_\ell(i+e_j)=e^{2\pi\mathrm i\ell_j/N_j}\phi_\ell(i)$ and $\phi_\ell(i-e_j)=e^{-2\pi\mathrm i\ell_j/N_j}\phi_\ell(i)$. Substitution into the $j$th stencil term gives $\kappa_jh_j^{-2}(2-e^{2\pi\mathrm i\ell_j/N_j}-e^{-2\pi\mathrm i\ell_j/N_j})\phi_\ell(i)=4\kappa_jh_j^{-2}\sin^2(\pi\ell_j/N_j)\phi_\ell(i)$. Summing over $j$ yields the asserted eigenvalue. [F1, algebra]

1.2 For one coordinate, the finite geometric sum $\sum_{r=0}^{N_j-1}e^{2\pi\mathrm i qr/N_j}$ equals $N_j$ if $q$ is divisible by $N_j$ and equals $0$ otherwise. Therefore distinct modes are orthogonal in the complexified grid inner product. There are exactly $\prod_jN_j$ such nonzero modes, equal to the dimension of the grid space, so they form a basis. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Substituting $U^n=a_n\phi_\ell$ into the zero-source update gives $(a_{n+1}-a_n)+\Delta t\lambda_\ell((1-\theta)a_n+\theta a_{n+1})=0$. Since $1+\theta\Delta t\lambda_\ell\ge1$, solving this scalar equation gives $a_{n+1}=g_\theta(\ell)a_n$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By step 1.2 every grid vector is a finite linear combination of these modes, and the update acts on each component by the factor from step 2.1. Thus the stated factors describe the full update. [step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The calculation is for periodic grids. It does not establish stability of a finite Dirichlet matrix or of a variable-coefficient stencil.

## Definition

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

## Statement

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $z=a+bi$ and $w=u+vi$.

[F1] Complex numbers have unique real coordinates and the coordinate addition and multiplication formulas ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]).

[F2] Conjugation and modulus are defined by $\overline{a+bi}=a-bi$ and $|a+bi|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]).

[F3] The real numbers are a complete ordered field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), and every nonnegative element of a complete ordered field has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

[F4] For nonnegative elements $r,s$ of an ordered field, $r\le s$ if and only if $r^2\le s^2$ ([[lem-of-square-monotone]]).

[F5] The square of every nonzero element of an ordered field is positive ([[lem-of-square-positive]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Coordinate expansion using [F1] and [F2] proves the two homomorphism laws, that conjugation fixes every real number, and that applying it twice is the identity. Thus conjugation is an involutive real-field automorphism. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Direct multiplication gives $z\overline z=a^2+b^2=|z|^2$. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.3 Lagrange's identity gives $$ (a^2+b^2)(u^2+v^2)-(au+bv)^2=(av-bu)^2\ge0. $$ The final inequality follows from [F5], with the zero case included. [F5, algebra]

2.1 By [F2] and [F3], $|z|\ge0$. If $z=0$, then $|z|=0$; conversely, $|z|=0$ makes $a^2+b^2=0$, and [F5] forces $a=b=0$. [F2, F3, F5, step 1.2]

3.1 Apply step 1.2 to $zw$ and use step 1.1: $|zw|^2=(zw)\overline{zw}=(z\overline z)(w\overline w) =|z|^2|w|^2$. Both sides of $|zw|=|z||w|$ are nonnegative, so uniqueness in [F3] proves multiplicativity. [F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1]

3.2 Hence $au+bv\le |z||w|$: if $au+bv\le0$ this follows from $|z||w|\ge0$; otherwise both quantities are nonnegative, step 1.3 and [F4] give the inequality after squaring. [F4, step 2.1, step 1.3]

4.1 Expanding with [F1] and [F2], then using step 3.2, gives $$ |z+w|^2=a^2+b^2+u^2+v^2+2(au+bv) \le (|z|+|w|)^2. $$ [F1, F2, step 1.2, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 Both sides of $|z+w|\le|z|+|w|$ are nonnegative, so [F4] turns the squared inequality in step 4.1 into the triangle inequality. [F4, step 2.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

## Remarks

- The inequality $\|Tx\| \le \|T\|\,\|x\|$ holds for every $x \in X$ by the
  unit-ball definition and rescaling.
- The unit-ball formula is the one used uniformly below, because it also covers
  the zero-space case without a separate convention.

## Statement

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathbb{N} = \omega$ is the smallest inductive set ([[def-inductive-set]], [[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-omega-smallest-inductive]]); $0 = \varnothing$, $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$.

[L1] $\omega$ is contained in every inductive set ([[lem-omega-smallest-inductive]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Suppose $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with $0 = \varnothing \in S$ and ($x \in S \Rightarrow \sigma(x) = x \cup \{x\} \in S$). [given]

2.1 Then $S$ contains $\varnothing$ and is closed under $x \mapsto x \cup \{x\}$, so $S$ is an inductive set. [step 1.1]

3.1 $\mathbb{N} = \omega \subseteq S$ because $\omega$ is a subset of every inductive set. [L1, step 2.1]

4.1 With $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ by hypothesis, $S = \mathbb{N}$. [step 3.1, given]

5.1 The property form is the set case with $S = \{n \in \mathbb{N} : P(n)\}$: $P(0)$ and $P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$ give $0 \in S$ and $\sigma$-closure, so $S = \mathbb{N}$, i.e. $P$ holds for all $n$; conversely the set form is the property form applied to $P(n) :\equiv n \in S$, so the two are equivalent. [step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

For $n\ge1$, there exists $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $|x|\le1$, and $\chi=0$ on $|x|\ge2$. For $R>0$, $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ satisfies $\partial^\beta\chi_R(x)=R^{-|\beta|}(\partial^\beta\chi)(x/R)$. The construction requires no choice.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $n\ge1$ and multi-indices as in [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]].

[F1] Exponentials dominate fixed powers at positive infinity ([[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]]).

[F2] The total chain rule holds ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[F3] Closed bounded subsets of Euclidean space are compact ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Define $a(t)=e^{-1/t}$ for $t>0$ and $a(t)=0$ for $t\le0$. If $s=1/t$, induction gives $a^{(k)}(t)=P_k(s)e^{-s}$ on $t>0$, with $P_0=1$ and $P_{k+1}(s)=s^2(P_k(s)-P_k'(s))$. By [F1], both $P_k(s)e^{-s}$ and $sP_k(s)e^{-s}$ tend to zero as $s\to\infty$. Extending each derivative by zero to $t\le0$ is therefore continuous; its difference quotient at zero also tends to zero. Induction proves $a\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with every derivative zero at zero. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Set $\sigma(t)=a(t)/(a(t)+a(1-t))$. For $t\le0$, the second summand in the denominator is positive; for $t\ge1$, the first is positive; for $0<t<1$, both are positive. Thus the quotient is smooth, $0\le\sigma\le1$, and $\sigma=0$ on $t\le0$, $\sigma=1$ on $t\ge1$. Define $\chi(x)=\sigma((4-|x|^2)/3)$. Repeated [F2] proves smoothness, and the two constant regions give the claimed unit and zero regions, including their boundaries. Its closed support lies in the closed radius-two ball and is compact by [F3]. [step 1.1, F2, F3]

3.1 Differentiating $\chi(x/R)$ once in coordinate $j$ gives $R^{-1}(\partial_j\chi)(x/R)$. Iterating this identity in the prescribed multi-index order gives the asserted factor, including $\beta=0$. No selection was made in any construction. [step 2.1, F2, given] ∎

## Definition

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R$ be open and let
$a:\Omega\to\mathbb R^n$, $c:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$.
The scalar first-order equation

$$u_t(x,t)+a(x,t)\cdot\nabla_x u(x,t)+c(x,t)u(x,t)=f(x,t)$$

is a **linear transport equation**.

Fix $(x_0,t_0)\in\Omega$. A **characteristic through $(x_0,t_0)$** is a
solution $X(\cdot)$ of the ODE

$$X'(s)=a(X(s),s),\qquad X(t_0)=x_0,$$

on an interval containing $t_0$. The corresponding space-time curve is
$s\mapsto (X(s),s)$. If these initial-value problems have unique solutions for
varying initial data, write $X(s;t_0,x_0)$ for the solution through
$(x_0,t_0)$. The resulting maps $x_0\mapsto X(s;t_0,x_0)$, on the domains
where they are defined, form the **characteristic flow** of the transport
field. Without uniqueness there are characteristics, but no single-valued
characteristic flow.
