## Definition

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

## Remarks

- **At $p=2$ this is the published operator norm.** The vector $2$-norm is the
  Euclidean norm ([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]),
  so the induced $2$-norm of a real matrix is the operator norm of the
  published spectral/SVD page; [[thm-operator-norm-is-the-largest-singular-value]]
  identifies it with the largest singular value. No second operator norm is
  introduced here.

- **Only rational $p\ge 1$ are used.** The published
  [[def-p-norms-on-rn]] exist for rational exponents only, and this definition
  inherits that restriction verbatim; no statement on this page ranges $p$
  over a real interval.

## Statement

Let $f \in \mathbb C[x]$ have degree $n \ge 1$. Then there exist distinct
complex numbers $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$ and positive integers
$m_1,\dots,m_r$ such that
$$ f(x)=c\prod_{j=1}^r (x-\alpha_j)^{m_j} $$
for some $c \in \mathbb C^\times$, with
$$ m_1+\cdots+m_r=n. $$
These exponents are uniquely determined by $f$. Equivalently, $f$ has exactly
$n$ roots counted with multiplicity.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A polynomial $f \in \mathbb C[x]$ of degree $n \ge 1$.

[L1] Every nonconstant polynomial in $\mathbb C[x]$ splits over $\mathbb C$ ([[cor-every-complex-polynomial-splits-into-linear-factors]]).

[L2] Splitting means a nonzero scalar times a product of linear factors ([[def-polynomials-that-split-and-splitting-fields]]).

[L3] The polynomial ring $\mathbb C[x]$ is a unique factorization domain ([[thm-polynomial-ring-over-a-field-is-a-ufd]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1] and [L2], there are $c \in \mathbb C^\times$ and complex numbers $\beta_1,\dots,\beta_n$ such that $$ f(x)=c\prod_{k=1}^n (x-\beta_k). $$ Let $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$ be the distinct values among the $\beta_k$, and let $m_j$ be the number of indices $k$ with $\beta_k=\alpha_j$. Then $$ f(x)=c\prod_{j=1}^r (x-\alpha_j)^{m_j}, $$ and by construction $m_1+\cdots+m_r=n$. [L1, L2, construct]

2.1 Suppose also that $$ f(x)=c'\prod_{j=1}^s (x-\gamma_j)^{n_j} $$ with $c' \in \mathbb C^\times$, distinct $\gamma_j$, and positive integers $n_j$. In the UFD $\mathbb C[x]$, each linear factor $x-\alpha$ is irreducible, hence prime. Therefore the exponent with which $x-\alpha$ appears in a factorization of $f$ is uniquely determined. After reordering, this gives $$ r=s,\qquad \gamma_j=\alpha_j,\qquad n_j=m_j \text{ for every } j. $$ So the multiplicities are well defined. [L3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Step 1.1 gives a factorization whose exponents sum to $n$, and step 2.1 gives uniqueness of those exponents. This is exactly the statement that a degree-$n$ complex polynomial has exactly $n$ roots counted with multiplicity. [step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

For an endomorphism $T$ of a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space,

$$\sigma_F(T)=\{\lambda\in F:\chi_T(\lambda)=0\}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite-dimensional $F$-vector space $V$ and $T\in\mathcal L(V)$.

[L1] In any basis, $\chi_T$ is the characteristic polynomial of the representing matrix; in dimension zero it is $1$ ([[def-characteristic-polynomial-of-an-operator]]).

[L2] A scalar $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $T-\lambda I_V$ is not invertible ([[prop-eigenvalue-iff-shift-is-not-invertible]]).

[L3] A finite-dimensional endomorphism is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero ([[thm-operator-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]]).

[L4] A root of a polynomial is a scalar at which its evaluation is zero ([[def-polynomial-evaluation-and-root]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $\dim V=0$, the spectrum is empty because there is no nonzero eigenvector, while [L1] gives $\chi_T=1$, which has no root. [L1, L4]

1.2 Suppose $\dim V=n\ge1$ and choose a basis with matrix $A=[T]$. Then $\chi_T(\lambda)=\det(\lambda I_n-A)=(-1)^n\det(A-\lambda I_n)$. [L1, algebra]

2.1 The scalar $(-1)^n$ is nonzero. Thus step 1.2, [L3], and [L2] give $\chi_T(\lambda)=0$ if and only if $T-\lambda I_V$ is not invertible if and only if $\lambda\in\sigma_F(T)$. [step 1.2, L2, L3, L4]

3.1 Steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove the set equality in every finite dimension and prove both directions of the equivalence. [step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

## Definition

A subset is convex when it contains the segment joining each pair of its
points ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). A function
$F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is proper if it never equals
$-\infty$ and is finite at at least one point. Its domain is
$\operatorname{dom}F=\{x:F(x)<+\infty\}$. Its epigraph is
$\operatorname{epi}F=\{(x,t):F(x)\le t\}$. It is closed convex when its
epigraph is a closed convex set. For a nonempty convex set $S$,
$\operatorname{aff}S$ is its smallest containing affine subspace and
$\operatorname{ri}S$ is its interior relative to $\operatorname{aff}S$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $m,p\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed, let
$f_0,g_1,\ldots,g_m$ be proper closed convex functions on $\mathbb R^n$,
let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$ have full row rank, and let
$b\in\mathbb R^p$. Full row rank means that the rows are linearly
independent, vacuously when $p=0$. The common domain is
$D=\operatorname{dom}f_0\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}g_i$. The primal
problem is to minimize $f_0(x)$ over $x\in D$ satisfying $Ax=b$ and
$g_i(x)\le0$. An inequality is trivial if $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $x\in D$;
trivial inequalities may be removed without changing the feasible set.
Unless stated otherwise, the inequalities below are the remaining,
nontrivial ones. The primal value is
$$
p^*=\inf\{f_0(x):x\in D,\ Ax=b,\ g_i(x)\le0\text{ for all }i\}.
$$

For $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+$ and $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, the extended
Lagrangian is
$$
L(x,\lambda,\nu)=\begin{cases}f_0(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)+\nu^T(Ax-b),&x\in D,\\+\infty,&x\notin D.\end{cases}
$$
The dual function and dual value are
$$
q(\lambda,\nu)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}L(x,\lambda,\nu),\qquad d^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0,\ \nu\in\mathbb R^p}q(\lambda,\nu).
$$
The dual supremum is attained when some admissible $(\lambda,\nu)$ has
$q(\lambda,\nu)=d^*$; the optimal duality gap is $p^*-d^*$ when both values
are finite.

Slater's condition means that there is
$x_s\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_0)\cap
\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g_i)$ with $Ax_s=b$ and
$g_i(x_s)<0$ for every remaining inequality. Relative interior is used in
the affine hull of each domain, so the domain need not have ambient interior.

## Remarks

The equality rows are assumed independent after consistent redundant rows are
removed. The theorem on this page assumes a finite attained primal value;
Slater's strict inequalities alone do not assert primal attainment.

## Statement

For the convex program and Lagrangian dual of
[[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]], every primal feasible
$x$ and every dual feasible $(\lambda,\nu)$ satisfy
$$q(\lambda,\nu)\le f_0(x).$$
Consequently, when the primal feasible set is nonempty, $d^*\le p^*$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A primal feasible point and a dual feasible multiplier pair.

[F1] On the common domain,
$L(x,\lambda,\nu)=f_0(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)+\nu^T(Ax-b)$ and
$q(\lambda,\nu)=\inf_x L(x,\lambda,\nu)$, with $\lambda\ge0$
([[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]]).

## Proof

1.1 Since $x$ is feasible, $Ax-b=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$. Since $\lambda_i\ge0$, this gives $L(x,\lambda,\nu)=f_0(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x)\le f_0(x)$. The infimum defining $q$ is no larger than this particular Lagrangian value, so $q(\lambda,\nu)\le f_0(x)$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The bound in step 1.1 holds for every primal feasible $x$ and every dual feasible pair. Taking the infimum over primal feasible $x$ and the supremum over dual feasible pairs gives $d^*\le p^*$ when the primal set is nonempty. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $A$ be a square matrix over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and let $b$ be a
vector of matching size. Define

$$K_0(A,b):=\{0\},$$

and for $m\ge 1$ define the $m$th **Krylov subspace**

$$K_m(A,b):=\operatorname{span}\{b,Ab,\dots,A^{m-1}b\}.$$

Thus $K_m(A,b)\subseteq K_{m+1}(A,b)$ for every $m\ge 0$.

## Statement

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, be symmetric with ordered eigenvalues
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n$. Let $r$ be the multiplicity of $\lambda_1$.
If $r<n$, assume $\lambda_1>\lambda_{r+1}$, and let $P$ be the orthogonal
projection onto the $\lambda_1$-eigenspace. Let $b\in\mathbb R^n$ be a unit
vector and, for $m\ge1$, define

$$K_m:=\operatorname{span}\{b,Ab,\ldots,A^{m-1}b\},\qquad \theta_m:=\max_{0\ne x\in K_m}\frac{x^{\mathsf T}Ax}{x^{\mathsf T}x}.$$

Thus $\theta_m$ is the largest Rayleigh–Ritz value on $K_m$; if Lanczos runs
through step $m$ without breakdown, it is the largest Ritz value of
$Q_m^{\mathsf T}AQ_m$. If $r=n$, then $A=\lambda_1I$ and $\theta_m=\lambda_1$
for every $m\ge1$. Suppose $r<n$.

1. If $Pb=0$, then $\theta_m\le\lambda_{r+1}$ for every $m$; no convergence
   to $\lambda_1$ is asserted.

2. If $Pb\ne0$, put
   $$\tau:=\frac{\|(I-P)b\|_2}{\|Pb\|_2}.$$
   If $\lambda_{r+1}>\lambda_n$, then for every $m\ge1$,
   $$0\le\lambda_1-\theta_m\le \frac{(\lambda_1-\lambda_n)\tau^2} {T_{m-1}\!\left(1+2\frac{\lambda_1-\lambda_{r+1}} {\lambda_{r+1}-\lambda_n}\right)^2}.$$
   For a simple top eigenvalue ($r=1$), $\tau$ is the tangent of the angle
   between $b$ and a unit top eigenvector, so the starting-angle denominator
   is explicit.

3. If $\lambda_{r+1}=\lambda_n$, then
   $$\lambda_1-\theta_1=(\lambda_1-\lambda_n) \frac{\|(I-P)b\|_2^2}{\|b\|_2^2},\qquad \theta_m=\lambda_1\quad(m\ge2).$$

When $r<n$, $Pb\ne0$, and exact Lanczos breakdown occurs at dimension $d$, then
$\theta_d=\lambda_1$ and $K_m=K_d$ for all $m\ge d$. These are exact-arithmetic
claims; they give no finite-precision grade-termination guarantee.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real symmetric $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, its ordered eigenvalues, the top-eigenspace projection $P$ when $r<n$, a unit start vector $b$, the Krylov spaces $K_m$, and the largest Rayleigh–Ritz values $\theta_m$ defined in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-lanczos-process-as-hermitian-arnoldi]]: exact Lanczos is Arnoldi applied to a symmetric matrix, with real nonnegative subdiagonal coefficients before breakdown.

[F2] [[thm-arnoldi-produces-an-orthonormal-krylov-basis-and-upper-hessenberg-factorization]]: before breakdown, the Arnoldi vectors form an orthonormal basis of $K_m$ and satisfy $AQ_m=Q_{m+1}\bar H_m$.

[F3] [[def-ritz-values-and-ritz-vectors-from-arnoldi]] and [[prop-ritz-residual-formula-for-an-arnoldi-ritz-pair]]: eigenvalues of $H_m=Q_m^{\mathsf T}AQ_m$ are Ritz values with vectors $u=Q_my$; if Arnoldi runs through step $m$ without breakdown and $H_my=\theta y$, then $Au-\theta u=h_{m+1,m}(e_m^{\mathsf T}y)v_{m+1}$.

[F4] [[thm-courant-fischer-min-max-principle]] and [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]: every real symmetric compression has a largest Rayleigh–Ritz value equal to its largest eigenvalue, and $A$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis.

[F5] [[lem-scaled-chebyshev-filter-bound-on-a-separated-interval]]: for $a>b>c$, the degree-$k$ scaled filter has value $1$ at $a$ and absolute value at most $1/T_k(1+2(a-b)/(b-c))$ on $[c,b]$.

[F6] [[def-arnoldi-process]]: each exact Arnoldi column has $Av_j=\sum_{i=1}^j h_{ij}v_i+w_j$; exact breakdown at column $d$ means $w_d=0$.

[F7] [[def-krylov-subspace-of-a-matrix-and-start-vector]]: $K_m(A,b)=\operatorname{span}\{b,Ab,\ldots,A^{m-1}b\}$.

## Proof

1.1 If exact Lanczos runs through step $m$ without breakdown, [F1], [F2], and [F7] give an orthonormal basis $Q_m$ of $K_m$ and a symmetric compression $H_m=Q_m^{\mathsf T}AQ_m$. By [F3], each eigenpair of $H_m$ lifts to an exact Ritz pair of $A$; by [F4], the largest eigenvalue of $H_m$ is the maximum Rayleigh quotient on $K_m$, namely $\theta_m$. If Lanczos breaks down earlier, no step-$m$ basis or Ritz assertion is used; $\theta_m$ remains defined directly by the Rayleigh–Ritz formula in the Statement. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F7]

1.2 Assume $r<n$. By [F4], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of $A$ whose first $r$ vectors span the range of $P$. If $Pb=0$, then $b$ is orthogonal to that eigenspace. For every integer $j\ge0$ and every top eigenvector $u$, symmetry gives $u^{\mathsf T}A^jb=(A^ju)^{\mathsf T}b=\lambda_1^j u^{\mathsf T}b=0$. Thus every vector in $K_m$ lies in the orthogonal complement of the top eigenspace, where all Rayleigh quotients are at most $\lambda_{r+1}$; this proves branch 1. [given, F4, F7, algebra]

1.3 If $r=n$, every eigenvalue is $\lambda_1$, so [F4] gives $A=\lambda_1I$. Every nonzero $x\in K_m$ then has Rayleigh quotient $\lambda_1$, proving the stated dimension-one/full-multiplicity branch. [given, F4, algebra]

1.4 Assume $Pb\ne0$ and $\lambda_{r+1}>\lambda_n$. Apply [F5] with $a=\lambda_1$, $b=\lambda_{r+1}$, $c=\lambda_n$, and $k=m-1$ to obtain a polynomial $p_{m-1}$ of degree at most $m-1$ with $p_{m-1}(\lambda_1)=1$ and $|p_{m-1}(t)|\le\delta_m$ on $[\lambda_n,\lambda_{r+1}]$, where $\delta_m:=1/T_{m-1}(1+2(\lambda_1-\lambda_{r+1})/(\lambda_{r+1}-\lambda_n))$. By [F7], $x:=p_{m-1}(A)b$ belongs to $K_m$, and spectral decomposition gives $Px=Pb$ and $\|(I-P)x\|_2\le\delta_m\|(I-P)b\|_2$. [given, F4, F5, F7, algebra]

1.5 Assume $Pb\ne0$ and $\lambda_{r+1}=\lambda_n$. The spectral decomposition gives $A=\lambda_n I+(\lambda_1-\lambda_n)P$. Hence $Ab=\lambda_n b+(\lambda_1-\lambda_n)Pb$, so [F7] gives $Pb\in K_2$ and it has Rayleigh quotient $\lambda_1$; this proves $\theta_m=\lambda_1$ for $m\ge2$. For $m=1$, [F7] gives $K_1=\operatorname{span}\{b\}$, and the same decomposition gives the displayed exact formula for $\lambda_1-\theta_1$. [given, F4, F7, algebra]

2.1 In the eigenbasis of [F4], write $x=Px+(I-P)x$. The two components are orthogonal, $A(Px)=\lambda_1Px$, and all eigenvalues on the second component lie in $[\lambda_n,\lambda_{r+1}]$. Therefore $$\lambda_1-\frac{x^{\mathsf T}Ax}{x^{\mathsf T}x} =\frac{\sum_{j>r}(\lambda_1-\lambda_j)x_j^2} {\|Px\|_2^2+\|(I-P)x\|_2^2} \le(\lambda_1-\lambda_n)\frac{\|(I-P)x\|_2^2}{\|Pb\|_2^2} \le(\lambda_1-\lambda_n)\delta_m^2\tau^2.$$ Since $\theta_m$ is the maximum Rayleigh quotient on $K_m$, it is at least the quotient of this nonzero $x$ and at most $\lambda_1$. This proves branch 2, including $m=1$ because $T_0=1$. [given, F4, step 1.4, algebra]

3.1 Finally, assume $r<n$, $Pb\ne0$, and exact Lanczos breaks down at column $d$. For $d>1$, no breakdown occurs at columns $j<d$. Starting from $q_1=b/\|b\|_2$, inductively suppose $q_1,\ldots,q_j$ form an orthonormal basis of $K_j$. By the exact Arnoldi definition [F1, F6], the residual $w_j=Aq_j-\sum_{i=1}^j h_{ij}q_i$ lies in $K_{j+1}$, is orthogonal to $K_j$, and is nonzero for $j<d$; hence its normalized vector $q_{j+1}$ lies in $K_{j+1}\setminus K_j$. Since $K_{j+1}$ is generated by $j+1$ vectors, $q_1,\ldots,q_{j+1}$ form a basis of $K_{j+1}$. Thus $q_1,\ldots,q_d$ form a basis of $K_d$. For $d=1$, $q_1$ directly spans $K_1$. Each $Aq_j\in K_d$ for $j<d$, and $Aq_d\in K_d$ because its orthogonalized residual $w_d$ is zero. Hence $AK_d\subseteq K_d$, and [F7] plus induction gives $K_m=K_d$ for $m\ge d$. [given, F1, F6, F7, induction, algebra]

3.2 Let $\mu_1=\lambda_1,\mu_2,\ldots,\mu_s$ be the distinct eigenvalues of $A$. Since $r<n$, $s\ge2$ and the denominators below are nonzero. Define $$p(t):=\prod_{i=2}^{s}\frac{t-\mu_i}{\lambda_1-\mu_i}.$$ Then $p(\lambda_1)=1$ and $p(\mu_i)=0$ for $i\ge2$. On the orthonormal eigenbasis from [F4], $p(A)$ therefore acts as the identity on the $\lambda_1$-eigenspace and as zero on every other eigenspace, so $p(A)=P$. Since $AK_d\subseteq K_d$ and $b\in K_d$, every power of $A$ applied to $b$ lies in $K_d$, whence $Pb=p(A)b\in K_d$. The nonzero vector $Pb$ has Rayleigh quotient $\lambda_1$, while no quotient can exceed $\lambda_1$; thus $\theta_d=\lambda_1$ and the exact-breakdown branch follows. [given, F4, step 3.1, algebra, induction] ∎

      url: "https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~saad/IterMethBook_2ndEd.pdf"
    - title: "Richard Barrett et al., Templates for the Solution of Linear Systems: Building Blocks for Iterative Methods, 2nd ed., Chapter 4 §4.3.1–4.3.2, printed pp. 57–63"
      url: "https://www.netlib.org/templates/templates.pdf"
dependency_level: 0

## Definition

Let $F$ be a field, and let $m,n,s\in\mathbb N$, where $\mathbb N$ includes
$0$. A **compressed sparse row (CSR) record** for an $m$ by $n$ matrix over
$F$ consists of integer arrays $r=(r_0,\ldots,r_m)$ and
$c=(c_0,\ldots,c_{s-1})$, and a value array $v=(v_0,\ldots,v_{s-1})\in F^s$,
satisfying

$$r_0=0,\qquad 0=r_0\le r_1\le\cdots\le r_m=s,\qquad 0\le c_t<n\quad(0\le t<s).$$

For each row $i<m$, its **stored entries** are the indices
$t$ with $r_i\le t<r_{i+1}$. The row is empty exactly when
$r_i=r_{i+1}$. Repeated column indices within one row and stored values
$v_t=0_F$ are permitted; each such entry remains a separate stored entry.

The represented matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ is defined entrywise by

$$A_{ij}:=\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}v_t\qquad(0\le i<m,\ 0\le j<n),$$

where $\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}$ is $1_F$ when $c_t=j$ and $0_F$ otherwise, and an
empty sum is $0_F$. Repeated entries in column $j$ are therefore added. The
number $s$ is the **stored-entry count**; it is not in general the number of
nonzero entries of $A$.

A CSR record is **canonical** when no row repeats a column and no stored value
is zero. In that case every nonzero matrix entry is stored exactly once and
$s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)$, where $\operatorname{nnz}(A)$ denotes the number of
nonzero entries of $A$. If $m=0$, the endpoint conditions force $s=0$ and the
row-pointer array has its single entry $r_0=0$. If $n=0$, the column-index
condition forces $s=0$ as well.

## Definition

Fix a field $F$. The **validated CSR matrix-vector product** takes integer
dimension candidates $m,n$, integer arrays $r,c$, a value array $v$ of elements
of $F$, and a vector candidate $x$ of elements of $F$. All input arrays are
finite; write $s=\operatorname{length}(v)$.

1. If $m\notin\mathbb N$, $n\notin\mathbb N$,
   $\operatorname{length}(r)\ne m+1$,
   $\operatorname{length}(c)\ne s$, or
   $\operatorname{length}(x)\ne n$, return the status `invalid-dimension`.
2. For $i=0,\ldots,m$, check that $r_i\in\{0,\ldots,s\}$; return
   `invalid-index` if a check fails. Check $r_0=0$ and $r_m=s$, and for each
   $i=0,\ldots,m-1$ check $r_i\le r_{i+1}$; return `invalid-index` if any
   check fails. For each $t=0,\ldots,s-1$, check $0\le c_t<n$ and return
   `invalid-index` if a check fails.
3. Initialize $y_i=0_F$ for $0\le i<m$. For each row
   $i=0,\ldots,m-1$, and then each stored index
   $t=r_i,\ldots,r_{i+1}-1$, update
   $$y_i\gets y_i+v_t x_{c_t}.$$
4. Return the status `ok` together with $y\in F^m$.

For valid CSR data this uses exact field operations. Validation examines only
finite arrays, and the row intervals partition the $s$ stored entries, so the
specified loops are bounded. This procedure makes no floating-point rounding,
backward-stability, convergence, runtime, or memory-bandwidth claim.

      url: "https://www.netlib.org/templates/templates.pdf"

## Statement

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n\in\mathbb N$, let a valid CSR record represent
$A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, and let $x=(x_j)_{j<n}\in F^n$. Define
$(Ax)_i:=\sum_{j<n}A_{ij}x_j$, the usual matrix-vector product from
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. Then the algorithm
[[alg-csr-matrix-vector-product-with-validation]] returns `ok` with output
$Ax$ in exact field arithmetic.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $m,n\in\mathbb N$, a valid CSR record representing $A$, and $x\in F^n$.

[L1] [[def-csr-matrix-with-stored-entry-semantics]]: $A_{ij}=\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}v_t$, with an empty sum equal to $0_F$.

[L2] [[alg-csr-matrix-vector-product-with-validation]]: each row starts at $0_F$ and accumulates $v_t x_{c_t}$ once for every $t=r_i,\ldots,r_{i+1}-1$.

[L3] [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]: matrix multiplication uses $(AB)_{ik}=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}$.

[L4] [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]: a finite sum is independent of its enumeration and an empty sum is its identity element.

[L5] [[def-field]]: multiplication distributes over addition.

[L6] [[def-function-space]]: $F^m$ is the set of functions $m\to F$; when $m=0$ it has exactly one element, the empty function.

[L7] [[lem-of-zero-mult]]: in a field, $0\cdot a=0$ for every $a$.

[L8] [[def-field]]: multiplication is commutative on all of $F$, and $x\cdot1=x$ for every $x\in F$; hence $1_F x=x$.

## Proof

1.1 Fix a row $i$. Initially its output coordinate is $0_F$, the empty partial sum. After $q$ entries of that row have been visited, induction on $q$ gives $y_i=\sum_{t=r_i}^{r_i+q-1}v_t x_{c_t}$: the next algorithmic update adds exactly the next summand. Taking $q=r_{i+1}-r_i$ yields $y_i=\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}v_t x_{c_t}$. [L2, induction, algebra]

2.1 By [L1] and [L3], $(Ax)_i=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}v_t x_j$. Repeated application of [L5], by induction on the finite number of summands, distributes the products over these sums. Re-enumerating the resulting finite sum over pairs $(j,t)$ as $(t,j)$ is permitted by [L4]. For each fixed $t$, exactly the term $j=c_t$ survives, so the result is $\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}v_t x_{c_t}$. By step 1.1 this equals $y_i$. [L1, L3, L4, L5, L7, L8, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $m=0$, both $y$ and $Ax$ are the unique empty vector by [L6]. If $m>0$, step 2.1 gives equality in every coordinate $i<m$, hence $y=Ax$. [L6, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n\in\mathbb N$, and let a valid CSR record have
$s$ stored entries. Its input arrays use exactly $s$ field-value slots, $s$
integer column-index slots, and $m+1$ integer row-pointer slots, for a total of
$2s+m+1$ data slots. On valid input, the algorithm
[[alg-csr-matrix-vector-product-with-validation]] performs exactly $s$ field
multiplications, $s$ field additions, and $m$ zero initializations. Its index
validation and loop-control work is $O(m+s+1)$. Counting the CSR arrays and
returned output but excluding the supplied vector $x$ and constant-size
workspace, it uses exactly $2s+2m+1$ data slots, hence $O(m+s+1)$ slots; for
$m\ge1$ this is $O(m+s)$. Here $O(g)$ means bounded by $Cg$ for a constant $C$ independent of
the dimensions and input values.

For a square record of order $m\ge1$ with at least one stored entry in each
row, $s\ge m$, so the work and storage are $O(s)$. For a canonical record as defined in
[[def-csr-matrix-with-stored-entry-semantics]], $s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)$;
without that convention, the cost is in terms of stored entries, not
$\operatorname{nnz}(A)$. These are arithmetic, index, and storage counts, not
runtime, memory-bandwidth, convergence, or factorization-cost bounds.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A valid CSR record with dimensions $m,n\in\mathbb N$ and $s$ stored entries.

[L1] [[def-csr-matrix-with-stored-entry-semantics]]: the arrays have lengths $m+1$, $s$, and $s$; the row pointers satisfy $r_0=0\le\cdots\le r_m=s$.

[L2] [[def-csr-matrix-with-stored-entry-semantics]]: a record is canonical when no row repeats a column and no stored value is zero; then $s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)$.

[L3] [[alg-csr-matrix-vector-product-with-validation]]: on a valid record the algorithm initializes $m$ outputs and visits each row interval $r_i,\ldots,r_{i+1}-1$, performing one multiply-add per visited index.

## Proof

1.1 The value, column-index, and row-pointer arrays have lengths $s$, $s$, and $m+1$, respectively, so their input representation contains exactly $2s+m+1$ data slots. [L1, algebra]

1.2 The number of visits in row $i$ is $r_{i+1}-r_i$. Summing these lengths telescopes to $r_m-r_0=s$; monotonicity makes the intervals disjoint and their endpoints cover every stored index once. Thus the accumulation loop executes exactly $s$ multiply-add updates, and the initialization loop executes exactly $m$ times. The two validation scans examine at most $m+1$ pointers and $s$ column indices, so validation and loop control take $O(m+s+1)$ work. [L1, L3, algebra]

1.3 The returned vector occupies $m$ additional field slots. Counting it with the CSR arrays, and excluding the supplied $x$ and fixed workspace, gives exactly $2s+2m+1$ data slots, hence $O(m+s+1)$. If $m\ge1$, then $m+s\ge1$ and the additive constant is absorbed into a fixed multiple of $m+s$. [L1, L3, algebra]

2.1 For a square record of order $m\ge1$ with every row storing at least one entry, summing its $m$ row lengths gives $s\ge m$; substituting into the preceding bounds yields $O(s)$. By [L2], a canonical record has $s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)$; no such equality is asserted when duplicate columns or explicit zeros are stored. [L1, L2, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Definition
Finite sums of vectors in $\mathbb R^n$ use the additive finite-list sum of [[def-linear-combination-and-span]]; sums of real coefficients use [[def-finite-sum]].

Fix $n\ge1$, an objective oracle $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{\text{nonfinite}\}$, a finite integer call budget $B\ge0$, positive tolerances $\varepsilon_x,\varepsilon_f$, and an ordered initial simplex $(v_0,\ldots,v_n)$. Call the ordered tuple nondegenerate when, for real coefficients $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$, $\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i(v_i-v_0)=0$ implies every $\lambda_i=0$. Use reflection $\alpha=1$, expansion $\gamma=2$, contraction $\rho=1/2$, and shrink $\sigma=1/2$. Ties in sorting objective values are broken by current vertex slot, lower slot first. When recording the best point seen, replace it only on a strict objective improvement, so ties retain the earliest evaluation; initial vertices are evaluated in slot order.

If the initial simplex is degenerate, return **degenerate-simplex**. If $B<n+1$, return **budget-exhausted** with zero calls and no best point. Otherwise evaluate initial vertices in slot order, counting every call. A nonfinite result returns **nonfinite-objective** and the best finite point seen, if any. For each committed simplex, let $x_b$ be its sorted best vertex, $x_w$ its worst, let $x_2$ denote the second-worst (the best when $n=1$), and set $c:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x_i$ using the sorted vertices $x_0,\ldots,x_n$. Define the diameter $D=\max_{0\le i,j\le n}\|x_i-x_j\|_2$, and spread $S=f(x_w)-f(x_b)$. Stop with **tolerance-met** exactly when both $D\le\varepsilon_x$ and $S\le\varepsilon_f$.

Otherwise evaluate reflection $x_r=c+(c-x_w)$. If $f(x_r)<f(x_b)$, evaluate expansion $x_e=c+2(x_r-c)$ and replace $x_w$ by $x_e$ iff $f(x_e)<f(x_r)$; a tie keeps reflection. If $f(x_b)\le f(x_r)<f(x_2)$, where $x_2$ is the second-worst vertex, replace $x_w$ by reflection. If $f(x_2)\le f(x_r)<f(x_w)$, evaluate outside contraction $x_{oc}=c+(x_r-c)/2$ and accept iff $f(x_{oc})\le f(x_r)$; equality accepts. If $f(x_r)\ge f(x_w)$, evaluate inside contraction $x_{ic}=c+(x_w-c)/2$ and accept iff $f(x_{ic})<f(x_w)$; equality fails. A failed contraction shrinks each nonbest vertex to $x_b+(v_i-x_b)/2$.

Count every objective call, including rejected trials. Before a needed call, if the budget is exhausted, return **budget-exhausted** with the last committed simplex and best finite point seen; do not partially commit an update. A nonfinite trial returns **nonfinite-objective** with the same committed simplex. If a proposed complete update is degenerate, return **degenerate-simplex** without committing it. After a valid update, recheck both tolerances. No general convergence guarantee is asserted.

## Definition
Finite sums of vectors in $\mathbb R^n$ use the additive finite-list sum of [[def-linear-combination-and-span]]; sums of real coefficients use [[def-finite-sum]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex. The finite-budget projected subgradient procedure takes $x_0\in C$, an integer budget $N\ge1$, and positive stepsizes $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{N-1}$. At iteration $k$, an oracle returns either failure or a pair $(f(x_k),g_k)$ with $g_k\in\partial f(x_k)$, where subgradient has the meaning in [[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]]. On a valid response set
$$x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k g_k),$$
where $P_C(u)$ is the unique nearest point in $C$ to $u$. On an oracle failure at iteration $k$, return status **oracle-failure**, the feasible current iterate, the completed update count, and the least-index best among values observed so far if any (otherwise report none); a full-horizon average is not returned. If all $N$ calls succeed, return status **budget-exhausted**, the final iterate, the weighted average $\bar x_N=(\sum_{k<N}\alpha_kx_k)/(\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k)$, and a least-index minimizer of observed values among $x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1}$. Report status and completed update count. This finite procedure makes no convergence claim.

## Definition
Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex; let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex; fix $t>0$, a serious-step fraction $m_s\in(0,1)$, a center $x_0\in C$, and an integer outer budget $N\ge1$. A valid oracle call at $y\in C$ returns $(f(y),g_y)$ with $g_y\in\partial f(y)$; otherwise it fails. Store every cut $m_y(z)=f(y)+\langle g_y,z-y\rangle$ from every successful call, with no memory cap, and set $M_k$ to the maximum of the stored cuts. If no cut exists, call the oracle at the current center. If this initialization call fails, return status **oracle-failure** with the current center, zero completed trials, and no candidate or model residual; otherwise store its cut. Find the unique minimizer
$$z_k=\arg\min_{z\in C}\left(M_k(z)+\frac{\|z-x_k\|_2^2}{2t}\right),\qquad P_k=f(x_k)-M_k(z_k).$$
If $P_k\le0$, return status **stationary-or-model-failure** with $x_k,z_k,P_k$. Otherwise evaluate at $z_k$. An oracle failure returns **oracle-failure**. Declare a serious step exactly when $f(x_k)-f(z_k)\ge m_sP_k$, set $x_{k+1}=z_k$ then, and otherwise take a null step and set $x_{k+1}=x_k$. Append the valid trial cut after either step. Return **budget-exhausted** after $N$ trials. This finite algorithm makes no generic convergence claim.

## Definition

Let $n\ge1$ and let $D=(d_1,\ldots,d_m)$ be a nonempty finite ordered list in $\mathbb R^n$. For coefficients $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m$, the finite vector sum $\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i d_i$ means the vector whose $k$th coordinate is $\sum_{j<m}\lambda_{j+1}(d_{j+1})_k$ for each $k<n$; this is the finite real sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. The list is **positive spanning** if every $w\in\mathbb R^n$ has such a representation with $\lambda_i\ge0$. Keep the order to make a deterministic poll. Define the directional score $\psi_D(v)=\max_{1\le i\le m}(-\langle v,d_i\rangle)$ for unit $v$, and the largest poll norm $D_{\max}=\max_{1\le i\le m}\|d_i\|_2$. These maxima exist because their indexing sets are nonempty and finite ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]). A positive uniform lower bound for $\psi_D$ is a separate theorem, not part of this definition.

## Statement

Let $K$ be compact in Euclidean $\mathbb R^n$ and let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $K\subseteq V$. There is $\delta>0$ such that for every $x\in K$, if $\|y-x\|_2<\delta$, then $y\in V$. If $K=\emptyset$, any positive $\delta$ works.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Compactness and openness in the Euclidean metric ([[def-metric-compactness]], [[def-metric-topology]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]); compactness is intrinsic to the subspace metric ([[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]]).

[F1] For each $x\in V$, openness gives $r>0$ with $B(x,2r)\subseteq V$ ([[def-metric-topology]], [[def-metric-ball]]).

[F2] Every open cover of compact $K$ has a finite subcover ([[def-metric-compactness]], [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]]).

[F3] A nonempty finite set of real numbers has a minimum that belongs to the set ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

## Proof

1.1 If $K=\emptyset$, take $\delta=1$. Otherwise form the family of all balls $B(x,r)$ with $x\in K$, $r>0$, and $B(x,2r)\subseteq V$. By [F1] this family covers $K$; [F2] supplies a finite subcover $B(x_i,r_i)$, $1\le i\le q$. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Since $K\ne\emptyset$, the finite subcover has at least one ball. The minimum $\delta=\min_{1\le i\le q}r_i$ belongs to the nonempty finite set of positive radii, so $\delta>0$ by [F3]. Given $x\in K$ and $\|y-x\|_2<\delta$, choose a covering ball containing $x$. Then for its index $i$, $\|y-x_i\|_2\le\|y-x\|_2+\|x-x_i\|_2<\delta+r_i\le2r_i$, so $y\in B(x_i,2r_i)\subseteq V$. [step 1.1, F3, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be totally differentiable at every point, and suppose its gradient is $L$-Lipschitz on $U$ for some $L\ge0$. If $x,y\in U$ and the whole segment $[x,y]$ lies in $U$, then
$$f(y)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|y-x\|_2^2.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Total derivatives and gradients [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]], the Lipschitz definition and Euclidean metric [[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], local continuity of totally differentiable maps [[thm-total-differentiability-gives-a-local-linear-bound-and-continuity]], Cauchy–Schwarz [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], derivative rules [[def-derivative]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], and the mean-value theorem [[cor-mean-value-theorem]].

[F1] The Lipschitz condition is $d_2(\nabla f(u),\nabla f(v))\le Ld_2(u,v)$; for $n\ge1$, $d_2(a,b)=\|a-b\|_2$ ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

[F2] A real function continuous on a closed interval and differentiable in its interior has a point where its derivative equals its secant slope ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

[F3] Total differentiability implies continuity, and the directional derivative along $d$ is $D_df(a)=\langle\nabla f(a),d\rangle$ ([[thm-total-differentiability-gives-a-local-linear-bound-and-continuity]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]).

[F4] The identity function has derivative $1$ by its difference quotient; the sum, scalar-multiple, and product rules follow from [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], and restricting a differentiable function to an interval preserves its interior derivatives ([[def-derivative]]).

[F5] Cauchy–Schwarz and norm homogeneity give $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$ and $\|sv\|_2=|s|\|v\|_2$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

[F6] Sums, scalar multiples, products, and polynomials of continuous real functions are continuous ([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]).

## Proof

1.1 Put $d=y-x$. If $d=0$, both sides are equal. For $d\ne0$, necessarily $n\ge1$. Define $\gamma(s)=x+sd$ and $I=\{s\in\mathbb R:\gamma(s)\in U\}$. Since $\|\gamma(s+h)-\gamma(s)\|_2=|h|\|d\|_2$, the affine path is continuous; openness of $U$ then makes $I$ open, and the segment assumption gives $[0,1]\subseteq I$. Put $\phi=f\circ\gamma$ on $I$. Total differentiability makes $f$ continuous at every point of $\gamma([0,1])$, so $\phi$ is continuous on $[0,1]$. For each $s\in(0,1)$, its difference quotient is the directional difference quotient of $f$ at $x+sd$ in direction $d$, so $\phi'(s)=\langle\nabla f(x+sd),d\rangle$. [given, F3, F5, construct]

2.1 Put $a=\langle\nabla f(x),d\rangle$, $g(s)=\phi(s)-\phi(0)-sa$, and $q(s)=g(s)-\frac{L}{2}s^2\|d\|_2^2$. By [F3] and [F6], $q$ is continuous on $[0,1]$; by [F4], it is differentiable on $(0,1)$ and
$$q'(s)=\langle\nabla f(x+sd)-\nabla f(x),d\rangle-Ls\|d\|_2^2.$$
By [F1] and [F5], the inner-product term is at most $L\|sd\|_2\|d\|_2=Ls\|d\|_2^2$ for $s\in(0,1)$. Hence $q'(s)\le0$. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F2] to $q$ on $[0,1]$: for some $s\in(0,1)$, $q(1)-q(0)=q'(s)\le0$. Since $q(0)=0$, this says $f(y)-f(x)-\langle\nabla f(x),d\rangle\le\frac{L}{2}\|d\|_2^2$, as required. [F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be an objective accessible only by function evaluations, and let $x_0\in U$. Fix an ordered finite positive-spanning poll list $D=(d_1,\ldots,d_m)$, initial mesh $\Delta_0>0$, cap $\Delta_{\max}\ge\Delta_0$, forcing function $\rho:(0,\Delta_{\max}]\to(0,\infty)$ with $\rho(\Delta)/\Delta\to0$ as $\Delta\downarrow0$, factors $0<\gamma_{dec}<1<\gamma_{inc}$, and integer poll budget $N\ge0$. Evaluate $f(x_0)$ first and include it in the best-point record. At poll $k$, inspect $x_k+\Delta_kd_i$ in list order, ignoring points outside $U$ without an objective call. Accept the first in-domain point $y$ satisfying $f(y)<f(x_k)-\rho(\Delta_k)$; then set $x_{k+1}=y$ and $\Delta_{k+1}=\min(\Delta_{max},\gamma_{inc}\Delta_k)$. If none succeeds, declare an unsuccessful poll, set $x_{k+1}=x_k$, and $\Delta_{k+1}=\gamma_{dec}\Delta_k$. Return the least-index best point among all evaluated points, current center, mesh, evaluation count, and status **budget-exhausted** after at most $N$ polls. A finite budget is not a stationarity certificate.

## Statement

Every invocation of [[alg-nelder-mead-finite-budget]] with finite call budget $B$ returns a status after at most $B$ objective calls. If it returns **tolerance-met**, both the simplex diameter and objective spread satisfy their stated tolerances. The status is a finite-budget result only and does not certify global or local optimality.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The exact branch rules, stopping test, call accounting, and return statuses in [[alg-nelder-mead-finite-budget]].

[F1] Every continuing outer iteration performs a reflection evaluation, while each additional branch evaluates finitely many trials and checks the budget before each call ([[alg-nelder-mead-finite-budget]]).

[F2] The procedure returns tolerance-met only after testing both diameter and spread against their tolerances ([[alg-nelder-mead-finite-budget]]).

## Proof

1.1 Each continuing iteration consumes at least one call for reflection. Every further expansion, contraction, or shrink evaluation also consumes a call, and the counter is bounded by $B$; before any call that cannot fit in the remaining budget, the procedure returns budget-exhausted. It therefore cannot continue indefinitely and returns a listed status after at most $B$ calls. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 The only tolerance-met branch is the explicit test $D\le\varepsilon_x$ and $S\le\varepsilon_f$ on a committed simplex, so that status implies both inequalities. None of the algorithm's finite statuses asserts a minimizer without an additional theorem. [F2, given, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

For every finite positive-spanning list $D=(d_1,\ldots,d_m)$ in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$, the score $\psi_D(v)=\max_i(-\langle v,d_i\rangle)$ on the unit sphere attains a strictly positive minimum. Write this minimum as $\kappa_D>0$. Thus for every $v\in\mathbb R^n$ there is $d_i\in D$ with $-\langle v,d_i\rangle\ge\kappa_D\|v\|_2$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Positive spanning and directional score [[def-positive-spanning-poll-set-and-angle]], Euclidean geometry [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], compactness and extrema ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

[F1] For every unit vector $u$, positive spanning writes $-u=\sum_i\lambda_i d_i$ with $\lambda_i\ge0$ ([[def-positive-spanning-poll-set-and-angle]]).

[F2] Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\langle u,d_i\rangle|\le\|u\|_2\|d_i\|_2$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

[F3] By the coordinatewise vector-sum convention, $\langle u,\sum_i\lambda_i d_i\rangle=\sum_{k<n}u_k\sum_{j<m}\lambda_{j+1}(d_{j+1})_k$. Finite distributivity and reordering the two finite sums, using finite-sum additivity/scaling and induction on their lengths, gives $\sum_i\lambda_i\langle u,d_i\rangle$. A finite sum of nonnegative real terms is nonnegative ([[def-positive-spanning-poll-set-and-angle]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

[F4] If $M=\max_i|a_i-b_i|$ for two nonempty finite lists, then $a_i\le b_i+M\le\max_jb_j+M$ for each $i$; taking maxima and reversing the lists gives $|\max_i a_i-\max_i b_i|\le M$ ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

[F5] The unit sphere is nonempty, closed, and bounded. For $n\ge1$, the standard vector $e_0$ has Euclidean norm $1$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). If $\|x\|_2\ne1$, choose $\varepsilon=|\|x\|_2-1|/2$; the reverse triangle inequality shows every $y$ with $d_2(x,y)<\varepsilon$ also has $\|y\|_2\ne1$, so the complement is open. Every unit vector lies in $B_2(0,2)$, so the sphere is bounded. Hence it is compact by Heine–Borel ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], [[def-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]], [[def-metric-ball]], [[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

[F6] [[thm-reals-ordered-field]] makes $\mathbb R$ a totally ordered field, in particular the product of two strictly positive reals is positive; [[lem-of-zero-mult]] gives multiplication by zero. Hence if $a,b\ge0$, either one is zero and $ab=0$ (using field commutativity if needed), or both are strictly positive and $ab>0$. Thus $ab\ge0$.

## Proof

1.1 Taking inner products of [F1] with $u$ and using [F3] gives $-1=\sum_i\lambda_i\langle u,d_i\rangle$. Since all $\lambda_i\ge0$, at least one index with positive coefficient has $\langle u,d_i\rangle<0$; otherwise every summand is nonnegative by [F6] and [F3] makes the sum nonnegative, a contradiction. Hence $\psi_D(u)>0$ for every unit $u$. [F1, F3, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F4], $|\psi_D(u)-\psi_D(w)|\le\max_i|\langle u-w,d_i\rangle|$, and [F2] bounds the right side by $D_{\max}\|u-w\|_2$, so the score is continuous. By [F5], the unit sphere is nonempty and compact. The extreme-value theorem gives a minimum attained at some unit $u_0$; step 1.1 makes that attained value strictly positive. For nonzero $v$, apply this bound to $u=v/\|v\|_2$ and multiply by $\|v\|_2$; for $v=0$ the inequality is immediate. [F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $N\ge1$ be an integer and run [[alg-projected-subgradient-method]] with all stated inputs. Every execution returns after at most $N$ oracle calls. On failure it returns the feasible current iterate and a best observed point if one has been observed, or none otherwise; it does not return a full-horizon average. If all calls succeed, the weighted average is defined and feasible, a best observed iterate exists, and the status is budget-exhausted after exactly $N$ updates.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty closed convex feasible set, a finite budget, positive stepsizes, and the oracle/failure rules of [[alg-projected-subgradient-method]].

[F1] Every point has a unique nearest-point projection onto a nonempty closed convex set ([[thm-nearest-point-in-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]]).

[F2] A convex combination of feasible points remains feasible ([[thm-finite-jensen-inequality-in-euclidean-space]]).

[F3] A nonempty finite list of real values has a minimum attained at one of its members ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]); scanning the list in increasing index order and replacing the record only on a strict decrease yields the least-index minimizer, by induction on the finite list length.

[F4] A finite sum of nonnegative terms is nonnegative, and a zero sum forces every term to be zero; therefore a nonempty finite sum of strictly positive terms is strictly positive ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

## Proof

1.1 Initially $x_0\in C$. At each successful oracle call, if $x_k\in C$, [F1] gives a unique projected point $x_{k+1}\in C$. Induction over the successful calls proves feasibility and unique definition of each iterate through at most $N$ calls. [given, F1, induction]

2.1 A failed call returns immediately; if no earlier value was observed, the optional best field is none, and otherwise [F3] supplies a least-index best among the finite observed list. If all calls succeed, $N\ge1$ and every $\alpha_k>0$, so $A_N=\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k>0$ by [F4]. The weights $\alpha_k/A_N$ are positive and sum to one by the scaling law for finite sums; [F2] makes the weighted average feasible, and [F3] gives a least-index best observed point. The finite loop completes exactly $N$ updates and returns budget-exhausted. [given, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Under the projected-subgradient update of [[alg-projected-subgradient-method]], let $x^*\in C$ and suppose the $k$th oracle call returns $g_k\in\partial f(x_k)$. Then
$$\|x_{k+1}-x^*\|_2^2\le\|x_k-x^*\|_2^2-2\alpha_k(f(x_k)-f(x^*))+\alpha_k^2\|g_k\|_2^2.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The projected update [[alg-projected-subgradient-method]], subgradient convention [[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]], and projection variational inequality [[lem-projection-onto-a-closed-convex-set-has-the-variational-inequality]].

[F1] For $p=P_C(u)$ and every $z\in C$, $\langle u-p,z-p\rangle\le0$ ([[lem-projection-onto-a-closed-convex-set-has-the-variational-inequality]]).

[F2] $g_k\in\partial f(x_k)$ implies $f(x^*)\ge f(x_k)+\langle g_k,x^*-x_k\rangle$ ([[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]]).

## Proof

1.1 Put $u=x_k-\alpha_kg_k$ and $p=x_{k+1}=P_C(u)$. Applying [F1] with $z=x^*$ gives $\langle u-p,x^*-p\rangle\le0$, hence $\langle u-p,p-x^*\rangle\ge0$. Expanding $\|u-x^*\|_2^2=\|u-p\|_2^2+\|p-x^*\|_2^2+2\langle u-p,p-x^*\rangle$ yields $\|p-x^*\|_2^2\le\|u-x^*\|_2^2$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Expand the right side as $\|x_k-x^*\|_2^2-2\alpha_k\langle g_k,x_k-x^*\rangle+\alpha_k^2\|g_k\|_2^2$. By [F2], $\langle g_k,x_k-x^*\rangle\ge f(x_k)-f(x^*)$; substituting proves the estimate. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex; let $t>0$, $v\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $m_i(y)=b_i+\langle a_i,y\rangle$ be a nonempty finite list of affine functions. Then
$$\Phi(y)=\max_i m_i(y)+\frac{\|y-v\|_2^2}{2t},\qquad y\in C,$$
has a unique global minimizer on $C$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Closed convex feasibility ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]], [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]), the Euclidean norm and Cauchy–Schwarz ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]), closed bounded compactness ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]), and attainment on compact sets ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

[F1] A finite maximum of affine maps obeys $|\max_i m_i(y)-\max_i m_i(z)|\le\max_i|m_i(y)-m_i(z)|$; each difference is $|\langle a_i,y-z\rangle|\le\|a_i\|_2\|y-z\|_2$ by Cauchy–Schwarz ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

[F2] The quadratic difference obeys $|\|y-v\|_2^2-\|z-v\|_2^2|\le(\|y-v\|_2+\|z-v\|_2)\|y-z\|_2$, by expansion and Cauchy–Schwarz ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

[F3] Continuity in a metric space is the epsilon-delta property at every point ([[def-metric-continuity]]).

[F4] $\mathbb R^0$ consists of one vector, its zero vector ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

## Proof

1.1 If $n=0$, [F4] says $\mathbb R^0$ is a singleton, so the nonempty feasible set $C$ is that singleton. The finite maximum and quadratic objective have one feasible value, and its sole feasible point is the unique global minimizer. For the remainder assume $n\ge1$. [F4, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F1] and [F2], $\Phi$ has a finite local Lipschitz bound on $C$ around each point: the finitely many $\|a_i\|_2$ are bounded, and the quadratic difference in [F2] has a bounded factor on a sufficiently small ball. Hence $\Phi$ is continuous on $C$ by [F3]. Choose $y_0\in C$ and let $c=\Phi(y_0)$. The sublevel set $S=\{y\in C:\Phi(y)\le c\}$ is nonempty. If $y\in C\setminus S$, continuity supplies an ambient ball around $y$ whose intersection with $C$ lies in $C\setminus S$; if $y\notin C$, closedness of $C$ supplies a ball disjoint from $C$. Thus every point outside $S$ has a ball disjoint from $S$, so $S$ is closed in $\mathbb R^n$. [F1, F2, F3, given, choose]

3.1 The first affine cut gives $\Phi(y)\ge b_1+\langle a_1,y\rangle+\|y-v\|_2^2/(2t)=\beta+\|y-(v-ta_1)\|_2^2/(2t)$, where $\beta=b_1+\langle a_1,v\rangle-t\|a_1\|_2^2/2$. Since $c=\Phi(y_0)\ge\beta$, every $y\in S$ satisfies $\|y-(v-ta_1)\|_2^2\le2t(c-\beta)$ and thus lies in the open ball of radius $1+\sqrt{2t(c-\beta)}$ about $v-ta_1$. So $S$ is bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) and compact by Heine–Borel. The continuous real-valued restriction $\Phi|_S$ attains its minimum by the extreme-value theorem; points outside $S$ have value greater than $c$, while the minimum on $S$ is at most $c$, so this is a global minimizer. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For every index $i$, affinity gives $m_i((p+q)/2)=(m_i(p)+m_i(q))/2\le(\max_jm_j(p)+\max_jm_j(q))/2$; taking the finite maximum over $i$ proves the model midpoint value is at most the average endpoint values. For distinct $p,q\in C$, the quadratic term satisfies $\|(p+q)/2-v\|_2^2=(\|p-v\|_2^2+\|q-v\|_2^2)/2-\|p-q\|_2^2/4$. After multiplication by $1/(2t)$ the quadratic term is strictly below the endpoint average. If both $p,q$ minimized $\Phi$, their midpoint would therefore have smaller value, a contradiction. The minimizer is unique. [given, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be convex, let $t>0$, $v\in\mathbb R^n$, and suppose $p$ minimizes $Q(y)=F(y)+\|y-v\|_2^2/(2t)$ with $Q(p)<+\infty$. Then for every $z$ with $F(z)<+\infty$,
$$Q(z)\ge Q(p)+\frac{\|z-p\|_2^2}{4t}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The extended-real convexity convention [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]] and Euclidean quadratic identity [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

[F1] Convexity gives $F((p+z)/2)\le(F(p)+F(z))/2$ for finite-valued endpoints ([[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]).

[F2] The midpoint identity is $\|(p+z)/2-v\|_2^2=(\|p-v\|_2^2+\|z-v\|_2^2)/2-\|p-z\|_2^2/4$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F3] Since $Q(p)<+\infty$ and the quadratic term is finite, $F(p)<+\infty$; together with the stated $F(z)<+\infty$, both endpoints are in the finite domain required for [F1].

## Proof

1.1 [F3] puts both endpoints in the finite domain. Apply [F1] to $p,z$ and combine with [F2], after multiplying the latter by $1/(2t)$, to obtain $Q((p+z)/2)\le(Q(p)+Q(z))/2-\|z-p\|_2^2/(8t)$. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Minimality gives $Q(p)\le Q((p+z)/2)$. Combining with step 1.1 and rearranging yields $Q(z)\ge Q(p)+\|z-p\|_2^2/(4t)$, including $z=p$ with equality. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every integer poll budget $N\ge0$, each invocation of [[alg-deterministic-direct-search]] returns after at most $N$ polls with a feasible current center and a best evaluated point.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An open domain $U$, finite-valued objective on $U$, feasible initial point, finite ordered poll list, and the mesh/forcing inputs of [[alg-deterministic-direct-search]].

## Statement

For a finite integer budget $N\ge1$, every invocation of [[alg-proximal-bundle-serious-null-method]] returns one of its specified statuses after at most $N$ trials. Every trial point used by the procedure is uniquely defined unless an earlier oracle-failure or stationary-or-model-failure status has already returned.

1.1 If no cut is stored, the initialization oracle either fails and returns with zero completed trials or supplies one valid cut. Thereafter the bundle is finite and nonempty; at each trial [F1] supplies a unique candidate unless an earlier status has returned. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Each trial either returns on oracle failure or $P_k\le0$, or evaluates one candidate and completes exactly one serious/null branch, appends its cut, and advances the counter by one. ## Statement

Consider an infinite continuation of the polling and mesh-update rules of [[alg-deterministic-direct-search]], using its admissible inputs and exact branch rules but with no finite poll-budget cap. Write its fixed finite positive-spanning poll list as $D$ and its forcing function as $\rho$. Suppose a subsequence of unsuccessful polls indexed by $k_j$ has $\Delta_{k_j}\to0$ and centers $x_{k_j}$ in a compact set $K\subseteq V$, where $V\subseteq U$ is open. Assume $f:U\to\mathbb R$ is totally differentiable at every point of $V$ and $\nabla f$ is $L$-Lipschitz there. Here an accumulation point means a limit of a subsequence in the Euclidean metric. Then every such point is stationary, meaning $\nabla f(\bar x)=0$. Compactness ensures at least one such accumulation point. This asymptotic claim concerns the untruncated continuation; a finite-budget return is not a stationarity certificate.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The poll and forcing rules [[alg-deterministic-direct-search]], positive angle [[lem-positive-spanning-poll-set-has-uniform-angle]], uniform neighborhood radius [[lem-compact-set-in-open-neighborhood-has-uniform-radius]], local descent [[lem-direct-search-local-descent-inequality]], and compact metric sequential compactness [[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]].

[F1] There is $\kappa_D>0$ with $\max_i(-\langle u,d_i\rangle)\ge\kappa_D$ for every unit vector $u$ ([[lem-positive-spanning-poll-set-has-uniform-angle]]).

[F2] For sufficiently short displacements from any center in compact $K$, the segment remains in $V$ ([[lem-compact-set-in-open-neighborhood-has-uniform-radius]]).

[F3] If the segment $[x,x+h]$ lies in $V$, then $f(x+h)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),h\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|h\|_2^2$ ([[lem-direct-search-local-descent-inequality]]).

[F4] A sequence is a function on the naturals, convergence is the metric limit, and every sequence in compact metric $K$ has a subsequence converging in $K$ ([[def-sequence]], [[def-metric-convergence]], [[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]], [[def-metric-compactness]]).

[F5] On $\mathbb R^n$ with $n\ge1$, the Euclidean metric is $d_2(x,y)=\|x-y\|_2$; thus the $L$-Lipschitz hypothesis gives $\|\nabla f(u)-\nabla f(v)\|_2\le L\|u-v\|_2$ ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

[F6] The finite poll list has a largest norm $D_{\max}=\max_i\|d_i\|_2$ ([[def-positive-spanning-poll-set-and-angle]]).

## Proof

1.1 Use the defined finite maximum $D_{\max}$ from [F6], and choose the uniform radius $\delta>0$ from [F2]. For all sufficiently large $j$, $\Delta_{k_j}D_{\max}<\delta$, so every segment from $x_{k_j}$ to $x_{k_j}+\Delta_{k_j}d_i$ remains in $V. [F2, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 If $\nabla f(x_{k_j})\ne0$, [F1] supplies a poll direction $d_i$ with $\langle\nabla f(x_{k_j}),d_i\rangle\le-\kappa_D\|\nabla f(x_{k_j})\|_2$. The poll is unsuccessful, so its in-domain trial value is at least $f(x_{k_j})-\rho(\Delta_{k_j})$. Apply [F3] to this direction and combine the two bounds to obtain $\kappa_D\|\nabla f(x_{k_j})\|_2\le\rho(\Delta_{k_j})/\Delta_{k_j}+(L\Delta_{k_j}/2)D_{\max}^2$. If the gradient is zero, the same inequality holds. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The right side tends to zero by the forcing condition and $\Delta_{k_j}\to0$, while $\kappa_D>0$; hence $\|\nabla f(x_{k_j})\|_2\to0$. For any accumulation subsequence converging to $\bar x\in K$, [F5] gives $\|\nabla f(x_{k_j})-\nabla f(\bar x)\|_2\le L\|x_{k_j}-\bar x\|_2\to0$, so $\nabla f(\bar x)=0$. By [F4] at least one accumulation subsequence exists. [given, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex, and run [[alg-projected-subgradient-method]] for $N\ge1$ steps with positive $\alpha_k$. Assume all $N$ oracle calls return valid pairs. Suppose a global minimizer $x^*\in C$ exists and the oracle vectors obey $\|g_k\|_2\le G$; let $R\ge\|x_0-x^*\|_2$. Set $A_N=\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k>0$ and $\bar x_N=A_N^{-1}\sum_{k<N}\alpha_kx_k$. Then
$$\min_{0\le k<N}\bigl(f(x_k)-f(x^*)\bigr)\le f(\bar x_N)-f(x^*)\le\frac{R^2+G^2\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k^2}{2A_N}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite algorithm [[alg-projected-subgradient-method]], its one-step estimate [[lem-projected-subgradient-one-step-estimate]], convexity [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]], and finite Jensen [[thm-finite-jensen-inequality-in-euclidean-space]].

[F1] For each $k$, $\|x_{k+1}-x^*\|_2^2\le\|x_k-x^*\|_2^2-2\alpha_k(f(x_k)-f(x^*))+\alpha_k^2\|g_k\|_2^2$ ([[lem-projected-subgradient-one-step-estimate]]).

[F2] For a convex function and nonnegative weights summing to one, its value at the weighted average is at most the weighted average of its values ([[thm-finite-jensen-inequality-in-euclidean-space]]).

[F3] Starting from $x_0\in C$, each successful update is the unique projection onto $C$ and remains feasible; the finite-budget result also establishes that the returned average is defined and feasible ([[alg-projected-subgradient-method]], [[thm-nearest-point-in-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]], [[lem-projected-subgradient-finite-budget-returns-status]]).

[F4] Since the stepsizes are positive, $A_N=\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k>0$, and the weights $\alpha_k/A_N$ are positive and sum to one by the scaling law for finite sums ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

[F5] The nonempty finite list of objective gaps has a minimum attained by one of its indices ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

## Proof

1.1 Rearrange [F1] and sum over $k=0,\ldots,N-1$. The squared-distance terms telescope, giving $2\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k(f(x_k)-f(x^*))\le\|x_0-x^*\|_2^2-\|x_N-x^*\|_2^2+\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k^2\|g_k\|_2^2\le R^2+G^2\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k^2$, since the last squared distance is nonnegative. Divide by $2A_N>0$ using [F4] to bound the weighted average of the objective gaps. [F1, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F3] the iterates lie in $C$, and by [F4] the normalized positive weights sum to one. Apply [F2] to get $f(\bar x_N)-f(x^*)\le A_N^{-1}\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k(f(x_k)-f(x^*))$. ## Statement

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-projected-subgradient-best-and-average-bound]], let $R>0$ and $G>0$ and choose the constant stepsize $\alpha_k=R/(G\sqrt N)$ for all $k<N$. Then
$$\min_{k<N}(f(x_k)-f(x^*))\le f(\bar x_N)-f(x^*)\le\frac{RG}{\sqrt N}.$$
Thus both reported gaps are $O(N^{-1/2})$ with constants $R,G$ fixed. The schedule is not used when $R=0$ or $G=0$; in those boundary cases the best-iterate gap is zero under the theorem's hypotheses and bounds below.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The best-iterate and weighted-average bound [[thm-projected-subgradient-best-and-average-bound]].

[F1] The bound is $[R^2+G^2\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k^2]/(2\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k)$ ([[thm-projected-subgradient-best-and-average-bound]]).

[F2] The Euclidean norm is definite, so $\|v\|_2=0$ implies $v=0$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

[F3] The algorithm's best observed list includes $x_0$, and $g_0\in\partial f(x_0)$ on a successful first call ([[alg-projected-subgradient-method]], [[lem-projected-subgradient-finite-budget-returns-status]], [[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]]).

[F4] For a constant real $a$, $\sum_{k<N}a=Na$ by the scaling law for finite sums ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

## Proof

1.1 For $R,G>0$, [F4] gives $\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k=N\,R/(G\sqrt N)=R\sqrt N/G$ and $G^2\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k^2=N\,R^2/N=R^2$. Substituting these values into [F1] gives $(2R^2)/(2R\sqrt N/G)=RG/\sqrt N$. [F1, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 If $R=0$, then $\|x_0-x^*\|_2=0$ and [F2] gives $x_0=x^*$; by [F3] the best observed list includes this optimizer, so its gap is zero. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

2.2 If $G=0$, the successful first call satisfies $\|g_0\|_2\le0$, so [F2] gives $g_0=0$. Then $g_0\in\partial f(x_0)$ and the subgradient inequality gives $f(y)\ge f(x_0)$ for every feasible $y$; hence $x_0$ is a global minimizer and the best-iterate gap is zero. These boundary cases require no zero stepsize. [given, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed, and convex, with nonempty closed convex domain $C=\operatorname{dom}F$. Fix $t>0$, a center $x\in C$, and a finite affine model $M\le F$ on $C$. Let $z$ minimize $M(y)+\|y-x\|_2^2/(2t)$ over $C$, set $e=F(z)-M(z)\ge0$, and let $p=\operatorname{prox}_{tF}(x)$. Then
$$\|z-p\|_2^2\le4te.$$
In particular, a sequence of such model errors $e_k\to0$ forces the model candidates to approach their exact proximal points in norm.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Bundle subproblem existence [[lem-proximal-bundle-subproblem-has-unique-minimizer]], proximal mapping [[def-proximal-mapping]], resolvent/existence [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]], and quadratic growth [[lem-proximal-objective-has-quadratic-growth-from-minimizer]].

[F1] $p$ is the unique minimizer of $Q_F(y)=F(y)+\|y-x\|_2^2/(2t)$ ([[def-proximal-mapping]], [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]]).

[F2] The convex function $Q_F$ obeys $Q_F(z)\ge Q_F(p)+\|z-p\|_2^2/(4t)$ ([[lem-proximal-objective-has-quadratic-growth-from-minimizer]]).

## Proof

1.1 Put $Q_M(y)=M(y)+\|y-x\|_2^2/(2t)$. Since $z$ minimizes $Q_M$ over $C$ and $p\in C$, $Q_M(z)\le Q_M(p)$. The pointwise underestimator gives $Q_M(p)\le Q_F(p)$, while $Q_F(z)=Q_M(z)+e$. Hence $Q_F(z)\le Q_F(p)+e$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F2] to $z$ and combine with step 1.1: $Q_F(p)+\|z-p\|_2^2/(4t)\le Q_F(z)\le Q_F(p)+e$. Subtracting the common finite value and multiplying by $4t>0$ proves the inequality. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed, and convex. Suppose $C=\operatorname{dom}F$ is nonempty, closed, and convex, and $F|_C$ is continuous. Consider an infinite full-memory continuation of [[alg-proximal-bundle-serious-null-method]] with fixed $t>0$ and $m_s\in(0,1)$, centers $x_k\in C$, finite affine models $M_k\le F$ on $C$ touching their centers ($M_k(x_k)=F(x_k)$), and exact candidates
$$z_k=\arg\min_{y\in C}\left(M_k(y)+\frac{\|y-x_k\|_2^2}{2t}\right).$$
Assume every predicted decrease $P_k=F(x_k)-M_k(z_k)$ is positive, each trial uses the stated serious/null acceptance test, the initial sublevel set $K=\{x\in C:F(x)\le F(x_0)\}$ is compact, and the aggregate-model errors $e_k=F(z_k)-M_k(z_k)$ satisfy $e_k\to0$. Then every accumulation point, meaning a limit of a subsequence in the Euclidean metric, is a global minimizer of $F$. At least one accumulation point exists. The vanishing-error premise is an additional assumption; full-memory cutting planes alone are not asserted to imply it.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The serious/null algorithm [[alg-proximal-bundle-serious-null-method]], model-subproblem existence [[lem-proximal-bundle-subproblem-has-unique-minimizer]], the aggregate-error estimate [[lem-aggregate-model-error-controls-proximal-candidate]], proximal resolvent [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]], extended-real subgradient definition [[def-extended-real-epsilon-subdifferential]], compact sequential compactness [[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]], and attainment on compact metric spaces [[thm-extreme-value-metric]].

[F1] Each candidate is unique, and the exact proximal point $p_k=\operatorname{prox}_{tF}(x_k)$ exists, is unique, and the proximal map is nonexpansive ([[lem-proximal-bundle-subproblem-has-unique-minimizer]], [[def-proximal-mapping]], [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]]).

[F2] The model error is nonnegative and $\|z_k-p_k\|_2^2\le4te_k$ ([[lem-aggregate-model-error-controls-proximal-candidate]]).

[F3] If $0\in\partial F(x)$, then $F(y)\ge F(x)$ for every $y$ by the extended-real subgradient definition ([[def-extended-real-epsilon-subdifferential]]).

[F4] A sequence is a function on the naturals, convergence is the metric limit, and every sequence in compact $K$ has a subsequence converging in $K$ ([[def-sequence]], [[def-metric-convergence]], [[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]], [[def-metric-compactness]]). Two limits in a metric space agree ([[lem-metric-limits-unique]]). A continuous real function on compact $K$ is bounded below ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]], [[def-metric-continuity]]).

## Proof

1.1 A serious step has $F(x_k)-F(z_k)\ge m_sP_k>0$; a null step leaves the center fixed. Thus centers remain in the initial sublevel set $K$, and $F(x_k)$ is nonincreasing and bounded below there by [F4]. The decreases $d_k=F(x_k)-F(x_{k+1})\ge0$ have bounded partial sums, since $\sum_{k<q}d_k=F(x_0)-F(x_q)$. If $d_k$ failed to tend to zero, some positive $\epsilon$ would be exceeded by infinitely many terms, making these partial sums unbounded; hence $d_k\to0$. [given, F4, algebra]

1.2 Let $x_{k_j}\to\bar x$ be any accumulation subsequence, which exists for at least one subsequence by [F4]. For any chosen convergent subsequence, compactness gives a further subsequence converging to a point of $K$; the uniqueness-of-limits fact in [F4] identifies that point with $\bar x$, so $\bar x\in K$. Applying compactness to the whole center sequence also supplies at least one accumulation subsequence. By nonexpansiveness in [F1], $p_{k_j}=\operatorname{prox}_{tF}(x_{k_j})\to p=\operatorname{prox}_{tF}(\bar x)$. By [F2] and $e_{k_j}\to0$, $\|z_{k_j}-p_{k_j}\|_2\to0$, so $z_{k_j}\to p$. Since $F|_C$ is continuous and all these points lie in $C$, $F(x_{k_j})\to F(\bar x)$ and $F(z_{k_j})\to F(p)$. [F1, F2, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 Suppose for contradiction that $\bar x$ is not a global minimizer. Then $p\ne\bar x$: otherwise the resolvent equivalence in [F1] gives $0=(\bar x-p)/t\in\partial F(\bar x)$, and [F3] would make $\bar x$ globally minimizing. By proximal minimality, $F(p)+\|p-\bar x\|_2^2/(2t)\le F(\bar x)$; therefore $\delta:=F(\bar x)-F(p)>0$. [F1, F3, step 1.2, algebra, assume-contra]

3.1 Along the chosen subsequence, $D_j:=F(x_{k_j})-F(z_{k_j})\to\delta$ by step 1.2, while $P_{k_j}=F(x_{k_j})-M_{k_j}(z_{k_j})=D_j+e_{k_j}$. Hence $D_j-m_sP_{k_j}=(1-m_s)D_j-m_se_{k_j}\to(1-m_s)\delta>0$. For all sufficiently large $j$ the step is serious and $d_{k_j}=D_j\ge\delta/2$, contradicting $d_k\to0$ from step 1.1. Thus every accumulation point is a global minimizer. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra, discharge-contradiction] ∎

## Definition

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

## Remarks

- **What "topology" means here.** $\mathcal{T}_d$ is defined above as a
  collection of subsets of $X$; the abstract notion of a topological space, a
  collection of subsets closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections
  taken as primitive data, is introduced on a later page and is not used
  here. What is proved
  here is that $\mathcal{T}_d$ has exactly those closure properties
  ([[thm-metric-open-set-algebra]]), which is what licenses the word.
- **Open and closed are not opposites.** A set may be neither ($[0,1)$ inside
  $\mathbb{R}$, once the usual metric is available from
  [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) or both ($\emptyset$ and $X$ always, and
  in some spaces every subset at once, as the discrete metric on the companion
  page shows). "Not open" is never a synonym for "closed".
- **Closedness is complementation, and nothing else, at this stage.** The
  description of closed sets by limits of sequences, and the description of the
  closure as an infimum of distances, are theorems proved later on this page
  ([[thm-metric-closure-characterisation]], [[thm-metric-sequential-closure]]),
  not part of the definition.

## Definition

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

## Remarks

- **The names "open ball" and "closed ball" are justified, not merely
  suggestive.** That $B(x,r)$ is an open set and $\bar B(x,r)$ a closed set in
  the metric topology is proved in [[thm-metric-open-set-algebra]]; the words are
  used here only as names for the three sets displayed above.
- **The closed ball is not in general the closure of the open ball**, and the
  sphere is not in general the boundary of either. Both failures are recorded on
  this page as [[fs-closed-ball-is-the-closure-of-the-open-ball]] and witnessed
  on the companion page. The safe reading of the three names is the displayed
  one and nothing more.
